: cf. Anacr. fr. 2. 9, ἐμῶν φρενὼν μὲν αὔραις Φέρειν ἔδωκα λύπας: Eur. Tro. 419, Ἀργεῖ’ ὀνείδη καὶ Φρυγῶν ἐπαινέσεις Ἀνέμοις φέρεσθαι παραδίδωμι: Hor. C. 1. 26. 2, tradam protervis ... ventis.
: this adv. meaning 'with due consideration' 'cautiously' is peculiar to Ap., cf. 2. 1134; 3. 83.

: for κυδάζειν 'to revile' cf. Aesch. fr. 91, οὔ τοι γυναιξὶ δεῖ κυδάζεσθαι: Soph. Aj. 722, κυδάζεται (pass.) toi=s pa=sin *)argei/ois.
The Schol. recognizes a noun κύδος (ὁ), 'abuse' as used by the Syracusans, and in the fragments of Epicharmus we find κυδάζω and κυδάζομαι.
: for the kindness of Heracles to Jason v. 341 sqq. Curtius explains ἐνηής as ἐνηvής, from root αv‐, av-eo.
: the gen. with ἀλείτης 'sinner' is peculiar. In Hom. we have the dative with ἀλιτρός, Il. 23. 595 δαίμοσιν ἀλιτρός.

div.p: Modelled on the famous lines, Il. 22. 159, ἐπεὶ οὐχ ἰερήιον οὐδὲ βοείην Ἀρνύσθην, ἅ τε ποσσὶν ἀέθλια γίγνεται ἀνδρῶν, Ἀλλὰ περὶ ψυχῆς θέον Ἔκτορος ἱπποδάμοιο.

div.seg: : the σχῆμα καθ’ ὅλον καὶ μέρος, by which the whole is in apposition with the parts instead of being in the gen.: cf. 4. 953, Od. 7. 103.
: the city was called Κίος from the name of the river (1178).
: = ἀνάστατον ποιήσειν. The verb is generally used of 'transplanting' a people.
: 'pledges,' cf. Soph. O.C. 858, μεῖζον ῥύσιον πόλει θήσεις.

: ζητοῦσι, ἐρευνῶσι. Schol. Cf. Od 21. 31, τὰς ἐρέων Ὀδυσῆι συνήντετο. Strabo (483, 2) describing Prusias, which was the later name of Cios, says, καὶ νῦν δ’ ἔτι ἑορτή τις ἄγεται παρὰ τοῖς Προυσιεῦσιν καὶ ὀρειβασια, θιασενόντων καὶ καλούντων ὜λαν, ὡς ἂν κατὰ ζήτησιν τὴν ἐκείνου πεποιηυένων τὴν ἐπὶ τὰς ὕλας ἔξοδον.
: Trachis in Thessaly where Heracles planted the Mysian hostages.

: the middle of ναίω is not used by Hom. Ap. uses it (1) c. acc. 'to settle or dwell in,' 2. 747. (2) c. acc. pers. in causal sense 'to make to dwell,' as here and in 4. 567; c. acc. rei 4. 275, ἄστη νάσσατο. (3) absolutely, meaning 'to settle or dwell in,' 1. 93. Hom. uses the passive in this sense, Il. 14. 119, Ἄργεϊ νάσθη, but ἀπενάσσατο, Od. 15. 254. In 2. 906 κατενάσσατο Θήβας means 'he settled at Thebes.' For the question of tmesis see on 2. 16. Linsenbarth denies tmesis here.
: this is a new formation: elsewhere Ap. uses νῆα. Rzach compares γρηῦν (Cramer, Anecd. Ox. iv 337. 28) and νηῦς (acc. pl.), Dem. Bithyn. iv 3 (Et. Mag. 437, 18).

κ. τ. λ.: 'a foreland running out, a broad expanse as viewed from the bay.' For this use of ἐκ cf. 4. 570, Il. 19. 375, ὅτ’ ἂν ἐκ πόντοιο σέλας ναύτῃσι φανήῃ. L. and S. say χθονὸς εἰσανέχ. means 'rising above the land,' but it means 'running into the land' i.e. from the point of view of the sailors, cf. 4. 291. For a different constr. v. 4. 1578.
: appulerunt. ἐπικέλλειν, like κέλλειν, was used either of the sailors running up a vessel with their oars, or of the vessel herself running ashore.

list.head: Summary
list.item: Amycus challenges the Argonauts (1-18)
Polydeuces takes up the challenge (19-24)
Preparations for the contest (25-66)
Amycus defeated and slain (67-97)
The Bebryces essay to avenge his death, but are routed by the Argonauts (98-153)
The heroes celebrate their victory by feast and sacrifice (154-163)
Through the skill of Tiphys they reach the Bithynian land (164-177)
Meeting with Phineus, who tells his sad tale (178-239)
Zetes and Calais promise to succour him (240-261)
Pursuit of the harpies by the sons of Boreas (262-300)
Prophecies of Phineus (301-425)
Return of the sons of Boreas (426-447)
Story of Paraebius (448-499)
Legend of Aristaeus and the Etesian winds (500-527)
Athene guides the Argo safely through the Symplegades (528-618)
Jason is downcast; his comrades strengthen him (619-647)
Apollo appears at the Thynian isle; rites in honour of him (648-719)
They come to the land of the Mariandyni (720-751)
Lycus, the king, welcomes them, and sends his son with them (752-814)
Fate of Idmon: funeral rites (815-850)
Death of Tiphys: Ancaeus chosen in his place: voyage resumed (851-910)
Apparition of Sthenelus: his shade appeased: they journey on (911-945)
The land of the Amazons: the land of the Chalybes (946-1008)
Strange customs of the Tibareni and Mossynoeci (1009-1029)
They reach the isle of Ares and are attacked by birds (1030-1089)
The sons of Phrixus are shipwrecked on the isle (1090-1133)
Jason receives them kindly; they tell the dangers which will beset him, and promise their aid against Aeetes (1134-1225)
Arrival at Colchis (1226-1283).

div.p: Cf. Val. Fl. 4. 99, Proxima Bebrycii panduntur litora regni. Pingue solum et duris regio non invida tauris. Rex Amycus , etc.

div.seg: : Strabo (464, 18) says that the Bebryces were of Thracian descent, and that their first settlement in Asia was in Mysia. Pliny (N.H. 5. 30) mentions, on the authority of Eratosthenes, that the Bebryces were one of the peoples in Asia who had utterly perished.

: 'the god of generation'; διὰ τὸ δεσπόζειν τοῦ ὑγροῦ καὶ πάσης τροφῆς, καὶ γενέσεως αἴτιον εἶναι, καθὸ τὸ ὕδωρ πάντων γεννητικόν. Schol: This is the doctrine of Thales, the earliest Greek philosopher; cf. Ritter and Preller, Hist. Phil. Gr. p. 6. Others explain 'god of the race,' like Ζεὺς γενέθλιος in Pind. O. 8. 16. Cf. Farnell, Cults iv 9.

: ἄδηλον ποῖόν ἐστι τὸ κύριον (i.e. which is the proper name). Schol. Three interpretations have been given: (1) a Bithynian nymph whose name was Melia, (2) a nymph of the class called Meliae (cf. Hes. Th. 187) whose name was Bithynis, (3) a Bithynian nymph of the class called Meliae (whose proper name is not given). Of these the first seems the best. Melia, daughter of Oceanus, was mother of Amycus by Poseidon, cf. Hyg. Fab. 17, Amycus Neptuni et Melies filius: Serv. ad Aen. 5. 373.

: Val. Fl. 4. 210,
Hic mihi lex caestus adversaque tollere contra
Bracchia, sic ingens Asiae plaga quique per Arcton
Dexter et in laevum pontus iacet haec mea visit
Hospitia; hoc functi remeent certamine reges.

κ.τ.λ.: 'he scorned in his o'erweening pride to ask them the purpose of their sailing and who they were.' ἄτισσε = οὐκ ἠξίωσε. This passage is usually mistranslated, e.g. de M., "il vint vers le navire s'enquérir de ce qui avait rendu l'expédition nécessaire, demander aux héros qui ils étaient; il les traita avec un souverain mépris, etc."
: = αὐτούς, cf. 4. 1209. Ap. probably followed Zenod. who defended μιν as a plural (v. schol. Il. 10. 127). There is no certain instance in Hom.; v. M. and R. on Od. 10. 212.
: cf. Theocry 22. 65, εἷς ἑνὶ χεῖρας ἄειρον ἐναντίδς · ἀνδρὶ καταστας.
: 'choose out and set before me.' L. and S. take ὁμίλου with ἀποκριδόν, but it depends on οἶον, cf. 1. 1240, Il. 11. 74, οἴη … θεῶν.

: 'here on the spot,' an adv. peculiar to Ap., cf. 3. 648, 4. 916, 1409. Rutherford (New Phryn. p. 121) attacks our poet for not recognizing that in Il. 10. 273, λιπέτην δὲ κατ’ αὐτόθι πάντας ἀρίστους, κατά belongs to λιπέτην, but, as Oswald points out, there are cases in Ap. in which κατά is in tmesis with the verb though standing immediately before αὐτόθι, e.g. 1. 1350 (?), 2. 892, 3. 889, and Hom. has παραυτόθι (or παρ’ αὐτόθι) in Il. 23. 147 where there is no question of tmesis.
: this verb is ἅπ. λεγ., cf. ἀπηλεγέως.
: cf. Il. 4. 157, κατὰ δ’ ὅρκια πιστὰ πάτησαν.
: for ἐφέψεται, on the mistaken analogy of ἐπιέννυμι, where the digamma prevents ἐπι becoming ἐφ; see note to 1.691.

div.p:
Cf. Val. Fl. 4. 222,
Talia dicta dabat, cum protinus asper Iason
Et simul Aeacidae simul et Calydonis alumni
Nelidaeque Idasque prior quae maxima surgunt
Nomina; sed nudo steterat iam pectore Pollux.

div.seg: : cf. Il. 19. 125, ἄχος ὀξὺ κατὰ φρένα τύψε.
: = ὑπισχνέομαι. In the ordinary sense of ὑπέχειν Ap. uses uncontracted forms, e.g. ὑποίσχεται (4. 169) on the analogy of καταίσχεται (Od. 9. 122).
: 'unflinchingly'; see note to 1.785. Theocritus has given us a most graceful and vivid picture of the contest which ensues in his Hymn to the Dioscuri (Idyll 22).

: see note to 1.895. The Schol. says: καὶ Ἀριστοτέλης δέ φησι τοῦτο ποιεῖν τὸν λέοντα--the passage referred to being apparently Hist. Animal. 9. 44, where a characteristic of the lion is said to be τὸν βαλόντα τηρήσαντα ἵεσθαι ἐπὶ τοῦτον.

: 'of close texture'; εὔστρεπτον, εὐπίλητον· παρὰ τὸ στείβω, ὅθεν καὶ στιβὰς καὶ στιβεῖς οἱ κναφεῖς. Schol. The word is only found here. Many editors prefer the explanation 'wellfulled' (based on στιβεῖς = κναφεῖς. Schol.), as avoiding an apparent inconsistency with λεπταλέον; but, surely, a robe may be of close texture even though it is finely woven.
: cf. 4. 169; λεπτός is the Homeric epithet.
: for the gifts of the Lemnian women v. 1. 846.
: 'a herdsman's staff.' Curtius connects the word with κάλ‐ως 'a string' and vρέπω, vρίπτω, werf-en, 'to hurl,' a loop of string being used to burl the staff; v. schol. Il. 23. 845.
: the wood of the oleaster was of extreme hardness (cf. 843); the club of Heracles was made of it, Theocr. 25. 208 sqq.

div.p: Cf. Milton, "As whom the fables name of monstrous size, Titanian or Earth-born, that warred on Jove" (P.L. 1 198).

div.seg:
: ἐπεὶ λέγεται ἡ Γῆ κατα ὀργήν, ὅτε τοὺς Τιτᾶνας κατεταρτάρωσεν ὁ Ζευς. γεννῆσαι τοὺς Γίγαντας. Schol.; cf
Aen. 4. 178,
Illam Terra parens, ira inritata deorum,
Extremam, ut perhibent, Coeo Enceladoque sororem
Progenuit.
: cf. Val. Fl. 4. 190, sidereo Pollux interritus ore.
: 'twinklings,' cf. h. Hom. Merc. 43, ἀπ’ ὀφθαλμῶν ἀμαρυγαί. Homer uses μαρμαρυγαί (Od. 8. 265). We find ἀμάρυγυα (3. 288), and ἀμαρύσσω (4. 178). The root μαρ is seen also in μαρμαιρω, marmor.
: see note to 1.672; cf. Val. Fl. 4. 233, Vixdum etiam primae spargentem signa inventae.

κ.τ.λ.: cf.
Aen. 5. 376, alternaque iactat Bracchia protendens, et verberat ictibus auras. See also 3. 1350.
: οὐ μὴν δ Ἀμυκος διεπείρασεν ἑαυτοῦ. καὶ διὰ τούτων δὲ δηλοῖ τὸ ὑπερήφανον αὐτοῦ. Schol.

: cf.
Aen. 4. 363, totumque pererrat Luminibus tacitis.

: 'bounded.' ὀρεχθέω is
found once in Homer, Il. 23. 30, βόες … ὀρέχθεον ἀμφὶ σιδήρω. Whatever may be its meaning there (v. Leaf), Ap. uses it in the sense of stretching towards, striving after, yearning; see note to 1.275. ὀρέγομαι is used in a similar way 878 infr. Curtius says ὀ‐ρεχ‐θε‐ω is related to ὀ‐ρεγ‐, 'to stretch,' as γη‐θε‐ω to γαv. Theocritus (11. 43) uses it of the sea rolling in to the beach, θάλασσαν ἔα ποτὶ χέρσον ὀρεχθῆν. With our passage Brunck compares
Aen. 5. 137, exultantiaque haurit Corda pavor pulsans, laudumque adrecta cupido .
: cf. Il. 7. 330, τῶν νῦν αἷμα … ἐσκέδασ’ ὀξὺς Ἄρης.

: the primitive boxing-gloves consisted of thongs of oxhide twisted round the hand, cf. Il. 23. 684, δῶκεν ἱμάντας ἐυτμήτους βοὸς ἀγραύλοιο: Theocr. 22. 80, σπείρῃσιν ἐκαρτύναντο βοείαις Χεῖρας καὶ περὶ γυῖα μακρά σφ’ εἵλιξαν ἱμάντας. We may assume that Ap. is using ἱμάντας here in the Homeric sense, though the Schol. says, ἱμάντας: τοὺς καλουμένους μύρμηκας. The μύρμηκες, like the caestus, were terrible weapons weighted with metal and studded with nails; cf. Anth. P. 11. 78:
Aen. 5. 405, ingentia septem Terga boum plumbo insuto ferroque rigebant . For illustrations of ancient boxing-gloves, see Gardiner, Greek Athletic Sports and Festivals, c. xix.
: see note to 1.138. Gardiner (p. 430) explains 'with hard ridges around them.'
: Ap. forms this on the analogy of τεθνηῶτες, ἑστηῶτες; cf. ἐσκλήκει, 201.
: Curtius (G.V. i 55) shows that in these subjunctive forms, which are common in Hom., the ι has crept in by mistake.
: this use of ἀτέμβομαι = μέμφομαι is peculiar to Ap., cf. 3. 99. In Hom. ἀτέμβω means 'to ill-treat,' ἀτέμβομαι 'to be reft of.'
: the only instance in the poem of this contraction in the imperative middle.
: cf Od. 18. 21, στῆθος καὶ χείλεα φύρσω Αἵματος.
: 'softly smiling,' cf. Hes. Th. 547, ἦκ’ ἐπιμειδήσας.
: 'without parley'; ἀδιστάκτως, ἀδιακρίτως, μηδὲν πρὸς τὴν ἀναίρεσιν προφασισάμενος. Schol.; cf. 4. 1005. For the ordinary meaning see note to 1.1201.
: ἀμφιδέω (= περιδέω) is a new compound; so too ἀμφιθρώσκω, ‐παλύνω, ‐μάρπτω are first found in Ap.
: like ἠείδειν (4. 1700) this is 3 pl.; so too ἠρήρειν (4. 947).
div.p: Curtius (G.V. ii 239) says, "The form in ‐ειν for the 3 pl., three times used by Ap. Rhod., is very peculiar. The learned Alexandrine gets into fine trouble for it with the Dutch critic (Cobet, Nov. Lect. p. 467): 'Apollonius ipse turpiter impegit. Quid eo homine facias qui ᾔδειν dixit pro sciebant?'! Certainly Ap. sometimes indulged in strange freaks, and perhaps this 3 pl. in ‐ειν was only an erroneous imitation of Homeric forms like βάν, ἔφαν, μίγεν, which even at the present day many regard as abbreviated from those in ‐σαν."
Cf. Val. Fl. 4. 252, Dixit et urgentis per sera piacula fati Nescius extremum hoc armis innectere palmas Dat famulis.

div.seg:
: = προσώπων; cf. Soph. Ant.
529, Eur. H.F. 1203. In Hom. ῥέθεα means 'the limbs,' e.g. Il. 16. 856, ψυχὴ δ’ ἐκ ῥεθέων πταμένη. According to Eustathius the use of ῥέθος for πρόσωπον was an Aeolic peculiarity.

div.p: For the simile cf. Val. Fl. 4. 268, spumanti qualis in alto Pliade capta ratis, trepidi quam sola magistri Cura tenet, rapidum ventis certantibus aequor Intemerata secat: Pollux sic providus ictus Servat et Oebalia dubium caput eripit arte.

div.seg: : 'as the wave strives eagerly to rush within the sides of the ship.' For this use of τοῖχος v. Tyrrell on Eur. Tro. 116.
κ.τ.λ.: 'and quickly he observed his rude boxing to see in what points his might was resistless, and in what points he was his inferior.'
: for the quantity cf. Od. 21. 91; the penult. is long in Il. 14. 271.

div.p:
'As when shipwrights, putting together in rows by means of sharp treenails the opposing timbers, smite
with their hammers, etc.'
div.seg: : usually explained of the δούρατα 'resisting' the γόμφοι, but cf. Heraclitus' paradox τὸ ἀντίξουν συμφέρον referring primarily to pieces of wood supporting each other by leaning in opposite directions, the stability of the structure being due to opposite strains; v. Burnet on Arist. E. 8. 1. 6. In Od. 5. 248 Odysseus hammers together his σχεδίη by means of γόμφοι and ἁρμονίαι (γόμφοισιν δ’ ἄρα τήν γε καὶ ἁρμονίῃσιν ἄρασσεν).
: a new and wrong formation = ὑλουργοί.
: 'laying in rows'; cf. Od. 14. 11, σταυροὺς ἔλασσε 'he ran a row of stakes.' ἐπιβλήδην is ἅπ. λεγ. L. and S. explain it laying on, urgently.
κ.τ.λ.: 'the sound of blow after blow echoes unceasingly.'

: ἐξηχεῖται, ἀκούεται. Schol.; it properly means 'is tossed or wafted by the wind' (cf. Od. 6. 131). The verb is used metaphorically in Il. 21. 386, δίχα θυμὸς ἄητο 'tossed to and fro'; cf. Ap. 3. 688, θυμὸς ἄηται. See also on 3. 288.

: 'a rattling of teeth' from the blows on the jaws; cf.
Theocr. 22. 126, πυκνοὶ δ’ ἀράβησαν ὀδόντες. L. and S. wrongly explain it 'a gnashing of teeth.'
: 'standing up to each other'; see note to 1.293.

div.p: Cf. Val. Fl. 4. 279, respirant ambo paulumque reponunt Bracchia. Theocritus mentions no such cessation.

div.seg: : Val. Fl. 4. 282, Vix steterant, et iam ecce ruunt inflictaque late Terga sonant.

: cf. Ov. Met. 9. 42,
Digredimur paulum; rursumque ad bella coimus....
Non aliter fortes vidi concurrere tauros,
Cum pretium pugnae, toto nitidissima saltu,
Expetitur coniux.
Virg. also adopts this simile, Aen. 12. 715.
: 'in the pasture'; cf. Eur. Bacch. 165, πῶλος ὅπως ἅμα ματέρι φορβάδι . φορβάς is an adj. also in 2. 1024; it is a subst. in 3. 276, 4. 1449.

: cf.
Aen. 5. 426, constitit in digitos arrectus uterque . For this 'rising on tip-toe,' foreign to the ancient science of boxing, see Gardiner, op. cit. p. 431.

: cf. Ov. Met. 12. 248,
Elatumque alte, veluti qui candida tauri
Rumpere sacrifica molitur colla securi
Illisit fronti Lapithae.
For βουτύπος cf. 4. 468.
: 'aimed a swinging downward blow at him.' The compound is ἅπ. λεγ.

: i.e. he swerved aside to
avoid his onset; cf. Theocr. 22. 123, ἀλλ’ ὅγ’ ὑπεξανέῖυ.

: 'received on the shoulder the sweep of his elbow'; i.e. Amycus aimed at his head, but when he swerved aside the onward sweep of Amycus' under-arm just (τυτθόν) grazed his shoulder. de M. mistranslates, "il garantit son épaule en élevant le coude."

κ.τ.λ.; 'Polydeuces, close beside him, getting his knee past the knee of Amycus, with a swift lunge smote him over the ear.' For παρὲκ … ἀμειβων cf. 1. 581, παρεξήμειβον 'they passed by.' In Il. 11. 547, ἐντροπαλιζόμενος, ὀλίγον γόνυ γουνὸς ἀμείβων, the meaning is 'retreating slowly,' pedetentim, lit. 'changing one knee for the other,' and de M. tries to keep the Homeric sense here, "faisant quelques pas vers Amycos, sans se hâter, il le frappa, etc." This seems impossible as the whole thing was over in a moment: "Polydeuces slips aside, and before his opponent has time to recover his balance or his guard, steps past him and deals him a swinging blow above the ear, which not only knocks him out but kills him" (Gardiner). There is a very similar passage, Quint. Smyrn. 4. 345, Αἶψα δ’ ἄρ’ ἀλλήλοισι καταντία χεῖρας ἄειραν Ταρφέα παπταίνοντες· επ ἀκροτάτοις δὲ πόδεσσι Βοίνοντες κατὰ βαιὸν ἑὸν γόνυ γουνὸς ἄμειβον Ἀλλήλων ἐπὶ δηρὸν ἀλευόμεου μέγα κάυτος. This use of κατὰ βαιόν led Köchly to
alter our text by punctuating after πῆχυν, and he is followed by Merkel.
: literally 'darting at,' ἅπ. λεγ.; cf. καταΐγδην, 1. 64.
: prae dolore, cf. Archil. frag. 9 (Bergk), οἰδαλέους δ’ ἀμφ’ ὀδύνῃς ἔχομεν πνεύμονας.

div.p: The Schol. tells us that according to Pisander and Epicharmus Amycus was not slain but thrown into chains. Theocritus (22. 131) says that Polydeuces spared his life, having exacted an oath that he would never again do violence to strangers. Val. Fl. follows our author, differing from him only in saying that the Bebryces fled immediately their king was slain (4. 315), Bebrycas extemplo spargit fuga; nullus adempti Regis amor; montem celeres silvamque capessunt.

div.seg:
: Seaton (Class. Rev. xv p. 29) admirably defends this use of ἀφειδεῖν = ἀμελεῖν. The reading ἀκήδησαν was adopted by Merkel on the authority of Choeroboscus, and is approved by Bonitz and Jebb. In Soph. Ant. 414, εἴ τις τοῦδ’ ἀφειδήσοι πόνου, Jebb reads ἀκηδήσοι, though, as Seaton points out, ἀφειο=ήσοι is defended by the use of ἀφειδής in Thuc. 4. 26, τοῖς δὲ ἀφειδὴς ὁ κατάπλους καθεστήκει, 'the landing was made recklessly.' ἀφειδεῖν = ἀμελεῖν is found again in 2 869 and 3. 930, while
the adj. is used in an active sense in 4. 1252, ἀφειδέες … δείματος. For the varying quantity of the penult. of Βέβρυκες v. App. 11 (k).
: Ap. keeps the Homeric quantity: Eur. and Theocr. lengthen the penult.

: 'hard,' 'seasoned' = ἀζαλέος (115). This meaning is recognized in Et. Mag. σκληρόν· ἀπὸ τῆς ἄζης, and in schol. B. Il. 15. 25. In Hom. ἀζηχής has two meanings: (1) 'very piercing' of sound (ἀ‐διηχής), (2) 'incessant' (ἀ‐διεχής).

: ἀκόντια ὁλοσίδηρα. Schol.; cf. Hdt. 5. 9, σιγύννας καλέουσι Κύπριοι τὰ δόρατα: Arist. Poet. 21. 3, τὸ σίγυνον Κυπρίοις μὲν κύριον, ἡμῖν δὲ γλῶττα. For varieties of spelling v. L. and S. See also on 4. 320.
: cf. Soph. Aj. 730. κολεῶν ἐρυστὰ διεπεραιώθη ξιφη.

div.p:
Cf.
Aen. 9. 754, atque illi partibus aequis Huc caput atque illuc humero ex utroque pependit.

div.seg: : for the pleonasm cf. Theogn. 815. βοῦς μοι ἐπὶ γλώσσῃ κρατερῷ ποδὶ λὰξ ἐπιβαίνων.
: cf. Il. 16. 324, βραχίονα δουρὸς ἀκωκὴ Δρύψ’ ἀπὸ μυώνων.

div.p: The construction of this line is a blend of Il. 5. 305, τῷ βάλεν Αἰνείαο κατ’ ἰσχίον, and 14. 446, τὸν … οὖτα κατὰ λαπάρην.

div.seg: : 'but the bronze spear sped merely along the surface of the skin beneath the belt and touched not the vitals.'
: lit. 'thus much and no more,' see note to 1.183; cf. Il. 9. 354, ἀλλ’ ὅσον ἐς Σκαιάς τε πύλας καὶ φηγὸν ἵκανεν.
: for the trans. use cf. Soph. O.T. 969, ἄψαυστος ἔγχους.
: this compound is ἅπ. λεγ. The simple τεταγών (ta-n-go) occurs in Il. 1. 591, ῥῖψε ποδὸς τεταγών.

div.p: For the comparison of warriors to wolves cf. Il. 4. 471; 16. 156; Aen. 2. 355.

div.seg: : πολλὰ ἐπιβλέποντες καὶ μετ’ ἐνθουσιασμοῦ. παμφαλᾶν γὰρ τὸ μετὰ πτοιήσεως ἐπιβλέπειν. Schol. This compound is ἅπ. λεγ. παμφαλάα = παπταίνω was used by Anacreon and Hipponax.

: ἔδει εἰπεῖν περὶ ἀλλήλοις πίπτοντα, οὐ γὰρ περὶ ἑαυτά, τὸ δὲ ἁμάρτημα τῶν μεθ’ Ὄμηρον. Schol. We find σφίσι used instead of the dual pronoun (referring to ἄμφω) in 3. 1023, ἐπὶ σφίσι βάλλον ὀπωπάς. It is used for the 1 pers. pl. (with reciprocal sense) in 1278 infr., and in 3. 909. In Il. to. 398, μετὰ σφίσιν is equivalent to μεθ’ ὑμῖν (v. Leaf). See also on 4. 1290.

div.p:
For the simile cf. Lycophr. 293,
ἀλλ’ ὡς μέλισσαι συμπεφυρμέναι καπνῷ Καὶ λιγνύος ῥιπαῖσι, κ.τ.λ.:
Aen. 12. 587,
Inclusas ut cum latebroso in pumice pastor
Vestigavit apes fumoque implevit amaro:
Illae intus trepidae rerum per cerea castra
Discurrunt magnisque acuunt stridoribus iras
, etc.: Geor. 4. 230.

div.seg: : we have the same wide use of ὅς as of ἑός (1. 1113n.). It is used (a) regularly for 3 pers. sing., (b) for 3 pers. pl. instead of σφός or σφέτερος, as here and in 1. 384, etc., (c) for 1 pers. sing., e.g. 4. 1015; Od. 9. 28, (d) for 2 pers. pl., 4. 1384.
: cf. Ar. Vesp. 457, τῦφε (τοὺς σφῆκας) καπνῷ.
: κῶμαι. Schol. In Soph., fr. 138, we find οἰητᾶν, which Hesych. explains by κωμητῶν. The deriv. is unknown. Müller suggests an affinity with Lacon. ὠβά.
: the land of the Chalybes; cf. 1005 infr. Ap. alone uses the adj. in this sense.

: for the form v. Rzach, p. 172. Ap., misled by Homeric forms
like δηιόωντες, δηιόωντο, which have the appearance of coming from a verb in ‐αω, assumed that there was a present δηιάω from which he formed this iterative tense. Besides many forms from the regular δηιόω, he also uses ἐδήιον from a present δηίω (3. 1374), a form which he may have borrowed from Eumelus (see note to 3.1372).

: περιτρεποντες, ἐπὶ τὴν ναῦν ἐλαύνοντες. Schol. It is ἅπ. λεγ. Cf. Od 9. 465, μῆλα περιτροπέοντες ἐλαύνομεν (v. M. and R.) They surrounded the sheep and drove them off in a body. For ἐτάμοντο cf. Il. 18. 528, τάμνοντ’ ἀμφὶ βοῶν ἀγέλας, 'cut off, intercepted': Od. 11. 402, βοῦς περιταμνόμενον. The Lat. versions wrongly render 'mactabant,' and so de M. 'immolaient.'

div.p: 'Consider what the Bebryces would have done in their cowardice.'
div.seg: : see note to 132 Many needless corrections have been proposed for ἀναλκείῃσιν, e.g. ἀτασθυλίῃσιν, ἀπηνείῃσιν, ἀγηνορίῃσιν, αλαζονίῃσιν, but the text is sound. If the B. fled before the other Argonauts, what would they have done had Heracles been there?

div.p:
Val. Fl. introduces this yearning
for Heracles before the fight, 4. 247, redit Alcidae iam sera cupido Et vacuos maesto lustrant tum lumine montes.

div.seg: : impers., 'never would the issue have been decided by boxing.'

: 'straightway with his club he would have made him to forget his proud might together with the ordinances which he proclaimed.' Merkel takes λελαθέσθαι in this causal sense. Hom. has the active so used, Il. 15. 60, Εκτορα … λελάθῃ (sc. Ἀπόλλων) ὀδυνάων. Old edd. explain 'under the club A. would have forgotten'; but cf. Il. 22. 457, μιν καταπαύσῃ ἀγηνορίης, and νάσσατο, 1. 1356.

div.p: 'will realize his fatal folly now that H. is far away.'

div.seg: : 'wreathing,' cf. Eur. Bacch. 323, κισσῷ τ’ ἐρεψόμεσθα.

: 'to which the stern-hawsers had been fastened at the foreland.' For ἀκτῇ ἔπι cf. ἀκτῇ ἐπὶ προβλῆτι, 366 infr. The ἀκτή is that mentioned in 1. 1361. This seems the simplest correction. περί was due to the πρ of πρυμνήσια. Merkel's τῇ καί τε περί is read by Seaton, and explained by de M. "les amarres du navire étaient fixées à l'arbre et aux alentours," i.e. the cables were fastened not merely to the tree, but also to the surrounding rocks. The tree, however, was sufficiently strong; it was described as εὐμεγεθες δένδρον by Androetas of Tenedos according to the Schol. With Merkel's reading I would prefer to take περί as a prep. 'round which the cables also were fastened,' but Ap. has only the simple dat. with ἀνάπτειν.
: "all the breathless beach lay tranced with the spell of the song" (Way).

: explained by the Schol. as Apollo, to whom
Therapnae in Laconia was sacred. More probably Polydences is meant. For the connexion of the Dioscuri with Therapnae cf. Pind. Aem. 10. 55.
: i.e. from the bottom of the trunk, where naturally the tree was strongest. de M. renders "du laurier en dernier lieu," i.e. the cable round the bay-tree was the last loosed. See on 160.
: cf. Od. 11. 244, κῦμα περιστάθη οὔρεϊ ἶσον Κυρτωθεν: Virg. G. 4. 361, curvata in montis faciem circumstetit unda.
: 'but yet even this is smoothed if by good hap it meet with a skilful steersman.'
: sollertia. The word is peculiar to Ap., cf. 4. 1273.

: 'over against,' like ἀντιπέρας in Thucydides. They anchored, opposite Bithynia, on the Thracian coast where the Bosporus joins the Euxine, Salmydessus, the dwelling of Phineus,
should lie to the left after entering the Euxine; Ap., for his own purposes, places it on the left of the Bosporus before coming to the Cyanean Rocks.

: according to hellanicus, a son of Agenor; according to Pherecydes and Antimachus, a grandson. He was married first to Cleopatra (239), daughter of Boreas, by whom he had two sons who were introduced in Sophocles' lost tragedies on the legend of Phineus. By his second wife, Eidothea, he was father of Thynus and Mariandynus.

: Apollodorus (1. 9. 21) likewise states that he was blinded for revealing to men the counsels of Zeus. The Schol. mentions another story that he was cursed by Aeetes and blinded by Helios for saving the sons of Phrixus. Servius (on Aen. 3. 209) says that he was blinded by Boreas for his conduct to his first two sons whom he cruelly tortured for their treatment of his second wife (cf. Diod. 4. 44). Sophocles (Antig. 970) says these two sons were blinded by Eidothea.
: neque tantillum (see note to 1.290); 'and nought he recked to reveal truly unto mortals the sacred purposes of Zeus himself.'

div.p:
Cf.
Aen. 3. 225,
At subitae horrifico lapsu de montibus adsunt
Harpyiae, et magnis quatiunt clangoribus alas
Diripiuntque dapes contactuque omnia foedant
Immundo.

div.seg: : in Hom. these 'Snatchers' are always personifications of the storm-winds (e.g. Od. 20. 66, 77). In Aesch. Eum. 50 we first have them described as ugly creatures with wings, and in later writers they are always represented as loathsome monsters; cf. Aen. 3. 210 sqq.

κ.τ.λ.: 'and no one could have endured the stench, I will not say when putting the food to his mouth, but even standing afar off, so foul was the smell from the fragments of the feast.'
μὴ καί must stand for μὴ ὅτι, nedum, ne dicam, a usage which we find again in 3. 589. λευκανίη is the gullet as opp. to the ἀσφάραγος or windpipe, cf. Il. 22. 325. For the strange use of the local ‐δε cf. Aristophanes' reading κεφολήνδε in Od. 14. 349. On Il. 11. 97 we are told by Schol. A. that Ap. would read ἐγκέφαλόνδε, deleting the following line (v. Introd. p. 50 n). For the v.l. λαυκανίηνδε see on 4. 18.
: this use of ἀποπνεῖν is confined to late Greek.
: 'there was an oracle from Zeus that when they came he should have joy of his food.'
: 'a lifeless wraith'; cf. Eur. H.F. 111, δόκημα νυκτερωπὸν ἐννύχων ὀνειράτων (of the aged chorus): Phoen. 1556. See also on 3. 466.
: cf. Seneca Oed. 657, baculo senili triste praetentans iter
: 'groping along'; cf. Od. 8. 196 καί κ’ ἀλαὸς … διακυίνειε τὺ σῆμα Ἀμφαφόων.
: 'feebleness.' This form is used only by Ap.; cf. ὀλιγοδρανία, Aesch. Pr. 548.
: Rzach points out that Ap. adopts the form which was favoured by Zenod. in Hom., while Aristarch. advocated χρόος (v. schol. Il. 13. 191).
: cf. Lucr. 6. 1270, pelli super ossibus una : Hor. Epod. 17.22, ossa pelle amicta lurida.
: 'faintness,' 'giddiness.' Aristotle couples the word with κραιπάλη in describing the after-effects of drunkenness (Probl. 3. 17. 3).
: cf. Od. 4. 180, θανάτοιο μέλαν νεφος ἀμφεκάλυψεν.
: 'dark,' 'misty'; used by Hom. as an epithet of θάνατος (Il. 5. 83, etc.)

: 'the stupor of exhaustion'; cf. ἀβληχρὸς θάνατος, Od. 11. 135. Curt. explains the form as ἀ prothet. and βληχρός (4. 152) connected
with μαλακός. The notion of the Schol. and Et. Mag. (200, 14) that βληχρός = ἰσχυρός is without foundation.

κ.τ.λ.: cf. the Homeric ὰνενείκατο φώνησέν τε. Virg. imitates Ap.,
Aen. 1. 371, suspirans imoque trabens a pectore vocem. For ὑπύτοιο see on 1. 222.
: Ap. uses this word in its later sense of Greeks in general. Its meaning in Il. 2. 530 is very doubtful. See also on 1. 243, 904.
: 'I ascribe this favour to'; cf. Plut. Anton. 46, Μοναισῃ τὴν χάριν ἀνάπτων. Distinguish Eur. Phoen. 569, χάριτας ἔς σ’ ἀνήψατο 'conferred favours on.'
: = πρός (in entreaties), an innovation of Ap. See on 1. 1150.
: only here c. gen., elsewhere used absolutely meaning 'exceedingly.' It is not found in Hom.
: Ap. differs from Hom. in using χραισμέω in positive sentences, cf. 249, 3. 643. The negative use occurs once, 2. 1225.

: cf. Eur. Phoen. 1535, βίοτον μέλεος ἐς τὸν αἰὲν ἑλκω χρόνον. ἀμήρυτον 'interminable' is a coinage of Ap. from μηρύεσθαι 'to wind thread,' and is explained by the Schol., τὸ θάνατον μὴ ἔχον. Brunck takes ἐς τέλος, not with ἕλκω, but with ἀμήρυτον = γῆρας ὃ οὔποτε μέλλω εἰς τέλος μηρύσεσθαι.

: 'swooping down as destroyers from some unseen quarter.' Köchly's correction ὔλεθροι seems necessary as the vulg. ὀλέθρου can hardly mean 'place of destruction' (alicunde, e loco funesto, Dübner). The phrase ἔκποθεν ἀφράστοιο occurs again in 824; and is imitated by Quint. Smyrn.,
3. 437, ἔκποθεν ἀπροφάτοιο λυγρῷ βεβλημένος ἰῷ. ἔκποθεν, alicunde, is a form originated by Ap. For ὔλεθροι cf. Plat. Rep. 491 b, πολλοὶ ὔλεθροι καὶ μεγάλοι, and for similar expressions in our poet v. 3. 777, 1135, 4. 242.
κ.τ.λ.: 'but my desire for food could more easily escape the notice of my mind, than I could escape the notice of the harpies.' For the use of the positive ῥεῖα instead of the comparative cf. 4. 501.
: = ἀποπνεῖ, 193; cf. Soph. fr. 147, οὐ μύρου πνέον.

div.p: 'not even if his heart were forged of adamant.'

div.seg: : Zetes and Calais (1. 212). For the relationship of Phineus to Boreas see note to 178
: at Salmydessus (v.n. 177). Aesch. Pr. 745, τραχεῖα πόντου Σαλμυδησσία γνάθος Ἐχθρόξενος ναύταισι, μητρυιὰ νεῶν.
: σμυγερός = μογερός is practically confined to Ap.: cf. ἐπισμυγερῶς, 1. 616 (a compound also found in Hom.).
: ὄντως. Schol., 'if the divine power has indeed assigned to us this honour.' For the misuse of πρόχνυ see note to 1.1118.

: 'for the censure of the immortal gods makes itself plainly manifest to men': an echo
of Il. 15. 490 sqq. The sons of Boreas fear the wrath of heaven in aiding one who is suffering for his impiety. Ap. uses both ἀρίζηλος and ἀρίδηλος (3. 615; 4. 727) in the sense of 'clearly manifest.' The former is the Homeric form, though Zenodotus would read ἀρίδηλος (with long ι) in Il. 2. 318. Curtius shows that in ἀρίζηλος the δj passes into ζ, in ἀρίδηλος the j has simply fallen out.
: 'lose the favour of'; cf. Il. 1. 562, ἀλλ’ ἀπὸ θυμοῦ Μᾶλλον ἐμοὶ ἔσεαι.
: 'fixed straight on him the sightless gaze of his wide-opened eyes'; cf. Val. Fl. 4. 435, oculos attollit inanes.
: ἡ ἐπικειμένη μοι ἀχλύς. Schol. In Od. 10. 493 Teiresias is described as μάντις ἀλαός (λάω = video).

div.p: 'may they not deal gently with me if I die forsworn.'
div.seg: : ἐπιόρκως. Schol. Cf. Il. 19. 264, εἰ δέ τι τῶνδ’ ἐπιορκον, ἐμοὶ θεοὶ ἄλγεα δοῖεν.
: 'by reason of his oath,' causal dat.; Merkel eironeously construes the dat. with ἔπειτα.
: for the gen., which is un-Homeric, cf. Soph. Aj. 50, καὶ πῶς ἐπέσχε χεῖρα μαιμῶσαν φόρου; (Jebb, wrongly I think, takes φόνου with ἐπέσχε.)

: 'having gulped down'; cf. Od. 4. 222, ὃς τὸ καταβρόξειεν. Another compound άναβρόξαι occurs in 4. 826; Od. 12. 240. The variant forms with ω, which we find in our mss. and in Hom., were due to an attempt to assimilate the verb to βιβρώσκω Hesych. has the gloss βρόξαι· ῥοφήσαι.
: this form agrees with Zenodotus' reading ἀστήσεσθαι for ἀνστήσεσθαι in Il. 2. 694. Rzach points out that Ap. is inconsistent in using ἄνστησον in 4. 1325, and suggests ἄστησον.

: cf. Il. 19. 415, Νῶι δὲ καί κεν ἅμα πνοιῇ Ζεφύροιο θέοιμεν, Τόν περ ἐλαφρότατον φάσ’ ἔμμεναι:
Aen. 1. 317, volucremque fuga praevertitur Eurum.

div.p: This simile, which is so common in epic poetry, is derived from Il. 10. 360, ὡς δ’ ὅτε καρχαρόδοντε δύω κύνε εἰδότε θήρης )\Η κεμάδ’ ἠὲ λαγωὸν ἐπείγετον, κ.τ.λ. We have it amplified in Aen. 12. 749 sqq.; cf. also Ov. Met. 1. 533 sqq.
This line is modelled on Od. 17. 294 (of the dog Argos), τὸν δὲ πάροιθεν ἀγίνεσκον νέοι ἄνδρες Αῖγας ἐπ’ ἀγροτέρας ἠδὲ πρόκας ἠδὲλαγωούς.
div.seg: : 'roes'; Curtius connects the word with περκ‐νός (Il. 24. 316).

div.p:
Cf.
Aen. 12. 754,
Haeret hians, iam iamque tenet, similisque tenenti
Increpuit malis, morsuque elusus inani est.

div.seg: : 'in vain.' Here, and in Call. Lav. Pall. 124, this adv. is connected with ἠλεός, ἠλίθιος; in 3. 342 and 4. 177, 1265 it is used in the Homeric sense of 'exceedingly' (ἅλις).
: cf. Od. 14. 37, ὀλίγου δε κυνες διεδηλήσαντο.
: two small islands in the Ionian Sea, south of Zacynthus, afterwards called the Strophades (296).

: the Schol. tells us that according to Hesiod it was Hermes who restrained them, and that our poet introduces Iris appropriately (ἀστείως) as she was a sister of the Ἄρπυιαι, being sprung from Thaumas and Electra.
: cf. Aesch. Pr. 803 (of the griffins), Ζηνὸς ἀκραγεῖς κύνες: ib. 1022 (of the eagle), Διὸς πτηνὸς κύων.
: 'that never again shall they return to harm him.'

: cf. Il. 15. 36, Στυγὸς ὕδωρ ὕς τε μέγιστος Ὄρκος δεινότατός τε πέλει μακάρεσσι θεοῖσιν:
Aen. 12. 816,
Adiuro Stygii caput implacabile fontis,
Una superstitio superis quae reddita Divis.
: the adj. ὀπιδνός, from ἴπις 'reverence,' 'awe,' is only found here.

: 'to speed.' Ap. alone uses σώομαι = σοῦμαι, σεύομαι; cf. 2. 1010, 3. 307. Distinguish σώεσθαι (from σώω =
σώζω) 2. 610. Epilycus (fr. 1. 803 Kock) has the Doric σῶμαι = σοῦμαι.

: cf.
Aen. 3. 210,
Strophades Graio stant nomine dictae
Insulae Ionio in magno, quas dira Celaeno
Harpyiaeque colunt aliae, Phineia postquam
Clausa domus, mensasque metu liquere priores.
: = μετονομάζουσι. Other new compounds with μετά are μεταλωφέω, ‐αλδήσκω, ‐παιφάσσω, ‐εννέπω, ‐χάζομαι, ‐τρωπάω, ‐τρέφω.

: 'soaring aloft.' Apoll. Lex. Hom. μεταχρόνιον· μετέωρον: Suid. μεταχρονίη· ἡ εἰς ὕψος φερομενη: Hesych. μεταίσιον· μεταχρόνιον (a corruption of μεταχρόνιον· μετάρσιον). Ap. is imitating Hes. Th. 269 (of the harpies), Αἵῥ’ ἀνέμων πνοιῇσι καὶ οἰωνοῖς ἅμ’ ἕπονται, Ὠκείῃς πτερύγεσσι· μεταχρόνιαι γὰρ ἴαλλον, where Goettling, following the Schol., explains 'celeres ad instar temporis.' In our passage L and Pariss. give μεταχθονίη, and the Schol. Flor. recognizes the two forms: τὸ δὲ μεταχθονίη γράφεται καὶ μεταχρονίη. καὶ σημαίνει ἑκατέρως τὴν μετέωρον. In 2. 587, 3. 1151, 4. 952, 1385 there is a preponderance of authority for μεταχρόνιος; in 4. 1269 μεταχθονίην seems the true reading, as the meaning 'up on to the land' is different. Editors vary: Brunck reads
μεταχθόνιος in every case, while Merkel uniformly adopts μεταχρόνιος. Wellauer and Seaton read μεταχρόνιος, except in 4. 1269. Ruhnken says, "Mihi vox non ex μετὰ et χρόνος, ut Scholiastes Hesiodi nugatur, sed ex μετὰ et χθὼν composita videtur; quamvis facile largiar doctiores etiam Graecos, depravatam vulgi consuetudinem secutos, μεταχρόνιος pro μεταχθόνιος scripsisse." Nonnus in the Dionysiaca uses the form μεταχρόνιος, which is also mentioned in Et. Mag. 581. 41. where its equivalent μετέωρος is explained παρὰ τὸν ὦρον, ὃ σημαίνει τὸν χρόνον.
: the adj. πινόεις (= πιναρός 'foul') is found earlier only in Hippocrates, though πίνος (200) is used in Tragedy.
: 'cleansing'; a verb confined to Alexandrian writers, cf. Theocr. 17. 134, χεῖρας φοιβήσασα μύροις.
: 'greedily,' cf. Od. 6. 250, ὁ πῖνε καὶ ἦσθε … Ἁρπαλέως.
: cf. Il. 19. 167. οἴνοιο κορεσσάμενος καὶ ἐδωδῆς.
: 'the ends of their voyaging'; cf. Il. 23. 350, ἑκάστου πείρατ’ ἔειπεν.
κ.τ.λ.: 'revealing the purposes of Zeus as they would come to pass in order even to the end.'
: μὴ τέλεια, ὰλλ’ ἔτι ἐνδέοντα λόγια τοῖς ἀνθρώποις ἐκφαίνειν, ἵνα καὶ τοῦ θείου χρείαν ἔχωσι. θέσφατα δὲ μαντοσύνης τὰ θεσπίσματα τῆς μαντικῆς λέγει. Schol.

div.p: The prophecy of Phineus is modelled on the advice of Circe to Odysseus, Od. 12. 37 sqq.; Virgil imitates both passages in Aen. 3. 374 sqq., where Helenus foretells what lies before Aeneas.

div.seg: : cf. ἠρήρειντο, 3. 1398. Brunck needlessly reads ἐνήρεινται on the ground that ἐρηρέδαται is the Homeric form.

: for the sense see note to 1.1028. In Il. 9. 7 the antepenult. is
short, and so Brunck proposed κορθύνεται here.
: 'you cleave your way.' For this absolute use, which is peculiar to Ap., cf. 398. Elsewhere (e.g. 775) he follows the Homeric usage, κύματα πείρειν, κέλευθον πείρειν, etc.
: = αὐθαίρετον, cf. Od. 16. 148; for another use v. 4. 231. For the constr. cf. 881 infr.
: cf. Od. 14 262, ἐπισπόμενοι μένεϊ σφῷ, 'giving the reins to,' 'following the dictates of.'
: cf. Prop. 4. 22. 14, Qua rudis Argoa natatinter saxa columba In faciem prorae pinus adacta novae. Homer mentions doves in connexion with the Symplegades in quite a different way, Od. 12. 62 sqq.

: if the reading is sound, the construction is extremely harsh. ἐφιέμεν (= ἐπιτρέπειν) is used for an imperative, and πειρήσασθαι depends on ἐφιέμεν, 'leave it to the dove to make trial of the passage.' The difficulty would be relieved if we could take ἐφιέμεν as used intransitively of the dove committing herself to the breezes, or else as used absolutely in the sense of ταρσὸν ἐφεὶς πνοιῇ (934 infr.). The meaning then would be, 'first make trial of it by means of a dove, sending her forth in front of the vessel to wing her flight.' We should thus be able to retain the vulg. πειρήσασθε, though Ap. often uses infinitives for imperatives even where imperatives precede, e.g. 4. 374, 761.
: 'flies.' This must be referred to δίεμαι (Il. 23. 475), but in 4. 498 δίεσθαι is from δίομαι 'to pursue.'
: 'plying stoutly'; cf. Pind. O. 13. 135, βέλεα καρτύνειν χεροῖν. ἑαῖς: = ὑμετέραις, see note to 1.1113.
: 'deliverance'; cf. Il. 16. 95, ἐπὴν φάος ἐν νήεσσι Θήῃς.

div.p: 'wherefore, abandoning all else, labour boldly at what will profit you most' (i.e. κωπηλατεῖν).
div.seg: : the Ionic superl. from ὄνειος utilis. The compar. ὀνήιον occurs in Nic. Al. 627 (v. Smyth, Ion. Dial. 555). L. and S. mistranslate our passage 'exert yourselves to the utmost.'
: 'I dissuade you not from praying to the gods beforehand.' Prayers without exertion are useless, cf. 1. 870.
: ἀλέαιτο occurs in Od. 20. 368. In 1. 490 we had ἐξαλέοιο, like ἀλέοιτο (?) in Il. 20. 147.

div.p: 'Though thrice so much ye account me abhorred of the Dwellers in Heaven--Yea though it were more than thrice--as I am by my grievous sin, Yet dare not to flout the omen, to thrust your galley therein!' (Way).

div.seg: : i.e. contrary to the omen given by the dove. In this sense παρέκ usually takes the acc. as in 341 (see note to 1.130).
: 'the clashing of the rocks'; cf. Pind. P. 4. 370, σύνδρομοι πέτραι (= συνδρομάδες).
: the Bithynians were a Thracian people who came from the Strymon into Asia, having been driven from Europe by the Teucri and Mysi (Hdt. 7. 75).
: the Rhebas is a small river on the Bithynian coast.
: 'doubling': cf. the use of flectere, Cic. Div. 2. 45, in flectendis promunturiis.
: Thynias was a small island one mile from the coast of Bithynia (Strab. 465, 32). Arrian, Peripl. 13, says that it had a port and naval station belonging to Heraclea.

div.p:
'Thence bending back no long
distance over the sea ye shall run up the vessel on the land of the Mariandyni which lieth opposite.'
div.seg: : this fem. form with the last syllable short is only found in late epic; cf. 4. 521. Hom. uses the neut. pl. Il. 2. 635. ἀντιπέραῑ ἐνέμοντο.
: dwelling to the N.E. of Bithynia, and, like the Bithynians, originally immigrants from Thrace (Strab. 245, 35). They are referred to in Hdt. 3. 90, 7. 72, 75. Heraclea Pontica was their chief city.

: all rivers called Acheron were supposed to communicate with the lower world. Diodorus (14. 31) mentions the legend that it was by the outlet of this river near Heraclea that Heracles dragged up Cerberus; cf. also Xen. An. 6. 2. 2.
: sc. ἄκρῃ, 'after leaving this headland': see note to 1.932.

: Ἐνέτη was a city of Paphlagonia. The Ἐνετοί are mentioned
in Il. 2. 851, Παφλαγόνων δ’ ἡγεῖτο Πυλαιμένεος λάσιον κῆρ Ἐξ Ἐνετῶν. The Veneti on the Adriatic were supposed to be an offshoot from them. The tradition that Pelops was a Paphlagonian is mentioned also in Diod. 4. 74, schol. Pind. O. 1. 37.
: 'the revolving Bear,' i.e. the Great Bear which revolves round the Pole; cf. 3. 1195.
: Strabo (103, 17) says that this Paphlagonian promontory helps to make the Euxine into two seas (διθόλαττον). Cf. Pliny N.H. 2. 6.

div.p: 'and over it the blasts from the north are divided into two currents': i.e. the promontory, facing north, was so lofty that it interrupted the northern blasts and reft them in twain.
'to such a height does it reach in the upper air as it faces the sea.' For κύρω c. dat. cf. 4. 945: Il. 23. 428: Call. Cer. 38, μέγα δένδρεον αἰθέρι κῦρον.

div.seg: : cf. Strab. 466, 54, Ὁ δὲ Αἰγιαλὸς ἔστι μὲν ἠϊὼν μακρὰ πλειόνων ἢ ἑκατὸν σταδίων· ἔχει δὲ καὶ κώμην ὁμώνυμον, ἧς μέμνηται ὁ ποιητὴς ὁταν φῇ (Il. 2. 855) Κρῶμνάν τ’ Αἰγιαλόν τε καὶ ὑψήλους Ἐρυθίνους. For another Αἰγιαλός v. 1. 178.

: the Halys, the chiefriver
in Asia Minor, rises in the Armenian Mts. and, after a tortuous course, discharges itself into the Euxine. Strabo (468, 16) derives its name ἀπὸ τῶν ἁλῶν, i.e. the salt-mines in its neighbourhood, but this is very dubious.
: cf. Od. 5. 403, κῦμα ποτὶ ξερὸν … Δεινὸν ἐρευγόμενον.
: cf. Strab. 469, 19; Xen. An. 5. 6. 9 (where the breadth is given as three plethra).
: this comparative from μικρός was originated by Ap. and adopted by later writers.

div.p: 'from this point further on a great bend rising up juts out from the land.' For ἀγκών cf. 4. 1583, ἀγκῶνος … ἀπὸ προύχοντος.

div.seg: : a periphrasis for Θερμώδων as is shown by the masc. participle διαειμένος (372). The Thermodon, whose winding course is described 970 sqq., rises in Pontus and flows, like the Iris, through the plain of Themiscyra, emptying into the Euxine: cf. Aesch. Pr. 751.
: 'flows,' a meaning only found in Ap. and Lycophron. In Hom. it means 'to weep,' as in 1. 271, etc.
: 'after passing through,' a participle only found here. cf. καταειμενος, 1. 939; for the false formation see on 1. 366.
: the three cities were Lycastia, Themiscyra, and Chadesia. τρισσός is not used by Hom.: in Hes. it means 'threefold.'

: Aeschylus, Pr. 742, speaks of the σιδηροτέκτονες Χάλυβες as ἀνήμεροι οὐδὲ πρόσπλατοι ξένοις. Xenophon, An. 5. 5. 1, describes the march of the Ten Thousand through the country of the Mossynoeci (379), Chalybes, and Tibareni (377).
: 'unyielding,' difficilem; cf. Dion. Per. 768, Χάλυβες στυφελὴν καὶ ἀπήνεα γαῖαν Ναίουσιν, μογεροῦ δεδαηκότες ἔργα σιδήρου.
: a cape (so called from the river Genes), where was a temple of Zeus Xenios, Strab. 469, 53.
: sc. ἄκρῃ, 'next to (beyond) this headland,' cf. 357.

: cf. Strab. 470, 20, ἐπὶ δένδρεσιν ἢ πυργίοις οἰκοῦσι. διὸ καὶ Μοσυνοίκους ἐκάλουν οἱ παλαιοί, τῶν πύργων μοσύνων λεγομένων: Dion. Hal. 1. 26, οἰκοῦσιν ἐπὶ ξυλίνοις πύργοις … μόσσυνας αὐτὰ καλοῦντες. For their habits v. 1016 sqq.

div.p: 'making their habitations in towers of wood.'

(382-3). These two lines have been rejected as interpolations since the time of Brunck. The second line occurs again 1017 infr. Brunck argues forcibly against their genuineness: -- "Duo illi versus neutiquam hic locum habent, et quam etymologiam continent, eam in Phinei vaticinio ponere non debuit Poeta. Vates minime λεπτολογεῖ, non ἐτυμολογεῖ; breviter et summatim singula adtingit, quae eadem postea in itineris narratione Poeta tractabit uberius et exornabit. Praeterea in elaborato, correcto, et ad unguem expolito poemate idem versus bis in eodem libro legi non debet, nec utroque in loco a Poeta positus fuit." Gerhard plausibly suggests that these two lines stood in the earlier recension after 381 (which may originally have been δουρατέοις θριγκυῖσιν ἐνοίκια τεκτήναντες), and being afterwards removed by the poet they have crept into the text from a marginal note of the copyist.
div.seg: : 'rugged,' τραχείᾳ καὶ ὑψηλῇ. Schol., cf. λισσάδες 731 infr. In the Od. Aristarch. explains λισσή and λίς as 'smooth,' a sense which our Schol. also recognizes (see note to 4.922). The grammarians oscillated between the two meanings (v. Et. Mag. and Hesych.). In Aesch. Supp. 795 λισσάς perhaps means 'rugged,' as also in Eur. H. F. 1148 (v. Wilamowitz).

: 'as the story goes.' The name of the island was Ἀρητιάς or Ἄρεος νῆσος. The Schol. says that Eur. in his Phrixus described the island as haunted by monstrous birds, driven by Heracles from Stymphalus in Arcadia, which discharged their own feathers as shafts; cf. 1036.
: see note to 1.1037. In 1090 sqq. we read how the sons of Phrixus were shipwrecked on the island, and guided the heroes to the Colchian land.

div.p: 'Beyond this island and the mainland facing it dwell the Philyres.' For περαίης see note to 4.78, 1. 923. In 1231 infr. we hear of an island called Φιλυρηίς off the coast of Pontus, opposite the district of the Philyres.

div.seg: : 'exceeding many,' see note to 1.466; the Becheires are mentioned in Dion. Per. 765, φῦλα Βεχείρων.
: a savage tribe dwelling above Trapezus (Strab. 470, 29).
: the south-eastern recesses of the Euxine. See on 1. 170.

: Procop., B. G. 4. 13. 14, mentions Κουτατίσιον, a small town on the Phasis, modern Kutais. This was probably the Cyte or Cytaea which was associated with the birth of Medea (Prop. 1. 1. 24). In Ap. Κυταιίς = Colchian, cf. Val. Fl. 6. 693, terris Cytaeis.
: the Schol. states, on the authority of Herodian, that the Phasis rose in these mountains.
: cf. Dion. Per. 691, ἔνθα τε Φᾶσις Κιρκαίου κατὰ νῶτον ἑλισσόμενος πεδίοιο: Avienus 876, Phasis ... Circaeaque lapsus in arva Incidit Euxinum. Circe was a sister of Aeetes.

: ἀντὶ τοῦ σκιόεν, κατὰ Ἰωνικὴν πρόσθεσιν τοῦ ι—. Schol. For this new formation on the false analogy of the masc. cf. δακρυόειν, 4. 1291. Rzach (p. 97) suggests that we might regard these as metrical makeshifts of the copyists, and restore the normal forms in accordance with Il. 24. 269, πύξινον ὀμφαλόεν εὖ οἰήκεσσιν ἀπηρός, but the mss. and the Schol. are against this. Later writers imitated Ap., e.g. Nonn. Dion. 25. 440, ἐρόειν: Nic. Ther. 748, πυρόειν.
: 'watches,' cf. Il. 7. 243, λάθρη ὀπιπεύσας. For the form see note to 4.469.
: 'on guard'; once used in Hom., Il. 15. 730, of Ajax protecting the ships, ἑστήκει δεδοκημένος. It is to be referred to δέχομαι rather than δοκέω. Cf. also Hes. Sc. 214.
: = ἡδύς, cf. h. Hom. Merc. 241. The Homeric νήδυμος in νήδυμος ὕπνος was regarded by later poets as made up of νή (intens.) and ἡδύς.

div.p: Cf. Il. 17. 695, δὴν δέ μιν ἀμφασίη ἐπέων λάβε. See also 3. 76.

div.seg: : cf. Il. 9. 61, ἐξείπω καὶ πάντα διίξομαι.
: = τεκμήριον, 'sign,' i.e. the flight of the dove.
'Peius: hos scopulos in reditu superantes. Potius: in expeditione facienda; nam hoc et haec verba et Phinei responsio liquide dant.' (Dübner, quoted by de M.).
: this adv. is found first in Hdt. (4. 201). Hom. uses ἀσπαστός sometimes in the Od., but ἀσπασίως.
: a city on the Phasis where Aeetes dwelt (Strab. 38, 12), and the name was extended to the land ruled by him. Aeschylus and Pindar first use the historical name Colchis.

: 'lies over against the boundary of the Pontus and the earth'; cf. Eur. Tro. 797, Σαλαμῖνος τᾶς ἐπικεκλιμένας ἱεροῖς ὄχθοις (i.e. of Attica). Colchis was regarded as the eastern boundary of the earth, cf. 1. 84.
: i.e. they will not have to return through the Symplegades.
: 'as far as.' Way wrongly renders, 'after Aia.'

div.p: Cf. 273 sqq.

div.seg: : cf. ἀυτμένα φυσιόωντε, 87 supr. The compound is used of the 'puffing' of dolphins in Hes. Sc. 211, δοιοὶ δ’ ἀναφυσιόωντες … δελφῖνες. Boesch has collected many exx. of verbs used absolutely in Hom. but c. acc. in Ap., e.g. φυσιάω, παλάσσομαι (1. 358), τεθηπα (3. 215), μύρομαι (3. 656), ἀπολήγω (4. 767), καναχέω (4. 907).
: 'how far off they had driven the harpies.' ἄπωθεν is loosely used, as it should denote motion from. The Schol. takes ἤλασαν as intrans.: ἀντὶ τοῦ ὅσον μακρὸν ἐπορεύθησαν.
: this adv. is peculiar to Ap., cf. 472, 3. 427.

div.p: 'Now if he (i.e. the god) would but grant light to thine eyes, I trow that I should rejoice as though I had reached home again.'

div.seg: : i.e. the gift of sight is gone beyond recall; cf. Il. 1. 526, τέκμωρ οὐ παλινάγρετον. In Call. Lav. Pall. 103 the blinding of Teiresias is described as οὐ παλινάγρετον ἔργον.
: 'for my sightless eyeballs are slowly wasting away.' See on 109.

div.p: "Nay, death let a god bestow right speedily, rather than this: Then, when I am dead, shall I enter at last into perfect bliss" (Way).

div.seg:
: 'as they held converse.' We find the same absolute use in 4. 1461; see on 1. 644. Virg. imitates these lines,
Aen. 6. 535, Hac vice sermonum roseis Aurora quadrigis Iam medium aetherio cursu traiecerat axem. In 3. 1224 we have ἠριγενὴς Ἠώς; so in Hom. ἠριγένεια is used either as an epithet or a synonym of Ἠώς.
: 'poor'; in Hom. 'feeble,' a meaning found in 3. 144, 4. 1489.
: 'will restrain by the will of Zeus': cf. Il. 15. 489, Διόθεν βλαφθέντα. Others take Διόθεν with ἰούσας.

div.p: 'for, work as he might, and toil as he might, poverty with harder pinch pressed sore upon him.'

div.seg: : cf. Il. 11. 801. ὀλίγη δέ τ’ ἀνάπνευσις πολέμοιο.
: 'a grievous atonement (literally compensation)': cf. Od. 12. 382, τίσουσι βοῶν ἐπιεικέ’ ἀμοιβήν.

div.p: The Schol. mentions as the source of this story a tale told by Charon of Lampsacus how Rhoecus, having won the favour of a nymph by saving her oak-tree, afterwards incurred her displeasure and was maimed by her.

div.seg:
: Hamadryades (ἅμα, δρῦς) were nymphs whose life was bound up in that of the tree with which they had come into being, and which was their
home. For this joint life of nymphs and trees v. Call. Del. 79-85. Pindar (frag. 146) refers to the Hamadryades: ἰσοδένδρου τέκμαρ αἰῶνος λαχοῖσαι.
: this recalls Aesch. Cho. 607, καταίθουσα παιδὸς δαφοινὸν δαλὸν ἥλικα (of Althea burning the torch on which the life of her son Meleager depended).

: there is no need to change this to ἀθέριξε to make it conform with 477. Both forms are mentioned by Hesych. and in Et. Mag. The fondness of Ap. for weak aorists in ‐σσα would rather favour ἀθέρισσε in 477, but that line is quoted in Et. Mag. with ἀθέριξε (v. Rzach, p. 139).
: 'for he fain would bide with me in my distress.'
: 'drew near'; cf. h. Hom. Ap. 3, ἐπισχεδὸν ἐρχομένοιο. This adv. takes the dat. in 604, and the gen. in 1283.

div.p: Cf. Il. 3. 267, ὤρνυτο δ’ αὐτίκ’ ἔπειτα ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων )\Αν δ’ Ὀδυσεύς.

div.seg: : cf. Od. 5. 59; 19. 389. For the case-forms in ‐φι v. Monro, H.G. 154-8. This suffix was connected with Lat. -bi (ti-bi, u-bi), Skt. -bhyas, -bhyam.
: winds blowing at stated times of the year (ἔτος), especially northerly and north-easterly winds; cf. Arat. 150.

: 'blew strongly.' Only here is ἐπιχράω used absolutely. In Hom. it is found c. dat. 'to attack,' in which sense Ap. uses it c. gen., 283 supr. In 4. 508 we have it c. inf. = instare 'to be urgent,' δίζεσθαι ἐπέχραον, and in 3. 431 c. acc. et inf., ἥ με vεῖσθαι ἐπέχραεν.
: there seems no reason for preferring ἀνωγῇ, as many editors do. The succour (ἀρωγή) given by Zeus is described in 524 sqq.

: a daughter of the Peneius beloved by Apollo, who carried her off from Mt. Pelion to Libya, where she gave its name to Cyrene; cf. Pind. P. 9. 5, τὰν (sc. Κυράναν) ὁ χαιτάεις ἀνεμοσφαράγων ἐκ Παλίου κόλπων ποτὲ Λατοΐδας | ἅρπασ’ ἔνεγκέ τε χρυσέῳ παρθένον ἀγροτέραν δίφρῳ τόθι νιν πολυμήλου | καὶ πολυκαρποτάτας θῆκε δέσποιναν χθονὸς | ῥίζαν ἀπείρου τρίταν εὐήρατον θάλλοισαν οἰκεῖν.
: τῆς Θεσσαλίας, ἀπὸ Αἵμονος υἱοῦ Ἄρεως. Schol. Thessaly was called after Thessalus son of Haemon (Strab. 381, 11).
: ταῖς ἐγχωρίαις. Schol.; 'set her amongst the nymphs of the land.' Cf. 4. 1322.
: a headland in Cyrene; cf. Call. Ap. 90, στὰς ἐπὶ Μυρτούσσης κερατώδεος.

: cf. 4. 1132. The cult of Aristaeus was very widespread, not merely in Greece proper, but also in Magna Graecia and the islands of the Aegean, lonian, and Adriatic seas. His deliverance of Ceos from drought and pestilence is described also by Diodorus (4. 82). In Thessaly and Arcadia he was worshipped as the protector of flocks and bees, cf. Virg. G. 1. 14, 4. 283. Cicero, N.D. 3. 45, calls him inventor olivae, and the oil-press was said to have been devised by him. See the exhaustive article in Pauly-Wissowa, Real-Encycl.

: 'Hunter and Shepherd'; epithets of Apollo also, cf. Pind. P. 9. 63, θήσονταί τέ νιν ὰθάνατον, | Ζῆνα καὶ ἁγνὸν Ἀπόλλων’, ἀνδράσι χάρμα φίλοις, ἄγχιστον ὀπάονα μήλων, | Ἀγρέα καὶ Νόμιον, τοῖς δ’ Ἀρισταῖον καλεῖν.

div.p: 'for the god, through the love he bore her, made her a nymph of that land, bestowing upon her length of days and joy in the chase.'

div.seg: : Achilles and many other of the Greek heroes were pupils of Chiron, δικαιότατος Κενταύρων (Il. 11. 832).
: 'compassed a marriage for him'; cf. Call. Dian. 265, ἀγαθὸν γάμον ἐμνήστευσαν. The Muses wedded Aristaeus to Autonoe, daughter of Cadmus (Hes. Th. 975, Apollod. 3. 4. 2).

: 'watcher'; Hesych. ἤρανος· βασιλεύς, ἄρχων, σκοπός, φύλαξ. In Hom. we have ἐπιήρανος 'well-pleasing,' and after Hom. ἐπιήρανος was used for ἀμυντικός, βοηθός. On the connexion of these words with ἦρα v. Buttm. Lexil. 62.
: a plain in Phthiotis in Thessaly, called after Athamas the father of Phrixus and Helle (Strab. 371, 47).
: a mountain range in Phthiotis, cf. Hes. Th. 632.
: the Cyclades; cf. Thuc. 1. 4, Μίνως … τῶν Κυκλάδων νήσων ἦρξέ τε καὶ οἰκιστὴς πρῶτος τῶν πλείστων ἐγένετο, κ.τ.λ.
: the parching heat of the 'Dog-days' is often referred to, e.g. Hes. Sc. 397, ὁπότε χρόα Σείριος ἄζει.
: mod. Zea. The story is commemorated on the coins of Ceos by a head of Aristaeus and a representation of Sirius, v. Head, op. cit. 482.
: i.e. Arcadian, cf. Il. 2. 608. There was a district Παρρασική (Thuc. 5. 33) on the frontiers of Messene.
: a king of Arcadia, cf. Paus. 8. 2. 1.

: 'god of rain (ἰκμάς)';
cf. Ζεὺς ὑέτιος, Arist. Mund. 7. 2:
Aen. 9. 670,
Iuppiter horridus austris
Torquet aquosam hiemem et caelo cava nubila rumpit.
: 'cool'; cf. Od. 4. 568, ἀήτας Ὠκεανὸς ἀνίησιν ἀναψύχειν ἀνθρώπους.

div.p: Cf. Diod. 4. 82, γενομένης δὲ τῆς θυσίας κατὰ τὴν τοῦ Σειρίου ἄστρου ἐπιτολήν, καθ’ ἣν συνέβαινε πνεῖν τοὺς ἐτησίας, λῆξαι τὰς λοιμικὰς νόσους.

div.seg: : 'are told of,' cf. 4. 264. It is an Alexandrian word, cf. Call. Jov. 76, αὐτίκα χαλκῆας μὲν ὑδείομεν Ἡφαίστοιο. Curtius compares the root of ἀείδ‐ω, ἀηδ‐ών, Skt. vad-ami.
: kept back by the Etesian winds which were contrary (498).

: Zeus, Hera, Poseidon, Demeter, Hermes, Hephaestus, Apollo, Artemis, Hestia, Ares, Aphrodite, Athene. The place where the altar was
built was afterwards called Ἱερόν; cf. Polyb. 4. 39, Dem. Lept. 29.

: i.e. the opposite (Asiatic) coast, distant about 4 stades. They had anchored on the Thracian shore where the Bosporus joins the Euxine, 176 supr. The sailing across is not mentioned, but πέρην implies it. This is Buttmann's view (Lexil. 91), and it is the most probable one. de M. explains, "au delà de la demeure de Phinée, plus près de la mer, d'où il pourra être aperçu par les navigateurs," but πέρην could hardly have this meaning. Brunck held that πέρην must mean πέλας, or else must be changed to πάρος or πέλας.

: cf.
Aen. 1. 130, nec latuere doli fratrem Iunonis.

div.p:
'As when one wanders from his country (as we poor mortals are often doomed to roam), and there is no land
distant (to his mind) but all ways are visible (to his mind's eye), he perceiveth in his thoughts his own home, and the way thither over land and sea alike flashes upon him; now this way, and now that, his fancy swiftly flies, and he striveth to behold it with his eyes.' This remarkable simile, in which we can trace the yearning of the Alexandrian exile, is an amplification of Il. 15. 80, ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἂν ἀίξῃ νόος ἀνέρος ὅς τ’ ἐπὶ πολλὴν Γαῖαν ἐληλουθὼς φρεσὶ πευκαλίμῃσι νοήσῃ "ἔνθ· εἴην ἢ ἔνθα" μενοινήῃσί τε πολλά.

div.seg: : from the words of the Schol., ἀλλὰ καὶ πάσας καταφανεῖς πόλεις, Merkel would restore πόληες, and it is certainly unlike the finished workmanship of Ap. to have two successive lines ending with the same word; yet cf. 1. 375-6.

: Wellauer points out that unless we omit δέ we have an anacoluthon after ἀλώμενος in 541; it would seem to be one of those cases in which the δέ of an apodosis repeats the δέ (541) with which the whole sentence was introduced, v. Monro, H.G. 334.

: cf.
Aen. 4. 285, atque animum nunc huc celerem, nunc dividit illuc.
: cf. Strab. 265, 28, ἥ τε Θυνιάς … καὶ Φινόπολις … συνάπτουσαι τῷ Σαλμυδησσῷ· ἔστι δ’ οὗτος ἔρημος αἰγιαλὸς καὶ λιθώδης, ἀλίμενος, ἀναπεπταμένος πολὺς πρὸς τοὺς Βορέας.
: 'surged up against'; only here c. acc.
: 'smote their ears unceasingly.' The deriv. of νωλεμές is uncertain. Düntzer connects it with ὀλ, ὄλλυμι 'imperishably'; Nitzsch with *ολέω, αἰόλλω 'immovably'; Fick with ἠρέμα (νη‐ορεμές).
: 'rowed with a will'; θελήμων is used by Ap. alone, cf. 4. 1657. ἐθελήμων occurs in Plat. Crat. 406 A.

: only here c. gen. 'saw last of all men' (not with οἰγομένας 'for the last time of all' as they open again a few lines later). It was ordained that the rocks should
remain fixed for ever once a ship had passed between them (605).
: cf. Il. 24. 358, σὺν δὲ γέροντι νόος χύτο.
: 'the boiling foam rose in clouds,' cf. βρασσόμενον, 323. Virg. has imitated this whole passage in the description of the storm, Aen. 1. 104 sqq.
: 'and high on the cliff was dashed the spume of the raging billow.'
: for the metaph. use cf. Soph. Ant. 1009, κηκὶς … ἔτυφε κἀνέπτυε.
: sc. πέτραι. As the dove lost its tail-feathers, so the Argo lost the carving on its stern (601).
: 'till the returning wave with its rush bore them within the rocks.' The clashing of the rocks had forced out a volume of water which rushed back when the rocks parted.

: 'easing' the ship,
which was labouring under the strain of the oars.
κ.τ.λ.: οὕτω φησίν, ἐπῆρεν τὸ κῦμα τὴν ναῦν ὡς καὶ ὑπὲρ τὰς πέτρας αὐτὴν γενέσθαι. Schol.

div.p:
Cf.
Aen. 5. 188,
At media socios incedens nave per ipsos
Hortatur Mnestheus: nunc, nunc insurgite remis.

div.seg: : 'as far as the ship would yield to the rowers, twice as far did it leap back at once' i.e. when they made a little way with the oars, the force of the waves carried them back twice as far. For ἄν with iterative secondary tenses v. Monro, H. G. 324.
: cf. Il. 13. 134, ἔγχεα δὲ πτύσσοντο θρασειάων ἀπὸ χειρῶν: Cat. 64. 183, lentos incurvans gurgite remos.
: cf. Eur. Bacch. 1066, κυκλοῦτο δ’ ὥστε τόξον.

: from Od. 5. 367. The passage is well rendered by Way, "On-rushing, up-towering, a breaker came, overarched like a cave; But suddenly light as a roller she rode the furious wave. Forward through yawning gulfs she plunged; but caught was her prow By a whirlpool sea-rush betwixt the Clashers."

: ἅπ. λεγ. See
on 95 supr. Another new compound with προπρο‐ is προπροβιαζόμενοι (1. 386) on the analogy of προπροκυλινδόμενος in Hom.
: Ap. alone uses Πληγάδες for Συμπληγάδες, cf. 645.
: 'were held fast,' i.e. the Argo could make no way on account of the current (ῥόος, 571).

: τῆς πέτρας ὰντελάβετο καὶ κατεσχε. Schol. "Then did Athene backward thrust one massy rock With her left hand, touching their bark with her right to speed her through" (Way). For ἀντισπάω 'to pull in an opposite direction' cf. Aesch. Pr. 337, ὁρμώμενον δὲ μηδαμῶς ὰντισπάσης. Only here c. gen. Most edd. supply νήια δοῦρα as obj., 'snatched the vessel away from the rock which was holding it fast.' Such a constr. is also unique, and the use of the sing. πέτρης is a strong objection to this view. Val. Fl. makes both Hera and Pallas hold the rocks apart while the vessel passed through. For the agency of Hera cf. 4. 786; Od. 12. 71, καί νύ κε τὴν ἔνθ’ ὦκα βάλεν μεγάλας ποτὶ πέτρας Ἀλλ’ Ἤρη παρέπεμψεν, ἐπεὶ φίλος ἦεν Ἰήσων.
: we have ἔωσαν, 4. 104; so ἔαξε, 2. 1109, but ἆξεν, 1. 1168.

: imitated in
Aen. 5. 214,
Et pater ipse manu magna Portunus euntem
Impulit. Illa noto citius volucrique sagitta
Ad terram fugit
; also in Aen. 10. 246 sqq.

div.p: Cf. Val. Fl. 4. 691, Saxa sed extremis tamen increpuere corymbis, Parsque (nefas) deprensa iugis. For ἀφλάστοιο κόρυμβα see note to 1.1089.
div.seg: : 'cut off as the vessel passed,' ἅπ. λεγ. We find the syncopated ἔθρισεν (θερίζὠ in Aesch. Ag. 541.

: 'immovably,' see note to 554 The use of the word here after its occurrence in 602 has roused suspicions. From νωλεμενές (a corruption in Vind.) Brunck read ἐμμενές, and Merkel suggested νωχελές, but no change seems necessary.

: "Nemo ante Iasonem Cyaneas interius vidit; et ipsae 'nondum ullas videre rates' (Val. Fl. 4. 563)" Hoelzlin. It cannot mean 'living,' as some have taken it, for this would require a present participle
: 'as well as the ship,' see note to 1.502. de M. translates "grâce au navire."
: 'easy to contend with (πάλη).' The word is used only by Ap.; cf. εὐπαλέως, 4. 193. δυσπαλής is much more common.

div.p:
Similarly Agamemnon in Il. 2. 110 sqq. pretends to repent of the
expedition, and advises the Greeks to return home.

div.seg: : 'in defiance of' 'in sheer opposition to.' In Hom. this prep. means 'sheer down from,' e.g. Od. 10. 559, καταντικρὺ τέγεος πέσεν.
: ἀντὶ τοῦ ἀνηλεῶς καὶ κατὰ μέλος κατακοπτόμενος καὶ κατατεμνόμενος (Et. Mag. 603, 28). κεδαίω = κεδάννυμι, a late Gr. form: Ap. also uses κεδόωνται (κεδάομαἰ, 4. 500.

: 'I have laid on me as a burden.' ἀνατίθημι is used of heaping a thing on a person, e.g. Il. 22. 100, Πουλυδάμας μοι πρῶτος ἐλεγχείην ἀναθήσει, and so ἄγκειμαι is here used as the passive. For the acc. cf. Eur. Supp. 717, ἐπικείμενον κάρα κυνέας: Ar. Pax 542, κυάθους προσκείμεναι.

div.p:
'as each day endeth, I watch in
anguish through the night'; cf. Od. 22. 195, νύκτα φυλάξεις.

div.seg: : ἀντὶ ἐμαυτοῦ. Schol. We find εἷο in its ordinary sense as 3 sing. refl. in 4. 460; see note to 1.362.
: 'for this man and for that'; cf. Hdt. 4. 68. ἐπιώοκηκε ὃς καὶ ὅς: Dem. 21. 141, τὰ καὶ τὰ πεπονθώς.
: Ion. for βαράθρων 'chasms,' cf Il. 8. 14, τῆλε μάλ’ ᾗχι βάθιστον ὑπὸ χθονός ἐστι βέρεθρον: Plat. Phaed. 112.
: 'shall I let fear get hold of me,' literally 'attach to myself fear.'
: ἄκρα οὕτω καλουμένη περὶ τὸν Λύκον ποταμόν· μέμνηται αὐτῆς Νύμφις ὁ Ἡρακλεώτης ἐν τῷ περὶ Ἡρακλείας. Schol.
: the comp. παρεκνέομαι is peculiar to Ap., cf. 941, 1243.

: i.e. Phrixus. According to the legend, Athamas married Nephele by the command of Hera, and she bore him Phrixus and Helle. He was, however, really enamoured of the mortal Ino, by whom he begat Melicertes. Nephele, in her jealousy, returned to the gods and tried to compass the ruin of Athamas. When famine broke out in the land, Ino bribed the messengers to Delphi to bring back an oracle that Phrixus must be sacrificed. Nephele rescued Phrixus and Helle, and sent them to Colchis on the ram with the golden fleece.
: 'meadownymph,' cf. Soph. Ph. 1454, νύμφαι τ’ ἔνυδροι λειμωνιάδες: Il. 20. 8, νυμφάων, αἳ … νέμονται … πίσεα ποιήεντα.
: the Calpe (or Calpas, Strab. 465, 20) was a river of Bithynia. There was also a port of Calpe, midway between Byzantium and Heraclea, which Xenophon mentions on the retreat ( Anab. 6. 4).
κ.τ.λ.: cf. Od. 10. 28, ἐννῆμαρ μὲν ὁμῶς πλέομεν νύκτας τε καὶ ἦμαρ.
: 'worked hard at the oars'; cf. Od. 20. 107, μύλαις δώδεκα πᾶσαι ἐπερρώοντο γυναῖκες. We have this verb also in 677, and in 1. 385, and the simple ῥώομαι (cf. ruo) in 4. 942.
: ἔνυγρον ἔτι οὖσαν. Schol. πεπλαδηκώς· σεσηπώς, ὑγρανθείς. Hesych. The word is prosaic, and is often used by Hippocrates of flaccid or flabby flesh. Cf. πλαδαρός, 3. 1398.
: this verb is ἅπ. λεγ.; cf. Nic. Th. 758, παρέστραπται δὲ καὶ ὄσσε.
: 'the dry breath comes in loud gasps from their mouths.' For ἄμοτον see note to 1.513.
: this absolute use for ὀρφναίη νύξ is only found here.
: cf. Il. 7. 433, ἦμος δ’ οὔτ’ ἄρ πω ἠώς, ἔτι δ’ ἀμφιλύκη νύξ, with Leaf's note. ἀμφι‐ denotes 'half' light, cf. twilight, Zwielicht. For the vague μιν see note to 1.941.

: cf. 1. 309. Jebb, on Soph. Phil. 1461, suggests that the name of the country Lycia was derived from the cult of Apollo Λύκιος 'the god of light'; so too the epithet λυκηγενής applied to Apollo in Il. 4. 101 may mean 'born of, or in, light.'

: not mentioned in Hom., but in the poems of the Epigoni
and Hesiod (Hdt. 4. 32). They dwelt beyond the northern blast, favoured by the Sun-god, in blissful serenity in a fruitful land; cf. Pind. P. 10. 56 sqq. The worship of Apollo was by some derived from them. The oracle of Delphi was founded by them (Paus. 10. 5. 4), and Leto came from the Hyperboreans to Delos (Hdt. 4. 33, Paus. 1. 18. 4); so too Diodorus (2. 47) says that they worshipped Apollo more zealously than any other people, being all, as it were, priests of Apollo.
: properly used of clustering grapes, cf. Anth. P. 5. 287, βότρυς χαίτης: Milton, P. L. iv. 301, 'hyacinthine locks Round from his parted forelock manly hung Clustering.'
: 'floated,' see note to 661 Cf. Il. 1. 529, ἀμβρόσιαι δ’ ἄρα χαῖται ἐπερρώσαντο ἄνακτος Κοατὸς ἀπ’ ἀθανάτοιο.
: cf. Il. 13. 18, τρέμε δ’ οὔρεα μακρὰ καὶ ὕλη Ποσσὶν ὑπ’ ἀθανάτοισι Ποσειδάωνος ἰόντος. See also on 3. 1218.

: Ἡρόδωρος οὖν φησιν Ἑῷον Ἀπόλλωνα προσαγορεύεσθαι καὶ βωμὸν αὐτοῦ εἶναι ἐν τῇ νήσῳ, οὐ καθὸ ὄρθρου ἐφάνη αὐτοῖς, ἀλλὰ καθὸ οἱ Ἀργοναῦται ὄρθρου εἰς αὐτὴν κατέπλευσαν. Schol. Ἑώιος for ἑῷος is only found in Ap., cf. 700. The Homeric form is ἠοῖος; see note to 4.841.

: 'be gracious,' cf. Od. 3. 380. Ap. also uses ἵλαθι (4. 1014), and ἵλατε (4. 984), which represent the regular formation from the stem ἱλα, and are found in Callimachus (e.g. Cer. 139). We also find ἱλάεσθαι (2. 847), ἱλάσκονται (1. 1139), ἱλήκοις (2. 708).

: λίθοις μικροῖς. Schol. L. and S. wrongly explain 'large blocks of stone,' as χερμάς, like the Homeric χερμάδιον, means strictly a stone that can be grasped by the hand, cf. Il. 16. 735,
πετρος … τόν οἱ περὶ χεὶρ ἐκάλυψεν. For a similar altar v. 1170 infr.
: versabantur; cf. Od. 9. 153, ἐδινεόμεσθα κατ’ αὐτὴν (νῆσον).

: κεμάς· ἡ νέα ἔλαφος. Schol.: cf. Il. 10. 361: Et. Mag. 503, 7, διαφορὰν δέ φασιν εἶναι κεμάδος καὶ νεβροῦ. κεμάδα γὰρ εἶναι τὴν ἐπικοιμωμένην τῷ σπηλαίῳ νεβρὸν δὲ τὸν μείζονα καὶ ἐπὶ βορὰν νεμόμενον. Ap. uses the word again in 3. 879, 4. 12.
: Od. 9. 158, αἶψα δ’ ἔδωκε θεὸς μενοεικέα θήρην.

: i.e. thigh-bones wrapped in a double layer of fat, δίπλαξ δημός (Il. 23. 243); cf. 1. 434. The Schol. suggests another explanation, ὅτι δύο εἰσίν. For the difference between the forms μηροί, μῆρα, and μηρία, see M. and R. on Od. 3. 456.

: cf. h. Hom. Ap. 272, ἀλλ’ ἀκέων προσάγοιεν Ἰηπαίηονι δῶρα. Apollo was invoked with the cry
ἰὴ παιών or ἰὼ παιάν, 'Praise to the Healer'; cf Call. Ap. 21, Soph. Tr. 221, O. T. 154 (ἰήιος). Aristoph. has ἰηπαιωνίζω,
Eq. 408 . καλόν is probably an adv. as in Il. 1. 473, καλόν ἀείδοντες παιήονα.

: the dragon guarding the shrine at Delphi, slain by Apollo. It is doubtful whether the nom. is Δελφύνης or Δελφύνη. Callimachus makes it fem. (fr. 364), and also Dion. P. (442). If it is feminine in our passage, πελώριος must be of two terminations as in Hes. Th. 179. The dragon was usually called Python.
: probably 'beardless,' a meaning only found here; cf. Hesych. γυμνή· ἄνηβος, Lat. investis. Others explain it literally as 'naked.' Schneider suggested τυννός, infans.
: cf. Φοῖβος ἀκερσεκόμης Il. 20. 39. Ennius has 'crinitus Apollo' (Fab. 247, Mueller).
: Leto was the daughter of the Titan Coeus, cf. Hes. Th. 404.
: Κωρύκιον ἄντρον ἐν Παρνασσῷ. Schol.; cf. Sandys on Eur. Bacch. 559.
: cheered him on in his struggle with the dragon; cf. Varro Atac. fr. 5, Te nunc Coryciae tendentem spicula nymphae Hortantes 'O Phoebe' et 'ieie' conclamarunt.

div.p: 'and thence this fair refrain in honour of Phoebus had its birth'; cf. Call. Ap. 96, ἰὴ, ἰὴ Παιῆον; ακούομεν, οὕνεκα τοῦτο Δελφός τοι πρώτιστον ἐφύμνιον εὕρετο λαός.

div.seg: : μέλπω included both song and dance, e.g. Il. 1. 471.
: 'with holy libations'; dat. of attendant circumstances.
: Dio Cass. (49. 18) uses Ὁμονοεῖον = templum Concordiae.
: cf. Od. 2. 421, ἀκραῆ Ζέφυρον, where M. and R. explain ἀκραῆ 'a wind that sets exactly in the right quarter'; Hesych. ἀκραῆ· ἄκρως πνέοντα, οὔτε σφοδρῶς, οὔτε ἐλλειπόντως.
: a large river flowing from Phrygia through Bithynia into the Euxine; cf. Il. 3. 187, Ov. P. 4. 10. 47 (where it is called Sagaris).
: a river in Bithynia bearing the same name as the king of the Mariandyni (v. 752); cf. Xen. An. 6. 2. 3.
: the Schol. says that the name of this marsh was derived from the daughter of king Lycus.
: the ropes of the sail (see note to 1.1276); ὅπλα is a general term for the tackle.
: through this headland the Acheron discharged itself into the sea; v. 355.
: 'wide-spreading.' This epithet is applied to the plane-tree in Plat. Phaedr. 230 b, πλάτανος … ἀμφιλαφής τε καὶ ὑψηλή. For other uses v. 4. 983, 1366.
: cf. Od. 7. 128, παντοῖαι πεφύασιν ἐπηετανὸν γανόωσαι.

div.p: 'and from this headland, and away from the base of it, a hollow glen runs sloping inward from the coast.' ὕπαιθα is difficult: I take it in the Homeric sense 'from under.' One of the explanations given by the Schol. is ἐκ πλαγίου, and, apparently on the strength of this, Lehrs translates 'cava ex obliquo convallis'; de M., 'à l'intérieur, tournée vers le continent, se creuse obliquement une vallée où est l'antre d'Adès.'

div.seg: : Virg. imitates this passage in describing the cave of Avernus, Aen. 6. 237.

: 'maketh the hoarfrost
congeal about it.' In Hom. the passive is used, e.g. Od. 14. 477, σακέεσσι περιτρέφετο κρύσταλλος. For the quantity of συνεχές see note to 1.1271.
: 'bluff.' In Hom. only used of the 'grim' appearance of human beings. Curtius connects it with βλάστη, βλωθρός, so that the primary meaning would be 'big,' 'burly.'
: the breezes from the recesses of the chasm of Hades.

: 'the eastern sea,' i.e. the Pontus. Though this reading is defended by the schol., εἰς τὴν πρὸς ἀνατολὰς θάλασσαν, Merkel would read either Ἠοίην, as the name of the gulf into which the Acheron discharges, or Ἰονίην (v. 4. 289).
: 'Saviour of sailors,' ἅπ. λεγ. Pliny, N.H. 6. 1, also calls the Acheron 'Sonautes.'

: Nisaea was the port of Megara; cf. Theocr. 12. 27, Νισαῖοι Μεγαρῆες ἀριστεύοντες ἐρετμοῖς. The epithet is added to distinguish the Megarians from their colonists in Hyblaean Megara in Sicily (Thuc. 6. 4). The Megarians, along with the Tanagraeans from Boeotia, founded
Heraclea Pontica on the coasts of the Mariandyni (Paus. 5. 26. 6). Sailing thither the colonists were caught in a storm and took refuge in the Acheron.

div.p: 'thither the sailors ran straight in with their vessel through the Acherusian promontory.' The meaning and derivation of εἰσωποί in Il. 15. 653, εἰσωποὶ δ’ ἐγένοντο νεῶν, are quite uncertain (v. Leaf). In our passage the meaning seems to be 'straight forward.' The Schol. explains: ἐναντίοι, ἐσώτεροι γενόμενοι. If the meaning in Il. l.c. is that they had the ships before their faces, i.e. got behind them, the meaning here may be that they ran in behind the promontory. Way translates, "Through the gorge of the cape Acherusian ran the heroes their prow, And seawardfacing abode."

div.seg: : this correction is necessary as ὁρμηθέντες cannot mean advecti. The corruption was due to 537 supr.
: οἱ φονευταί. Schol.; cf. Hdt. 1. 117. Soph. uses the form αὐτοέντης, O.T. 107. For the termination ‐εντης cf. Hesych. συνέντης· συνεργός.
: 'they established friendship'; cf. Call. fr. 199, ἀρθμὸν δ’ ἀμφοτέροις καὶ φιλίην ἔταμον: h. Hom. Merc. 524.
: the city. The Schol. wrongly says, τὸν βασιλέα φησίν, οὐ τὴν πόλιν. Κίον: see note to 1.1177.
: for ἀβολέω = ἀντιβολέω 'meet' cf. 3. 1145, Call. fr. 455, ἀβάλε (= utinam) μηδ’ ἀβόλησαν.

: for the unusual causal
dative cf. 1. 449. Hom. has the gen., e.g. Il. 8. 124, Ἔκτορα δ’ αἰνὸν ἄχος πύκασε φρένας ἡνιόχοιο.

: the queen of the Amazons had received the girdle from Ares, and when the daughter of Eurystheus coveted it, Heracles was sent in quest of it. In 966 sqq. we are told how he won it; cf. also Eur. H.F. 407, Diod. 4. 16, Hdt. 4. 9, 10.
: 'at the time of the death of.'
: θρήνοις· τὰ γὰρ ἐλεγεῖα ἐπὶ ἐπιτυμβίοις ἐχρῶντο οἱ παλαιοί. Schol. The word was not used earlier than the fifth century, and was generally derived from ἒ ἒ λέγειν 'to cry woe! woe!' Eur. I.T. 146.
: i.e. at the funeral games, cf. 1. 1304.
: οἱ μέν φασι Διὸς παῖδα, ἕνα τῶν Ἰδαίων Δακτύλων (1. 1126), οἱ δὲ τὸν πρεσβύτατον τῶν Μαριανδυνοῦ παιδων. ὁ δὲ Μαριανδυνὸς Φινέως ἢ Φρίξου ἢ Κιμμερίου λέγεται παῖς εἶναι. Schol.
: 'in like fashion'; others explain 'without resistance,' ultro.
: a river of Bithynia, mod. Filyás.

div.p: 'have despoiled me, while H. was far off, gradually cutting away large slices of my kingdom.'

div.seg: : 'boundary-stones' (= ὅροι). In Hom. οὖρον is a measure of distance, e.g. Il. 10. 351, οὖρα … ἡμιόνων (v. Leaf), 23. 431, δίσκου οὖρα. Ap. was thinking of Il. 22. 489, ἀπουρίσσουσιν ἀρούρας.

: 'low-lying marshy meadows,' καθύγροις τόποις. Schol.; cf. Il. 4. 483, Theocr. 25. 16. From Theocr. 13. 40, ἡμένῳ ἐν χώρῳ, the word has been usually connected with sedere. Buttm. connects it with ἠιών, Classen with ἕννυμι (i.e. well-watered meadows clad with verdure).
: Scylax mentions this river as the boundary between the territory of the Bithyni and Mariandyni.

: cf.
Aen. 2. 777, non haec sine numine divum Eveniunt.
: 'weak'; (1) from ἀπέδον 'not standing firm,' (2) a lengthening of ἤπιος, cf. οὐτιδανός.
: 'as one of your company'; cf. Soph. O.T. 212, Βάκχον … Μαινάδων ὁμόστολον. The constr. c. dat. is peculiar to Ap., cf. 3. 558.
: = usque ad; a unique use of ὄφρα.
: a fut. mid. from ἵζω only found here.
: a rare Dor. fut. for ἱλάσονται or ἱλάσσονται, see note to 693
: cf. Il. 13. 602, τὸν δ’ ἄγε μοῖρα κακὴ θανάτοιο τέλοσδε.
: haunting the marshes or meadows (λειμωνιάδες), see note to 655

: the 'risings' either
in the uneven bed of the river or along its banks. It means rising ground also in Il. 10. 160, ἐπὶ θρωσμῷ πεδίοιο.

: this form is interesting as showing that Ap. regarded the Homeric ἀνέπαλτο (ἀνεπᾶλτὀ, Il. 8. 85, 20. 424, etc., as coming, not from ἀναπάλλομαι, as is generally assumed from Il. 23. 692, but from ἀνεφάλλουαι.

div.p: Cf. Il. 13. 546, οὔτασ’ ἐπαΐξας, ἀπὸ δὲ φλέβα πᾶσαν ἔκερσεν.

div.seg: : as this verb in Hom. takes the dat. of the weapon with which the thrust is made, Merkel restored αἰγανέῃ; cf. Il. 4. 307, ἔγχει ὀρεξάσθω.
: adv. 'in flight,' cf. Il. 11. 446, φύγαδ’ … ὑποστρέψας. The adj. φυγάς is not epic.
: cf. 3. 543, ἀφλάστῳ περικάππεσεν: Soph. Aj. 828, πεπτῶτα περὶ ξίφει.
: cf. Eur. Alc. 19, ἣ νῦν κατ’ οἴκους ἐν χεροῖν βαστάζεται Ψυχορραγοῦσα.

: cf. Eur.
Heracl. 560, σῇ γὰρ ἐνθανεῖν χερὶ Θέλω. Ap. forms several new compounds with ἐγκατα viz. ἐγκαταβάλλω, ‐θνήσκω, ‐λέγω, ‐ναίω, ‐πίπτω.
: this constr. is only found here, and is on the analogy of κωλύεσθαι c. inf.

: prae dolore, v.n. 96; so the Schol. κηδείῃ: τῷ πένθει τῷ περὶ τοῦ νεχροῦ. L. and S., with most editors, translate it 'funeral' here. Homer uses κῆδος for grief for a dead comrade, e.g. Il. 22. 272, κήδε’ ἐμῶν ἑτάρων (mourning for them).
: = μεγαλοπρεπῶς. For this usage, foreign to Homer, cf. Hdt. 6. 70, ὁ δὲ ὑπεδέξατο αὐτὸν μεγαλωστί.
: offerings at his tomb. In Od. 2. 99 ταφήιον φᾶρος is a winding-sheet.
: 'a barrow was raised'; cf. Il. 7. 336, τύμβον … χεύομεν.

κ.τ.λ.: cf. Il. 7. 86, σῆμά
τέ οἱ χεύωσιν ἐπὶ πλατεῖ Ἑλλησπόντῳ· Καὶ ποτέ τις εἴπῃσι καὶ ὀψιγόνων ἀνθρώπων Νηὶ πολυκλήιδι πλέων ἐπὶ οἴνοπα πόντον. See also 4. 252.

: 'a ship's roller of wild olive wood.' For κοτίνοιο see note to 34 For φάλαγξ see note to 1.375. We have ἐκ denoting material again in 3. 1325 and in Il. 22. 152, ἐξ ὕδατος κρυστάλλῳ. The Schol. says that it was one of the rollers used at the launching of the Argo which was now set up as a σῆμα. Merkel needlessly reads νήιος, as the hypallage is quite justifiable, cf. 4. 4, etc. de M. thinks that it was the trunk of a wild olive cut into the shape of a φάλαγξ, arguing that it was improbable that the Argonauts would carry these rollers with them, as they had not even a spare oar to replace that broken by Heracles (1. 1170); v. Seaton. Cl. Rev. x. 169. The general notion of the σῆμα is derived from Od. 12. 14, where an oar is set up over the barrow of Elpenor.
: 'if this too I must declare unswervingly as the minister of the Muses.' See on 1. 22.
: here used like βαλέσθαι, 'to lay the foundations.'

div.p: The inhabitants of Heraclea were bidden by an oracle of Apollo to make offerings to their πολισσοῦχος (guardian of the city) who was buried there. They, not knowing that the tomb was the tomb of Idmon, and believing that it was the tomb of Agamestor, a local hero, made offerings to him.
For this form of question addressed to the Muses who prompt his song cf. 1090.

div.seg: : 'brief'; in Hom. usually an epithet of men 'shortlived.' Cf 3. 690.
: here, and in 4. 1060, Ap. uses εὐνάζω, elsewhere εὐνάω.

: ἐν ὅσῳ ἔθαψαν τὸν Ἴδμονα, ἐν τοσούτῳ καὶ ὁ Τῖφυς νοσήσας ἐτελεύτησεν. Schol. This use of εἰσότε is very strained; in 4. 800, 1212 it has its normal meaning 'until.' In Od. 2. 99 εἰς ὅτε means 'against the time when.'

: 'in very truth': cf. Il.
15. 488, δὴ γὰρ ἴδον ὀφθαλμοῖσι.
: 'in silence.' The adv. is ἅπ. λεγ., for the adj. see note to 935
: 'were downcast in spirit.' L. and S. unnecessarily assume that the verb is trans. here. The compound is peculiar to Ap., and is intrans. in 3. 1400.
: for ἀπό 'away from' cf. ἀπὸ θυμοῦ, 253.

div.p: 'still further would they have been stayed in their anguish.'

div.seg: : ἀντὶ τοῦ διαφερόντως. Schol.; cf. Il. 16. 699, περιπρὸ γὰρ ἔγχεϊ θῦεν. For the accentuation of such forms as περιπρό, ἀποπρό, διαπρό, ἐπιπρό, v. La Roche, Textkr. p. 200.
: 'heedless of our emprise'; see note to 98
: ἐπιίστωρ has three meanings in Ap.: (1) peritus, here and in 4. 1558, (2) conscius, 4. 16, cf. Od. 21. 26, (3) testis, 4. 89.
: the Alexandrian use of ἰάπτειν iacĕre in the sense of βλάπτειν is never found in Homer.
: 'using all these words of exhortation'; cf. παραιφασίῃσι, 324.
: 'his heart bounded with joy,' or 'went out to him in his joy'; cf. ὀρέχθει, 49.
: for the constr. cf. 326, 4. 1261, Il. 3. 417. We find the dat. in 4. 401, ὀλοίμεθα πάντες ὀλέθρῳ. Gerhard and Wellauer regard this line as a survival from the first recension.

div.p: Cf. Il. 7. 73, ὑμῖν μὲν γὰρ ἔασιν ἀριστῆες Παναχαιῶν· Τῶν νῦν ὅν τινα θυμὸς ἐμοὶ μαχέσασθαι ἀνώγει, κ.τ.λ. If we retain μὲν of the mss., which is supported by the Homeric parallel, we must eject line 881, but ἐν seems to be required by the constr.

div.seg: : for the gen. cf. Od. 2. 404, μὴ δηθὰ διατρίβωμεν ὁδοῖο.

: cf. Il. 9. 517, μῆνιν ἀπορρίψαντα:
Aen. 1. 202, revocate animos, maestumque timorem Mittite.
: for this use of δέ in the apodosis cf. 1. 681.

div.p: 'wherefore I forebode for us a doom as dire as that of the dead.' For προτιόσσομαι see note to 1.895.

div.seg: : according to Herodorus it was Erginus who took the helm after the death of Tiphys; so too Val. Fl. (5. 65) says that the oaken beam of the Argo demanded that he should succeed.
: Ap. here uses the dat. with αἰνέω on the analogy of ἐπαινέω 'to approve of,' e.g. Il. 18. 312, Ἔκτορι μὲν γὰρ ἐπῄνησαν. When it means 'to praise' it takes the acc., 4. 503, 748.
: a river in Paphlagonia; cf. Val. Fl. 5. 73, Inde, premente noto, tristes Acherusidos oras Praeterit et festa vulgatum nocte Lyaei Callichoron.

: the mountain Nysa, from which Dionysus was supposed to have derived his name, was variously placed in Thrace, Libya, India, etc., wherever the worship of the god prevailed; v. Sandys on Eur. Bacch. 556.
