: cf. Arrian, Indica 5, καὶ πρὸ Ἀλεξάνὸρου Διονύσου μὲν πέρι πολλὸς λόγος κατέχει ὡς καὶ τούτου στρατεύσαντος ἐς Ἰνδοὺς καὶ καταστρεψαμένου Ἰνδούς, κ.τ.λ.: Diod. 2. 38: Prop. 3. 17. 22, Indica Nysaeis arma fugata choris.
: for the worship of Dionysus at Thebes v. Eur. Bacchae; Verrall, The Bacchants of Euripides; Norwood, The Riddle of the Bacchae.
: ἤτοι φοβερὰς διὰ τὰ μυστήρια τοῦ θεοῦ, ἢ ὅτι φοβεραί εἰσιν αἱ νύκτες. Εὐριπίδης ( Bacch. 486), Νύκτωρ τὰ πολλὰ σεμνότητ’ ἔχει σκότος. Schol.

: 'the Resting Place'; cf. Amm. Marc. 22. 8. 22, Aulion antrum est, et fluenta Callichori ex facto cognominati quod superatis post triennium Indicis nationibus, ad eos tractus Liber reversus, circa huins ripas virides et opacas orgia pristina reparavit et choros.

div.p:
Of this account of Sthenelus the
Schol. says: τὴν δὲ περὶ τοῦ Σθενέλου τᾴφου ἱστορίαν ἔλαβε παρὰ Προμαθίδα, τὰ δὲ περὶ τοῦ εἰδώλου αὐτὸς ἐπλασεν. See Introd., p. 22.

Cf. Val. Fl. 5. 89, Sthenelus, qualem Mavortia vidit Amazon Cumque suis comitem Alcides ut condidit armis, Talis ab aequorei consurgens aggere busti Emicuit. For Heracles' encounter with the Amazons v. 778, 966.

div.seg: : the Homeric form is Περσεφόνεια. Pindar first uses Φερσεφόνα. For the various forms v. Jebb on Soph. Ant. 894, where the name is explained as "she who brings (vegetation) to the light (φαν)."
: in Il. 13. 138 used of the brow of a hill.

: the meaning of this word in Hom. is quite uncertain. Autenrieth explains it "with the crest fashioned in four ridges or bands"; Leaf (Il. Vol. 1, App. B) says that the φάλοι were metallic projections, survivals of the horns which formed an ornament on the helmet of the primitive peoples on the coasts of the Mediterranean. Cf. τρυφαλείας, 1060.

: Merkel defends this against
μέλαν by comparing μέγας αἰθήρ, 2. 567, μέγας βυθός, 4. 1618.

: ἁγνίζειν meant to purify the corpse by the rites which religion required (v. Jebh, Soph. Ant. 545); then from giving the corpse the rite of fire it came to mean 'to burn' as here; cf. Eur. Suppl. 1211, ἵν’ αὐτῶν σώμαθ’ ἡγνίσθη πυρι.
: cf. Val. Fl. 5. 100, Odrysius dux (i.e. Orpheus) ... Percutit ... lyram nomenque relinquit harenis.

: the sheet-lines, see note to 1.566-7, 1276-7. Cf.
Aen. 5. 830,
Una omnes fecere pedem, pariterque sinistros,
Nunc dextros solvere sinus.

div.p: "setting its wings to the blast it is borne swiftly on, and there is no tremor in its flight, as it floats serenely on its motionless pinions."
div.seg: : the flat surface of the outspread wings, cf. Anth. P. 12. 144, διφυῆ ταρσὸν ἀνεὶς πτερύγων.
: used also of setting sails, Anth. P. 10. 1, πᾶσαν ἐφεὶς ὀθόνην.

: cf.
Aen. 5. 216, mox aere lapsa quieto Radit iter liquidum, celeres neque commovet alas : Aesch. Pr. 394, λευρὸν οἶμον αἰθέρος ψαίρει πτεροίς: Arat. Phaen. 278, αὐτὰρ ὅγ’ εὐδιόωντι ποτὴν ὄρνιθι ἐοικώς (which Ap. is imitating).
: τὴν ὁρμήν. Schol. In Aesch. Pr. 126, ῥιπαὶ πτερύγων means the rustling of wings. L. and S. assume a special meaning for ῥιπή in our passage, 'the wing as an instrument of swift motion.'
: the Alex. poets used this adj. of things, whereas earlier it was always confined to persons. In Hom. it implies mental tranquillity, never mere silence as in 861 supr., 3. 219 (v. Buttm. Lexil.).
: the comp. ἐνευδιάω 'to float in the clear sky' is ἅπ. λεγ.

: this Paphlagonian river derived its name (1) from Artemis having bathed there, (2) from the virgin freshness of the country through which it flowed, διὰ χωρίων ἀνθηρῶν φερόμενος καὶ διὰ τοῦτο τοῦ ὀνόματος τετυχηκώς, Strab. 465, 40. There was a river of the same name in Samos, see note to 1.187.
: 'flowing into the sea,' cf. Od. 5. 460. Elsewhere Ap. always uses ἁλιμυρής (= ἅλιος), see note to 1.913.
: a town of Paphlagonia mentioned in Il. 2. 853. Sesamus was afterwards called Amastris (Strab. 466, 42).

: Strabo (467, 6) says that the town was situated on two rocks called from their colour Ἐρυθρῖνοι. The five towns mentioned in these two lines are all found in the list of the Paphlagonians in Il. 2. 851 sqq.
: the box-trees of Cytorus were famous; cf. Virg. G. 2. 437, undantem buxo ... Cytorum : Cat. 4. 13, buxifer Cytorus . πύξον εἰς Κύτωρον ἄγειν = 'to carry coals to Newcastle.'

: Dion. P. (975) also uses the term Assyrian of the Leuco-Syrians
of Pontus and Cappadocia, amongst whose towns Sinope was included. The Cappadocians were called Λευκόσυροι to distinguish them from the darker southern Syrians.

div.p: According to the general legend it was Apollo who carried off Sinope (daughter of the river-god Asopus) from Boeotia to the place which afterwards bore her name.

div.seg: : 'outwitted by the promise she had secured.'
: cf. the Homeric ἐν φιλότητι μιγῆναι.
: only here have we the acc. with ἰθύω, which elsewhere (e.g. 3. 1060) takes the gen. of the object directly aimed at or sought.
: cf. Il. 14. 213, Ζηνὸς … ἐν ἀγκοίνῃσιν ἰαύεις.
: Tricca was a city in Thessaly on the Peneius; cf. Il. 2. 729.

div.p: Having been separated from Heracles in his expedition against the Amazons they had settled at Sinope. For ἀποπλαγχθέντες cf. 1. 316.
'going forth to meet them they showed them truly who they themselves were.'
div.seg: : cf. Hes. Th. 34, σφᾶς δ’ αὐτὰς πρῶτόν τε καὶ ὕστατον αἰὲν ἀείδειν. In Hom. σφας only occurs once (Il. 5. 567), and is enclitic with short vowel, elsewhere σφεας.

div.p: Val. Fl. (5. 115) also mentions that the sons of Deimachus left Sinope and joined the Argonauts.
div.seg: : Ap. did not follow Aristarchus' canon by which these shorter forms were banished from Hom. Gerhard shows that the majority of the later epic poets adhered to this canon.

: Ζεφύρου. Schol., cf. Hes. Th. 379, Ἀργέστην Ζέφυρον; strictly the N. W. wind, Pliny N. H. 18. 34, Corus, Graecis dictus Argestes. In Hom. ἀργέστης is an epithet of Νότος, so too in Ap. 4. 1628; cf. Hor. C. 1. 7. 15, Albus ut obscuro deterget nubila caelo Saepe Notus.

div.p: For these rivers v.n. 366-7.

div.seg: : the alluvial deposit at the mouths of these rivers forming Leucosyria (946 n.).
: 'enclosing a harbour,' ἅπ. λεγ. The headland is Themiscyra, cf. 371.
: Diodorus (4. 16) also tells how Melanippe, daughter of Ares and queen of the Amazons, was ransomed from Heracles by her sister. Cf. 778.
: a constant epithet of ζωστήρ in Hom.
: 'wasstirred up against their going further.' νισς. is dat. incomm.
κ.τ.λ.: 'and no river sends forth over the earth so many diverse streams all issuing from itself.'

div.p:
'it would lack four of a hundred,
were one to reckon each.'
div.seg: : literally 'four times,' i.e. the unit would require to be repeated four times more before reaching a hundred. Merkel reads τετράδος, but the use of τετράς would be as irregular as τετράκις. τετράκις for τέσσαρες is defended by ἑπτά for ἑπτάκις in 3. 860.
: literally 'reckon on the five fingers'; cf. Od. 4. 412, ἐπὴν πάσας πεμπάσσεται: Aesch. Eum. 751, πεμπάζετ’ ὀρθῶς ἐκβολὰς ψήφων.

div.p:
Cf. Plin. N.H. 6. 4, Thermodon ... praeterque radices Amazonii montis lapsus:
Aen. 11. 659,
cum flumina Thermodontis
Pulsant et pictis bellantur Amazones armis
, etc.

'Thence it spreads over the rising country which lieth opposite extending inland. Wherefore its channels are tortuous, and it winds unceasingly, now this way, and now that, wherever it can find low-lying land, one stream afar off, and another near. Many of its branches have no name; we know not where they are drained off. But the river itself, uniting with a few of its streams, discharges its waters openly into the inhospitable Pontus beneath the arching headland.'

div.seg: : 'tortuous,' cf. Dion. P. 75, ἐπίστροφον ὅρμον ἔχουσα. Elsewhere this adj. means 'conversant with,' e.g. Od. 1. 177, ἐπίστροφος ἦν ἀνθρώπων.
: ἅπ. λεγ. The streams are swallowed up by the sands.

: Strabo (248, 21) mentions how this name, which was given to the Pontus owing to the rigour of the climate and the fierceness of the Scythians, was afterwards changed to Εὔξεινος when the Ionians founded cities on its shores.
: cf. Il. 17. 363, οὐ γὰρ ἀναιμωτί γ’ ἐμάχοντο.

: 'gentle,' literally 'affable'; cf. Od. 18. 128, ἐπητῇ ἀνδρὶ ἔοικας:
Aen. 3. 621, nec dictu affabilis ulli . In Od. 21. 306 we have ἐπητύς 'courtesy.'
: cf. Od. 9. 112, τοῖσιν … οὔτε θέμιστες (of the Cyclopes).
: a plain near the Thermodon mentioned by Pherecydes. Doias and Acmon (992) are said by the Schol. to have been brothers.

: usually said to be the daughter, not the wife, of Ares. Ap.
follows Pherecydes in deriving the Amazons from Ares and Harmonia.

: Brunck reads διὰ τρίχα, i.e. διακεκριμέναι τρίχα. but the mss. are against him, and also the fact that κεκρ. κατὰ φῦλα is modelled on Il. 2. 362, κρῖν’ ἄνδρας κατὰ φῦλα. Since Woli's day διὰ τρίχα has always been read in Hom., v. Spitzner and La Roche on Il. 2. 655, διὰ τρίχα κοσμηθέντες (= τρίχα διακοσμηθέντες).

: Pherecydes, according to the Schol., mentioned a town Lycastis, inhabited by Amazons, between Themiscyra and Chalybia. Hecataeus mentioned Chadesia as a city of the Leucosyri, i.e. Cappadocians (v.n. 946).

: only here of the act of planting. In Hom. it is used for a
plantation, orchard, etc., as opposed to ἄρουρα.
: cf. ἀτειρέα γαῖαν, 375; στυφλὸς γῆ, Soph. Ant. 250.
: 'cleaving the earth,' a verb first used by Alex. writers.
: 'receive in exchange a price by which they live.' ὦνος is explained by the Schol. as τὸ τῆς τροφῆς τίμημα. L. and S. wrongly, 'articles of traffic.' βιοτήσιος is ἅπ. λεγ.

: elsewhere (e.g. 3. 769) Ap. always uses ὀτλέω, which is found also in Call. and Lyc. ὄτλος is used in Tragedy, e.g. Aesch. Th. 18, παιδείας ὄτλον. Curtius derives these words from the rt. τελ, ταλ (τλάὠ with prothetic ο. Shaw suggests that the spondaic ending of the line emphasizes the weary hardships of their lives; cf. 1. 272, where we have the same effect.

div.p: This curious custom of the couvade or 'man-childbed,' by which the father of a new-born child pretends to endure the pains of maternity, was observed amongst the Corsicans (Diod. 5. 14), and Strabo (137, 4) mentions it as prevailing amongst the Celtiberi. In modern times travellers, from Marco Polo downwards, tell of it in China, Assam, Borneo, Guiana, etc.; v. Tylor, Early History of Mankind p. 293.

div.seg: : a mountain near Trapezus; Arrian Peripl. 12, Ἱερόν, ἐν ᾧ ναός ἐστι Διὸς Οὐρίου.
: this subst. is an ν-stem in Ap.; Xen., who is the first to use it, has it as an ν-stem in sing. and an ο-stem in pl., An. 5. 4. 26, μόσσυνι … μοσσύνοις.
: 'usage,' 'custom,' literally 'a way pointed out (δείκνυμι).' In the sense of 'justice' it was 'the course which usage prescribed,' v. Jebb, Introd. Hom. p. 48.

div.p: So Xen. (l.c.) says of them: ἐν ὄχλῳ ὄντες ἐποίουν ἅπερ ἂν ἄνθρωποι ἐν ἐρημίᾳ ποιήσειαν, μόνοι τε ὄντες ἔπραττον ἅπερ ἂν μετ’ ἄλλων ὄντες.
Xen.: ἐζήτουν δὲ καὶ ταῖς ἑταίραις αἷς ἦγον οἱ Ἔλληνες ἐμψανῶς ξυγγίνεσθαι, νόμος γὰρ ἦν οὗτός σφισι.

div.seg:
: cf. Hes. Op. 36
διακρινώμεθα νεῖκος Ἰθείῃσιδίκαις (opp. to σκολιαὶ δίκαι, 219): Il. 23. 580.

: 'wretched man!' There is no sure instance of this meaning in Hom., the meaning there being 'hard,' either in the physical sense 'full of endurance' (καρτερικός), or 'hard-hearted'; v. Leaf on Il. 10. 164.

div.p: Cf. Mela 1. 19, reges suffragio deligunt, vinculisque et arctissima custodia tenent, atque ubi culpam prave quid imperando meruere, inedia totius diei afficiunt.

div.seg: : 'near dawn,' sub diluculum. For κνέφυς in this sense, cf. Ar. Eccl. 291. πρῷ πάνυ τοῦ κνέφους, so ἅμα κνέφᾳ = ἅμ’ ἡμέρᾳ, Xen. Hell. 7. 1. 15.
: Ap. was the first to form this aorist on the analogy of ἔλλαβε, ἔλλαχε.

div.p: See on 384.
Cf. Il. 13. 598, καὶ τὸ μὲν (ἔγχος) ἐκ χειρὸς ἔρυσεν μεγάθυμος Ἀγήνωρ, Αὺτὴν δὲ ξυνέδησεν ἐυστρεφεῖ οἰὸς ἀώτῳ, Σφενδόνῃ.

div.seg: : 'baldrick,' 'swordbelt.' Used for a bandage also in Eur. Phoen. 1669, ἀμφὶ τραύματα … τελαμῶνας βαλεῖν.
: i.e. before the bird could discharge its shaft.

: these words have been generally suspected and variously emended. The whole line could well be done without. If the text is sound, αὐτάρ must be used taking up the previous ἀλλά, in the same way as δέ is used after parentheses, and ἔπειτα must mean 'forthwith' (Hesych. ἔπειτᾱ τάχιστα). This meaning may be found in 558 supr., and in Il.
18. 357 Schol. A.B. explain ἔπειτα by παραυτίκα, νῦν.
: the birds floating on the Stymphalian mere; cf. Lucr. 5. 131, uncisque timendae Unguibus Arcadiae volucres Stymphala colentes . For this labour of Heracles v. Apollod. 2. 5. 6.

: this bronze rattle, fashioned by Hephaestus, was given for the purpose to Heracles by Athene. According to others H. devised it for himself, cf. Diod. 4. 13, κατασκευάσας χαλκῆν πλαταγὴν … ἐξεφόβει τὰ ζῷα, καὶ πέρας τῇ συνεχείᾳ τοῦ κρότου ῥᾳδίως ἐκπολεμήσας καθαρὰν ἐποίησε τὴν λίμνην. Our mss. strongly favour the paroxytone accent, and the Schol. Par. says Ἡρωδιανὸς τὴν πλαταγὴν ὀξύνεσθαι φησὶν ἐν τῇ καθόλου· βέλτιον δὲ ἴσως τὴν μὲν πλαταγήν, τὸν ἦχον, ὀξύνειν, τὴν δὲ πλατάγην, τὸ κρόταλον, παροξύνειν.
: a compound formed by Ap. on the analogy of ἀερσίποδες, Il. 18. 532.

: 'helmets.' Fick explains the word as τετρυφάλεια 'having four φάλοῑ, cf. τετράφαλος 920 supr. The old view was that it stood for τριφάλεια, 'having three φάλοι.' Buttm. derived it from τρύω, a helmet having its φάλος pierced to receive the λόφος.

: Rzach rightly explains this as the pl. of the aor. imper. ἄρσον, which we find in Od. 2. 353. For the sigmatic aor. with thematic vowel ε (cf. ἄξετε, Il. 3. 105) v. Monro, H.G. 41, Curt. G.V. ii 282 sqq. Wellauer takes ἄρσετε as futurum pro imperativo, but there is no epic fut. ἄρσω, and the imperatives in 1061, 1063 preclude this possibility. Similarly ὄρσετε in 1067 is an aor. imper.
: Ap. uses three other forms of this adv., ἀμοιβαδίς, ἀμοιβαδόν, ἀμοιβηδίς.

div.p: This simile is from Il. 16. 212, ὡς δ’ ὅτε τοῖχον ἀνὴρ ἀράρῃ πυκινοῖσι λίθοισι Δώματος ὑψηλοῖο, βίας ἀνέμων ἀλεείνων, (\Ως ἄραρον κόρυθες τε καὶ ἀσπίδες ὀμφαλόεσσαι.
div.seg: : = κατερέψηται; cf. Ar. Vesp. 1294, ὡς εὖ κατηρέψασθε καὶ νουβυστικῶς Κεράμῳ τὸ νῶτον ὥστε τὰς πληγὰς στέγειν.
: 'dwelling'; in Hom. a fence or enclosure, ἑρκίον αὐλῆς, Il. 9. 476.

div.p: 'one tile succeeds another continuously and is joined thereto.'

div.seg: : 'drawing near to.' de M., "après avoir échoué (i.e. beached) le navire," adopting from Vars a distinction between κέλλω aborder and χρίμπτω échouer, for which there seems no sufficient justification. Vars says (op. cit. 151), "à côtè de l'expression νῆα κέλσαι ou ἐπικέλσαι (Homère), on peut considérer le mot χριμψασθαι commune expression technique signifiant' échouer sur le sable, h. Hom. Ap. 439, ἡ δ’ ἀμάθοισιν ἐχρίμψατο ποντοπόρος νηῦς." κέλσαι, however, is used of this landing, 1090 infr.
: 'peacefully,' see note to 3.521; cf. Soph. fr. 563, ὑπὸ στέγῃ Πυκνῆς ἀκούειν ψακάδος εὑδούσῃ φρενί.

: see note to 1.1201. Cf.
Virg. G. 1. 373, nunquam imprudentibus imber Obfuit.

div.p: 'so the birds discharged shaft after shaft upon the Argonauts, flying high up over the sea towards the mountains of the land beyond the waves.' They flew to Scythia whence they had come.

div.seg: : cf. 851. For the counsel of Phineus v. 388 sqq.

: like υἱῆας, 1119, this is a new formation from a stem vἱευ--. Ap. also uses forms from three other stems: (a) stem υἱ: υἷος, υἷα, υἷε, υἷες, υἱάσιν, υἷας, (b) stem υἱο: υἱός, υἱόν, υἱέ (voc.) (c) stem υἱυ: υἱέος, υἱέα, υἱέε, υἱέες, υἱέας, υἱεῖς (voc.); v. Rzach.
: see note to 399 These lines closely resemble Call. fr. 113, Ἀρχόμεν’, ὡς ἥρωες ἀπ’ Αἰήταο Κυταίου Αὖθις ἐς ἀρχαίαν ἔπλεον Αἱμονίην.
: 'laid as a charge upon them'; cf. Od. 1. 327, νόστον … ὃν … ἐπετείλατο Παλλάς.
: i.e. the day on which the heroes landed.

div.p: 'marking the watery path of Arcturus by the rain.' For διερήν see note to 1.184. The storms attending the rising of Arcturus are referred to in the Prol. to Plaut. Rudens spoken by Arcturus; cf. Virg. G. 1.204.
'now throughout the day Boreas made the leaves to rustle softly on the mountains, breathing lightly through the ends of the branches.'

div.seg: : ὁ ἐλαφρῶς πνέων, ἀπὸ τοῦ ἄω τὸ πνέω. Schol. L. and S. wrongly 'aloft.' The word occurs in Aesch. Pr. 452, ἀήσυροι μύρμηκες where it is explained (1) 'light as air,' 'tiny,' (2) 'moved by the wind,' 'agile.' Curtius finds the same termination in βλοσυρός.
: 'in giant might.' To this passage belongs Varro Atac. fr. 6, frigidus et silvis Aquilo decussit honorem.
: 'with roaring blasts;' cf. Od. 12.408, κεκληγὼς Ζέφυρος.
: 'and the murky blackness was fixed like a wall about them.'
: 'within a little of death;' παρ’ ὀλίγον ἐκ τοῦ θανάτου. Schol. παρέξ is not used elsewhere in this sense; παρὰ μικρόν, παρ’ ὀλίγον, παρὰ βραχύ are common.

: for the acc. cf. Hdt. 4. 151, ἑπτὰ ὲτέων οὐκ ὗε τὴν Θήρην: Od. 6. 131, λέων ὑόμενος. For ἀθέσφατος cf. Il. 3. 4, χειμῶνα φύγον καὶ ἀθέσφατον ὄμβρον. Hesych. ἀθέσφατον· ὅσον οὐδ’ ἂν θεὸς φατίσειεν δῑ ὑπερβολὴν πλήθους (v. the discussion in Buttm. Lexil.).
: the shipwrecked men and the Argonauts.
: one of the sons of Phrixus and Chalciope, daughter of Aeetes.
: cf. Cali. Jov. 81, ἕζεο δ’ αὐτός, Ἄκρῃς ἐν πολίεσσιν, ἐπόψιος οἵ τε δίκῃσιν Λαὸν ὑπὸ σκολιῇς οἵ τ’ ἔμπαλιν ἰθύνουσιν.
: cf. Il. 5. 91, ὅτ’ ἐπιβρίσῃ Διὸς ὄμβρος. See 1. 678, 3. 344.
: 'our sorry craft'; Aeetes, apparently, had given them a crazy vessel for their voyage, wishing to compass their death, as an oracle had warned him of dangers to himself from his own family.

: this conjecture
of Merkel is, on the whole, the most satisfactory; see note to 326
: for the object of their voyage v. 1095.
: this appeal closely resembles that of Odysseus to Nausicaa, Od. 6. 178, δὸς δὲ ῥάκος ἀμφιβαλέσθαι, Εἴ τί που εἴλυμα σπείρων (i.e. wrapper of the linen) ἔχες ἐνθάδ’ ἰοῦσα.

div.p:
Cf. Od. 9. 269, Ἀλλ’ αἰδεῖο, φέριστε, θεούς· ἱκέται δέ τοί εἰμεν, Ζεὺς δ’ ἐπιτιμήτωρ ἱκετάων τε ξείνων τε, Ξείνιος, ὃς ξείνοισιν ἅμ’ αἰδοίοισιν ὀπηδεῖ:
Aen. 1. 731, Iuppiter, hospitibus nam te dare iura loquuntur.

div.seg: : cf. Od. 9. 364, εἰρωτᾷς μ’ ὄνομα κλυτόν, where some of the old commentators explain "the name by which I am called," but more probably κλυτόν means 'illustrious.' This is the only place where Ap. uses ὄνομα not οὔνομα.

div.p:
Cf. Ov. Met. 15. 497, Fando aliquem Hippolytum vestras, puto, contigit aures , etc.;
Aen. 2. 81,
Fando aliquod si forte tuas pervenit ad aures
Belidae nomen Palamedis.

div.seg: : as in 4. 120 the poet says that the ram was slain by command of Hermes, while here it asks itself to be slain, de M. assumes that these contradictory traditions represent different recensions. Seaton (Cl. Rev. vi 396) points out that this is not a necessary assumption, any more than when we are told (2. 602) that it was Athene, and again (4. 786) that it was Hera who helped the Argo through the Symplegades.

: 'the god of flight'; Φύξιος Ζεὺς παρὰ Θεσσαλοῖς, ἤτοι ἐπειδὴ
τὸν ἐπὶ Δευκαλίωνος κατέφυγον κατακλυσμόν, ἢ διὰ τὸ φυγεῖν τὸν Φρίξον αὐτόν. Schol. Cf. Lyc. 288, καλῶν ἐπ’ εὐχαῖς πλεῖστα Φύξιον Δία.
: 'above all other gods'; cf. Od. 2. 432, λεῖβον … Ἐκ πάντων δὲ μάλιστα Διὸς γλαυκώπιδι κούρῃ.

: without asking the usual ἕδνα (see note to 1.977); cf. Il. 9. 146, τάων ἥν κ’ ἐθέλῃσι, φίλην ἀνάεδνον ἀγέσθω. Bentley altered the form in Hom. to ἀνέεδνος, i.e. ἀν‐έvεδνος, and was followed by Bekker. See Curtins, Et. 579.
: in Hom. always used of the gods.

: cf. Il. 18. 175, ἐρύσσασθαι … Τρῶες ἐπιθύουσι. On the disputed point whether the compound is to be resolved into ἐπιθύω (with ι lengthened in arsis) or into
ἐπ‐ἰθύω (with υ irreg. lengthened) v. L. and S. and Leaf on Il. l.c.

: 'busied themselves about,' 'ministered unto them' (Way); de M. wrongly 'embrassèrent.' Ap., like Hom., uses this verb of a great variety of activities, e.g. 1. 562, 571: 2. 761; 4. 1145 (ἄμφεπεν). He also uses it in the post-Homeric sense of 'worshipping,' 'paying homage to,' 1. 1102. See on 3. 547.
: 'kinsmen,' see note to 1.53. Cretheus and Athamas were brothers, and Jason was the grandson of Cretheus, Argus of Athamas.
: 'eagerly they placed themselves round the altar.'
: 'roofless,' ἅπ. λεγ. Roofless temples are often mentioned in Pausanias, e.g. 2. 18. 3, 24. 4.
: the altar was made of pebbles, cf. 694. For other instances of the gen. materiae v. 231, 3. 232, 1285.

: there is no reason to alter this to μέγας, as Brunck and others have done, to produce a contrast between the size of this stone and the small pebbles of which the altar was made. The rude image of the Mother of the Gods at Pessinus was a black stone, cf. Arnob. 7. 49, lapis quidam non magnus ... coloris furvi atque atri.
: the Armenians sacrificed horses (Xen. An. 4. 5. 35); so too the Massagetae (Hdt. 1. 216). "Horse sacrifices are said to prevail among the modern Parsees" (Rawlinson).

: 'of which they tend unfailing herds'; cf. Od. 7. 99,
πίνοντες καὶ ἔδοντες, ἐπηετανὸν γὰρ ἔχεσκον. Curtius derives ἐπηετανόν from ἐπί and αἰεί (Boeot. ἠΐ), the ending being the same as the Lat. -tinus. de M. tr. "elles sacrifiaient des chevaux qu'elles avaient nourri pendant une année," following the old deriv. from ἐπί and ἔτος.

div.p: Cf. Call. quoted on 1123.

div.seg: : 'who are god-fearing and unjust,' = οἵ τε θεουδέες καὶ οὐ δίκαιοι (Merkel). Wellauer wrongly construes οἵ τε θεουδέες ἐσμὲν οὐ λήθομεν Διά, οὐδὲ δίκαιοι λήθουσι. Our poet had in mind Od. 9. 174, πειρήσομαι οἵ τινές εἰσιν Ἤ ῥ’ οἵ γ’ ὑβρισταί τε καὶ ἄγριοι οὐδὲ δίκαιοι (= καὶ ἄδικοι) =Ἠε φιλόξεινοι, καί σφιν νόος ἐστὶ θεουδής. The conjecture ἠδέ for οὐδέ is easy but bad.
: 'he snatched your father from death at the hands of a stepmother (i.e. Ino)'; see note to 653 Cf. Pind. P. 4. 161, κριοῦ … τῷ ποτ’ ἐκ πόντου σαώθη ἔκ τε ματρυιᾶς ἀθέων βελέων.

: cf. 1. 386, Eur. Med. 3, Cat. 64. 1,
Peliaco quondam prognatae vertice pinus
Dicuntur liquidas Neptuni nasse per undas
Phasidos ad fluctus et fines Aeetaeos.

κ.τ.λ.: 'for I am sent to fulfil sacrifices of atonement to Phrixus, the cause of the wrath of Zeus against the sons of Aeolus.' Cf. Pind. P. 4. 158, where Pelias says to Jason, δύνασαι δ’ ἀφελεῖν | μᾶνιν γθονίων, κέλεται γὰρ ἑὰν ψυχὰν κομίξαι (to 'lay') | Φρίξος ἐλθόντας πρὸς Αἰήτα θαλάμους. Brunck says Φρίξοιο depends on ὑπέρ understood, but it seems to be a possessive gen. 'the sacrifices which belong unto, or, are due to, P.' Way mistranslates "Lo, thus do I sail to atone for their deed Who would sacrifice Phrixus."

: 'to accomplish.'
Merkel reads ἀλθήσων from ἀλθαίνω 'to heal' which is used of expiation in Lyc. 1122, κακὸν μίασμ’ ἔμφυλον ἀλθαίνων κακῷ, so de M. "accomplir des sacrifices expiatoires." χόλον is acc. in apposition to the sentence, but it is a very harsh use, as it is the fact that the spirit of P. has not been appeased, and that the fleece has not been brought back, which is the cause of the wrath of Zeus.
κ.τ.λ.: 'vexed that they should be busied on such a quest'; see note to 56
: 'shall not hold back from aiding you in the hour of need.'

div.p: 'but Aeetes hath rooted in him a spirit of murderous cruelty.'
div.seg: : 'is endued with,' cf. Pind. I. 2. 29, χαρίτεσσιν ἀραρώς: Eur. El. 948, κάλλει ἀραρώς.

: 'he maintains that he is,' 'he avows himself to be,' διαβεβαιοῦται. Schol.; cf. 3. 337, 579. Homer uses στεῦται c. inf. fut. of boasting, e.g. Il. 9. 241, στεῦται γὰρ νηῶν ἀποκόψειν ἄκρα κόρυμβα. Aristarch. explained it κατὰ διάνοιαν δρίζεσθαι, i.e. to have the mind determined. Curtius assigns it to the root stu 'to set up' (στῦλος, σταῦρος, instaurare), Meyer to Skt. stu 'celebrare' (στόμα, etc.).
: 'battle-cry.' For the awful voice of Ares cf. Il. 5. 859, ὁ δ’ ἔβραχε χάλκεος Ἄρης Ὄσσον τ’ ἐννεάχιλοι ἐπίαχον, κ.τ.λ.
: cf. Il. 6. 101, οὐδέ τίς οἱ δύναται μένος ἰσοφαρίζειν.
: 'around and about,' cf. h. Hom. Cer. 277, περί τ’ ἀμφί τε κάλλος ἄητο. ἀμφί properly meant 'on both sides.'
: περὶ τὸν Καύκασόν, φασιν, ἐν τῇ Τυφαονίᾳ πέτρᾳ κεραυνωθεὶς ὁ Τυφὼς ἰχῶράς τινας ἀφῆκεν, ἐξ ὡν ἐγένετο ὁ τὸ δέρος φυλάσσων ὄφις. Schol.
: i.e. the drops of gore from which the serpent sprang.

: this lake, on the confines of Syria and Egypt, was in the centre of a huge morass. Diod. (16. 46) tells how the army of Artaxerxes was almost swallowed up there in 350 b.c.; cf. Milton (P.L. 11 593), "that Serbonian bog Betwixt Damiata and Mount Casius old Where armies whole have sunk." According to the general legend Typhon was buried under Aetna or Pithecusa ( Aen. 9. 716).

: properly a greenish-white colour, luteus pallor. Cf. 3. 298,
Aen. 4. 499, pallor simul occupat ora.

: 'my good friend.' In Hom. it is generally used as a term of respect by one who is younger, νεωτέρου πρὸς πρεσβύτερον σεπτικὴ προσφώνησίς
ἐστι τὸ ἠθεῖε (Ariston. on Il. 22. 229). Curtius connects ἠθεῖος 'trusty' with ἦθος (σvεθ).
: in Hom. the gen. is used to express that in which one is inferior, e.g. Il. 24. 385, οὔ τι μάχης ἐπιδεύετ’ Ἀχαιῶν.
: for the constr. cf. Od. 21. 406, φόρμιγγος ἐπιστάμενος καὶ ἀοιδῆς.

div.p: 'I have good hope that the tribes of the Colchians will avail him not.' For χραισμήσειν see note to 218

div.seg: : cf. ἀκραής, 721; in Hom. only as a v.l. for ἀκραής.
: formed on the analogy of ὑπεκπροέλυσαν, Od. 6. 88.

div.p:
Cf. Virg. G. 3. 92,
Talis et ipse iubam cervice effundit equina
Coniugis adventu pernix Saturnus, et altum
Pelion hinnitu fugiens implevit acuto.

div.seg: : Pelion in Thessaly; cf. Call. Del. 118, Πήλιον ὦ Φιλύρης νυμφήιον: Ov. Met. 7. 352, Pelion umbrosum, Philyreia tecta. For Πελασγῶν see note to 1.580.
: it is, perhaps, possible to retain ἔνθ’ as Merkel does, supplying the verb of motion.
: cf. Hes. Th. 1002, Pind. P. 3. 1, Ov. Fast. 5. 380, Chiron Semivir, et flavi corpore mixtus equi ... Phillyrides.

: 'bore as offspring to a changing sire.' Kronos
changed his form at the moment of generation, and so Chiron was διφυής.

div.p: For these tribes v.n. 394 sqq.

div.seg: : generally explained 'galling bonds (ἀλύσσω, πέδη),' but there is nothing certain known about it. It occurs in Hes. Th. 521, where Hesych. explains it as δεσμοῦ εἶδος ἀναφεύκτον (?), and the Schol. as = ἀλυτοπέδη. Others apparently regarded it as connected with λυγίζομαι 'to writhe, wriggle,' i.e. 'fetters out of which one could not wriggle.'

div.p: Ap. is imitating Hes. Th. 521, Δῆσε δ’ ἀλυκτοπέδῃσι Προμηθέα ποικιλόβουλον Δεσμοῖς ἀργαλέοισι μέσον διὰ κίον’ ἐλάσσας. Καὶ οἱ ἐπ’ αἰετὸν ὦρσε τανύπτερον, αὐτὰρ ὅγ’ ἦπαρ Ἤσθιεν ἀθάνατον, τὸ δ’ ἀέξετο ἶσον ἁπάντῃ Νυκτός, ὅσον πρόπαν ἦμαρ ἔδοι τανυσίπτερος ὄρνις Cf. also Aesch. Pr. 1022 sqq.

div.seg:
: cf. Aesch. Ag. 52, πτερύγων ἐρετμοῖσιν:
Aen. 1. 300, volat ... Remigio alarum.

div.p: According to one tradition Heracles when abandoned by the Argonauts (1. 1283) delivered Prometheus from his torments. Val. Fl. (5. 155) represents this deliverance as taking place while the Argonauts, all unconscious of it, were passing by in sight of the Caucasus.

div.seg: : the yard on which the square sail hung; cf. Od. 5. 254.

: the receptacle at the stern which received the mast when
lowered. As its shape is purely conjectural (v. M. and R. Od. Appendix), it is impossible to determine how the sails and yard were placed in it, or on it, along with the mast. Vars and Torr identify the μεσόδμη and ἱστοδόκη, but see Class. Rev. x 169.
: lowering it backwards till it lay lengthways. For another use see 1. 315.
: = ἐγχωρίοις. As an instance of this custom the Schol. refers to the sacrifices offered by Alexander the Great at Ilium.

: 'to receive
in a good hour the mooring cables of the ship.'
: here, as in 3. 909, σφεῖς is used of the 1 pers., a use parodied by Lucian, Pseudosophist. 576. See on 128.

div.p: 'or whether there be some other method of approach which shall secure our ends.' For ἐπήβολος, which the Schol. explains by ἀσφαλής, see note to 1.694.

div.seg: : 'afloat,' i.e. the vessel was not drawn up on the shore; cf. Il. 14. 77, ὕψι δ’ ἐπ’ εὐνάων ὁρμίσσομεν.

: 'a backwater screened by trees.' Preston suggests that this passage may have furnished Virgil with the idea of the description in Aen. 7. 30 of the Trojans sailing up the Tiber under the shade of overhanging trees.

list.head: Summary
list.item: Invocation of Erato (1-5)
Hera and Athene take counsel to aid Jason (6-35)
They visit Aphrodite to get the help of Eros (36-110)
Aphrodite persuades Eros (111-166)
Jason reveals his plans to his comrades (167-209)
Jason, with the sons of Phrixus, comes to the palace of Aeetes (210-274)
Medea is smitten by the shafts of Eros (275-298)
Aeetes hears impatiently the words of Argus and Jason, and declares the ordeal for winning the fleece, to which Jason consents (299-438)
Medea's heart is heavy with foreboding (439-470)
Council of the heroes: they resolve to send Argus to Chalciope to win Medea's aid (471-575)
Gathering of the Colchians: Aeetes plots evil against the Argonauts (576-608)
Medea, in her anguish, yields to the entreaties of Chalciope (609-743)
Conflict of emotions in Medea's heart: at last she resolves to bring her magic drugs to Jason (744-824)
Medea goes to the temple of Hecate to meet Jason (825-911)
Meeting of Jason and Medea: Medea gives him the drugs, and Jason vows never to forsake her (912-1145)
Jason rejoins his comrades, and Medea returns to her home (1146-1162)
Telamon and Aethalides receive from Aeetes the dragon's teeth (1163-1190)
Jason sacrifices to Hecate by night (1191-1224)
Aeetes in his panoply goes forth to view the ordeal (1225-1245)
Jason prepares himself for the struggle (1246-1277)
He yokes the fire-breathing bulls, and vanquishes the earth-born warriors who spring from the dragon's teeth (1278-1407).

div.seg: : this invocation of Erato, the Muse of love and the poetry of love, is imitated by Virgil, Aen. 7. 37, Nunc age, qui reges, Erato, quae tempora rerum , etc., but, as Conington points out, the address to Erato there is much less appropriate.
: Ap. did not follow Zenod. and Aristarch. who read παρίσταο in Il. 10. 291.

: the same form occurs in 4. 1565; ἐνίσπες in 1. 487, 832. Both are found in Hom.,
Od. 3. 101, νημερτὲς ἐνίσπες , 4. 642, νημερτὲς ἔνισπε (v. Curt. G.V. 1 195).

κ.τ.λ.: 'for thou hast thy portion in the destinies of Cypris also'; cf. Ov. A.A. 2. 15,
nunc mihi, si quando, Puer et Cytherea, favete:
Nunc Erato, nam tu nomen amoris habes.
: Ap. mistook the Homeric perfect ἔμμορε for an aorist, and formed ἔμμορες. For ἔμμορε = *μέμορε v. Curt. G.V. 11 131.
: 'wherefore there is joined to thee a name whose burden is love (Ἐρατώ, ἔρως).'

: Rzach shows that Wellauer is quite wrong in reading
οἷ on the analogy of 1. 893, as the use of οἷ for the first and second person is only possible in a reflexive sense.
: i.e. the reeds of the δάσκιον ἕλος, 2. 1283.
: tentabat. It takes the gen. in 1. 495, πείραζεν ἀοιδῆς , as always in Hom. From the opening scenes of this book Virgil borrowed the idea of the dialogue between Juno and Venus in Aen. 4. 90 sqq.

: the variations in the mss. are attempts to mend the metre, which is that of
Il. 1. 342, τοῖς ἄλλοις· ἦ γὰρ ὅγ’ ὀλοιῇσι φρεσὶ θύει.

: in Hom. πολέες, etc., are always masc., and so Brunck would read πολλάς, but in Alex. writers these forms are often fem., e.g. Call. Del. 28, πολέες … ἀοιδαί ,
Dian. 42, πολέας … νύμφας.
: Ap. formed this compound on the false analogy of ἐνδοιάζω, which was from the Homeric ἐν δοιῇ εἶναι 'to be in doubt.' For δοιάζω see on 770 infra.

: cf.
Il. 3. 217, κατὰ χθονὸς ὄμματα πήξας. See also 1. 784.
: παραγενόμεναι καὶ ἐπελθοῦσαι. Schol.; in earlier epic used only of things, not persons.

: the notion of a god Eros, the child of Cypris, is not found
in Homer.

: the only example in Ap. of a subjunctive with short vowel from a non-sigmatic aorist. There is one in Hom. also, ἐπεντύνονται,
Od. 24. 89 ; v. Curt. G.V. 11 262.

div.p: 'nor know I aught that wakes desire'; cf. Eur. Hipp. 478, φίλτρα θελκτήρια ἔρωτος.
div.seg: : used generally like χρέος or χρῆμα (L. and S. wrongly 'destiny'). Ap. also uses it in the sense of 'purpose' or 'object,' e.g. 173; 'need,' e.g. 1. 649; 'fate,' e.g. 1. 440.

: an epithet applied only to Hephaestus and variously explained: (1) utroque pede claudus, from γυιός; this violates the rule that adjj. in ‐εις are only formed from nouns (v. Ameis-Hentze on Od. 8. 300); (2) 'strong-armed' or 'ambidextrous'; so, amongst others, Autenrieth, who says that γυῖα primarily meant the hands, as is shown by ἐγγυαλίζω and ἐγγύη; (3) 'with a crooked limb on each side,' from a noun *γύη 'crook'; so Leaf on Il. 1. 607.

: the ἕρκος was the wall surrounding the courtyard (αὐλή) in the Homeric house, and the word was also used for the αὐλή itself. αἴθουσα (sc. στοά) was the open colonnade in the αὐλή which received the sun's rays; hence its name.

div.p:
Cf.
Od. 8. 273, βῆ δ’ ἴμεν ἐς χαλκεῶνα, κακὰ φρεσὶ βυσσοδομεύων, Ἐν δ’ ἔθετ’ ἀκμοθέτῳ μέγαν ἄκμονα.

div.seg: : Hiera, or Lipara; cf. Aen. 8. 416 sqq. where the forges of the Cyclopes to which Vulcan descends are described. In Il. 18. 369 the forge of Hephaestus is in the heavens; in Od. 8. 283 it is in Lemnos.
: 'wandering' (like Delos). For the other interpretation, 'clashing' (πλήσσω), v. M. and R. on Od. 12. 61.

: cf.
Od. 19. 55, κλισίην δινωτὴν ἐλέφαντι καὶ ἀργύρῳ where Merry says δινωτήν refers to the legs and rails being 'rounded' of ivory and 'decorated' with silver, while Monro explains 'turned with ivory and silver carried round the wood-work'; cf. Leaf on
Il. 3. 391, δινωτοῖσι λέχεσσιν 'adorned with circles or spirals' of silver or the like, inlaid. See also on 4. 222.
: literally 'covered with hair over her white shoulders,' ὤμοις being the local dat.; cf. 4. 179.
: cf. Ov. Am. 1. 5. 10, candida dividua colla tegente coma.
: only used here for a comb for the hair.
: 'uncombed,' ἀκτενίστους. Schol. In Ar. Lys. 657, where it is used as an epithet of κόθορνος, this adj. means 'untanned.'

div.p: de M. observes that in the interview which follows we have "un pendant aux Syracusaines du poète alexandrin (Théocrite). Au lieu de deux petites bourgeoises, tracassières et bavardes, Apollonius met en scène de vraies grandes dames de la cour des Ptolemées, telles que les Bérénice ou les Arsinoé." See Introd. p. 34.

div.seg: : for this as a term of respect see note to 2.1219. The Schol. observes that it is strictly applicable only to Hera, not Athene, from the Homeric point of view, while later writers regarded both Hera and Athene as younger than Cypris.
: Ap. is peculiar in using this word to mean 'after a long time,' cf. 4. 645. In 590 infr. δηναιόν means 'for a long time.' The Homeric meaning is 'long-lived.'

: cf.
Il. 18. 385, Τίπτε, Θέτι τανύπεπλε, ίκάνεις ἡμέτερον δῶ, Αἰδοίη τε φίλη τε; πάρος γε μὲν οὔ τι θαμίζεις.
: 'is stirred with fear of a mischance.'
: "for that nigh is the deed and the hour of doom" (Way). For ὄρωρεν see note to 1.713.
: Ixion had grievously insulted Hera, and was for ever chained to a revolving wheel in Hades; cf. Pind. P. 2. 22 sqq.
: Pindar (l.c.) speaks of τὸν τετράκναμον δεσμόν, 'the four-spoked bond,' i.e. the wheel to which Ixion was bound.
: for his neglect of Hera v. 1. 14.
: only here c. gen.; cf. ἄτιμος ἐκφορᾶς, Aesch. Th. 1024 . The wrath of the gods when deprived of sacrifices is often mentioned, e.g. Il. 9. 534, Soph. Aj. 175, Eur. Hipp. 147.

div.p:
Cf.
Aen. 11. 537, neque enim novus iste Dianae Venit amor, subitaque animum dulcedine movit.

div.seg:
: 'as I made trial of the righteousness of men'; cf.
Od. 17. 485,
kai/ te qeoi\ cei/noisin e)oiko/tes a)llodapoi=sin,
pantoi=oi tele/qontes e)pistrwfw=si po/lhas,
)anqrw/pwn u(/brin te kai\ eu)nomi/hn e)forw=ntes.

div.p: 'and down the mountain side tumbled the roaring torrents'; cf. Hes. Th. 367, ποταμοὶ καναχηδὰ ῥέοντες.

div.seg:
: 'the rapids'; cf.
Il. 21. 262, χώρῳ ἔνι προαλεῖ (of rapidly falling ground). This adj. is usually connected with ἅλλομαι, but Leaf regards its origin as unknown.
: a compound only found here; cf. Orph. Arg. 64, ἔξοχα γὰρ μερόπων ἠγάζετο (sc. Ἤρη) καὶ φιλέεσκε Δεινοβίην ἥρωα περικλυτὸν Αἴσονος υἷα.

div.p: 'nor will Pelias atone for his outrage unless thou vouchsafe the return of Jason.' The vulg. ὀπάσσῃς is solecistic; for the regular sequence of moods cf. Ar. Eccl. 162, οὐκ ἂν προβαίην … εἰ μὴ ταῦτ’ ἀκριβωθήσεται.

div.seg: : 'speechless amaze,' literally 'standing dumb (ἐνεός),’ ἅπ. λεγ. Cf. 2. 409. Ruhnken was led to this correction by a gloss in Hesych. ἀνεοστασίη· θάμβος, and he himself was inclined to prefer ἀνεοστασίη from ἄνεως (v.n. 503).

: the same redundancy occurs in
Od. 4. 704, δὴν δέ μιν ἀμφασίη ἐπέων λάβε.
: ἱκετεύουσαν. Schol. This meaning, known to Trag., is never found in Hom.; cf. ἀντιάζω (1. 703 n).

κ.τ.λ.: 'mayest thou find
nought more base than Cypris, if I, when thus entreated, should scorn thee in word or in aught that these frail hands can do; nor ask I favour in return.' Brunck compares Ter. Heaut. 1. 1, Malo quidem me dignum quovis deputem, Si id faciam.
: cf. Anth. P. 7. 657, εἰσὶν ἀμοιβαῖαι κἀν φθιμένοις χάριτες.

: the nearest parallel to this curious constr. seems to be Eur. I.A. 1594, ταύτην μάλιστα τῆς κόρης ἀσπάζεται, where μάλιστα is treated like μᾶλλον. Somewhat similar is the use of the gen. after superlative adjj., e.g.
Od. 11. 482, σεῖο … οὔτις ἀνὴρ … μακάρτατος. For ἤ after a superl. cf. Hdt. 2. 35, πλεῖστα θωυμάσια ἔχει [Αἴγυπτος] ἢ ἡ ἄλλη πᾶσα χώρη, if the reading is sound (v. Stein).
: Ap. alone uses ἀναίδητος for ἀναιδής, cf. 4. 360.
: i.e. when he sees you face to face.

div.p: Similarly in Lucian Deor. Dial. xi Cypris complains to Selene of the conduct of her son, and tells her how she had chastised him in vain.

'and in very truth I was minded in my piteous plight to break his evil-sounding shafts, bow and all, before his face, such grievous threats did he utter in his wrath, that if I kept not my hands far from him while still master of his passion, hereafter I might reproach myself alone.'
div.seg: : the use of κακότης in Ap. is in favour of explaining 'in my helplessness,' though we might render 'plagued with his naughtiness.'

: cf.
Od. 22. 70, οὐ γὰρ σχήσει ἀνὴρ ὅδε χεῖρας ἀάπτους.
: see note to 2.56; cf. Hdt. 5. 46, ὅρα μὴ ἐξ ὑστέρης σεωυτὸν ἐν αἰτίῃ ἔχῃς.
: οὐκ εὖ κεῖται, ἀντὶ τοῦ ἐμοὶ γὰρ λαμβάνεται. Schol.; see note to 1.893.

: cf.
Il. 24. 223, ἄκουσα θεοῦ καὶ ἐσέδρακον ἄντην. Ziegler would read ἀλλήλας in 101, as ἄντην in Hom. is always used absolutely (so too 1010, 1066 infr.), and in late epic takes the gen.
: cf. Soph. O.T. 1061, ἅλις νοσοῦσ’ ἐγώ : Isocr. 2. 7, ἱκανὸς γὰρ αὐτὸς ἔφη ἀτυχῶν εἶναι.

: this constr. is on the analogy of χειρὸς ἔχειν, or ἑλεῖν, τινα. In Hom. ἐπιμαίομαι in the sense of 'feeling,' 'handling' takes the acc.; in the sense of 'desiring,' the gen. Ap. uses the acc. in 816 infr., but the gen. in 4. 18.
: 'he will cease' from his waywardness; cf. 951. In Hom. this verb takes the gen., cf. 1. 1271.

: cf.
Il. 11. 77, δώματα καλὰ τέτυκτο κατὰ πτύχας Οὐλύμποιο.

: the Schol. says that these words are ambiguous, meaning either χωρὶς τοῦ Διός or χωρὶς τῶν ἄλλων ἐν τῇ Διὸς ἀλωῇ. The latter meaning seems right, though de M. renders 'loin de Zeus.' Ap. uses ἀπάνευθε, seorsum, both as adv. (e.g. 2. 153) and as prep. (e.g. 1. 863).

: Ὄμηρος οὐχ ὑπὸ Διὸς ἡρπάσθαι ἀλλ’ ὑπὸ θεῶν φησιν, οὐδὲ δἰ ἔρωτα καὶ πόθον, ἀλλ’ ὥστε Διὶ οἰνοχοεύειν. Schol.; cf.
Il. 20. 234,
to\n kai\ a)nhrei/yanto qeoi\ *dii\ oi)noxoeu/ein,
*ka/lleos ei(/neka oi(=o, i(/n' a)qana/toisi metei/h.
The writers after Hom. spoke of Ganymede as the favourite of Zeus, e.g. Plat. Phaedr. 255 c, Eur. Or. 1392.

: the game of 'knuckle-bones' is mentioned in
Il. 23. 88, ἀμφ’ ἀστραγάλοισι χολωθείς. It was a favourite game of boys, cf. Plut. Alcib. 2. Pliny ( N.H. 34. 55) describes the famous statue by Polycletus of the Astragalizontes, two boys playing with astragali, which Ap. probably had before his mind.

: see note to 1.459. Cf
Anth. P. 12. 46, Ἔρωτες Ὡς τὸ πάρος παίξεσθ’ ἄφρονες ἀστραγάλοις.

div.p: 'Now greedy Eros held beneath his bosom the palm of his left hand filled full with knuckle-bones.'
div.seg: : a form only found here; in Hom. ἐνίπλειον. We have ἔμπλειος in 1281.

: 'greedy' seems the most appropriate sense here. The Lat. translators render it by 'protervus,' and so de M. 'l'insolent.' The Schol. explains ἱ μαργαίνειν ποιῶν, and Ellis on Cat. 64. 95, Heu misere exagitans immiti corde furores Sancte puer, curis hominum qui gaudia misces , says: 'Love is μάργος, a raging madman, Ap. 3.120, and not only the rouser of strife and grief in others (4.446, 7) but himself full of turmoil, τετρηχώς (3.276).'
: ἅπ. λεγ.; the usual form is ὀκλάξ (1308).
: sc. ἀστραγάλω, 'he still had two left, as he kept throwing one after another in vain.'

: 'throwing forward,' casting one after another. The use of this word seems to decide that the game was one of dice-throwing, the loser forfeiting his dice, though Seaton (Cl. Rev. 1 170) argues strongly that it was ἀρτιασμός (par impar), and explains ἐπιπρ. as 'staking,' quoting in support Becq de Fouquières (Jeux des Anciens 284 sqq.), "il n'avait plus que deux osselets, qu'il aventurait l'un après l'autre."
: 'having lost them as well as the others.'
: 'grasping him by the chin.' κατέχεσθαι is not used c. gen. in Hom., though ἔχεσθαι c. gen. is common.

div.p: 'Why dost thou laugh, thou unutterable rogue? Hast thou tricked him in this fashion, and unfairly triumphed over his innocence?'

div.seg: : only here has περιπέλομαι the sense of 'overreaching,' like περιέρχομαι in Hdt. 3. 4, σοφίῃ γάρ μιν περιῆλθεν. In 1150 it means 'to surround.'

: this acc., which occurs also in Call. fr. 111, is formed on a false analogy for the regular νήιδα (v. 32), the δ being primary (root vιδ). πάιν (4. 697) is a similar false formation; v. Rzach p. 78.

: a Cretan nymph, sister of the Curetes, who nursed the
infant Zeus in the Dictaean cave (1. 509); cf. Call. Jov. 47, σὲ δὲ κοίμησ’ Ἀδρήστεια Λίκνῳ ἐνὶ χρυσέῳ, where Spanheim refers to the Cretan coins of the age of Trajan on which the child Zeus is represented seated on a sphere. The ball, the plaything of his childhood, came to be regarded as typifying the universe.

: 'toy,' cf. 146; used in the pl. by Hom. of gifts bringing peace (μειλίσσω, μείλιχος), e.g.
Il. 9. 147, ἐγὼ δ’ ἐπὶ μείλια δώσω, a meaning which we have in 594 infr., 4. 1190, 1549.
: this comp. is ἅπ. λεγ. The gen. χειρῶν is on the analogy of that with δέχεσθαι.

div.p: 'The circlets of it are wrought of gold, and around each of them wind double curving rings; but the joinings are hidden, for a spiral of blue runs over all of them.' The ball seems to have been made of a number of separate circlets of gold, which were kept in position by two rings encircling them on the outside. The joinings of the κύκλα and ἁψῖδες were concealed by the spiral of blue.

div.seg: : probably of κύανος, lapis lazuli, or the imitation of it made of glass stained with carbonate of copper; cf. Il. 11. 24 sqq., where its iridescence on Agamemnon's breastplate is described, κυάνεοι δὲ δράκοντες … ἴρισσιν ἐοικότες.

: cf. 4. 296, which is imitated in
Aen. 2. 697 (of a shooting star), tunc longo limite sulcus Dat lucem.
κ.τ.λ.: 'by thy shafts do thou bewitch the daughter of Aeetes with love for Jason.' ἐπί denotes the end or object.
: 'fainter'; cf. 2. 453. Her gratitude would be less if the service were delayed.
: τὰ παίγνια, δῑ ὧν οἱ παῖδες μειλίσσονται. Schol. (v. 135).
: see note to 2.554. The constr. is θεᾶς ἀυφιμεμαρπὼς ἔχεν τοῦ χιτῶνος.

: 'drawing his cheeks towards her.' In ἐρύω (εἰρύὠ, in which the two roots vερυ 'to protect' and vερυς 'to drag' were confused, the quantity of the aor. varies as in Hom.; in 2. 586 ἀνείρυσε has short penult.

: 'be witness'; cf. 1. 466, 2. 257. For the custom of swearing by the head cf.
Aen. 9. 300, per caput hoc iuro ; ib. 4. 357, testor utrumque caput : Ov. Her. 3. 107, perque tuum nostrumque caput quae iunximus una.
: 'gathered together.' a compound only found here; Et. Mag. 83, 3, συναμησάμενος· σωρεύσας, συνάξας, ἢ θερίσας.

div.p: 'Forthwith he girt around him with a golden strap the quiver which was resting against a tree.'

'He passed from the palace of Zeus through (or, into) the fruitful orchard.' This is inconsistent with 114, where we are told that the boys were playing Διὸς θαλερῇ ἐν ἀλωῇ. Ap. seems to have used the Homeric διὲκ μεγάροιο, forgetting that it did not harmonize with what he had previously said. To translate 'he passed right through the fruitful orchard of the palace of Zeus' would remove the inconsistency, but the order of words is rather against it. Gerhard's μεγάλοιο, as he admits himself, is tame and otiose. The Schol. says that this passage is derived from Ibycus, διὰ τούτων τῶν στίχων παραγράφει τὰ εἰρημένα ὑπὸ Ἰβύκου ἐν οἷς περὶ τῆς Γανυμήδους ἁρπαγῆς εἶπεν ἐν τῇ εἰς Γοργίαν ᾠδῇ.

div.seg: : regularly used in epic poetry in enumerating a rapid succession of details.

: according to the Homeric conception in the Iliad there was an opening from the summit of Mt. Olympus into the vault of heaven, which was closed by a thick cloud as a door, e.g. 5. 749,
*au)to/matoi de\ pu/lai mu/kon ou)ranou= a(\s e)/xon =*(wrai
*th=|s e)pite/traptai me/gas ou)rano\s *ou)/lumpo/s te
*)hme\n anakli=nai pukino\n ne/fos h)d' e)piqei=nai.
ἐξήλυθεν: here c. acc. as in Hdt. 7. 29, ἐξῆλθον τὴν Περσίδα χώρην, cf. Lat. egredi c. acc. In 2. 202, ἐκ δ’ ἐλθὼν μεγάροιο , we have the gen. as in Hom., and so in 1. 844, πυλάων ἐξέμολεν.
: Preston suggests that from this Milton took his idea of the sunbeam bearing the angel Uriel 'slope downward' to the earth (P.L. iv. 589).

κ.τ.λ.: these words must be taken parenthetically, 'for there are two poles which rise up, the summits of trackless mountains, the highest points of earth.' Ap. leaves the reader to infer that the downward flight of Eros was by the northern heights. The use of δέ, standing for γάρ by parataxis, in introducing a reason or explanation is common in Hom. (v. M. and R. on Od. 1. 433: Monro, H.G. 333). The obscurity of the passage arises from the blending of the Homeric notion of Olympus with the notion of the two poles which is not Homeric. ὁ ἄνω πόλος and ὁ κάτω πόλος are described in Arist. de Mundo 2. 5; Arat. 21 sqq. The poets constantly spoke of the lofty mountains, such as Olympus and the shadowy Rhipaean peaks, rising up to heaven in the north and forming the northern πόλος (cardo, vertex, Virg. G. 1. 242), and so too Atlas in the south. Mercury in his flight in
Aen. 4. 246 sqq. lights first on Mt. Atlas. ἀνέχουσι is probably intrans. (cf. 217, 851, 1383), though the Latin translators render, 'duo poli sustinent vertices,' and de M., 'deux poles soutiennent les hauteurs.'
: the use of ᾗχί τε = ᾗχι is common in later epic poetry, and is an extension of the Homeric ἔνθα τε = ἔνθα; "where first upborne The blushing sun unfolds the rays of morn" (Preston).
: this epithet of γαῖα is not found in Hom., but it occurs in the Homeric hymns and in Hesiod.
: the Schol. explains the variant αἰθέρι as δοτικὴ (dat.) ἀντὶ αἰτιατικῆς (acc.), but Ap. does not use ἀνά c. dat. (in 2. 699 there may be tmesis), though it is found nine times in Hom.
: as in Il. 7. 407; elsewhere ἐφανδάνει, e.g. 34 supr.

: cf.
Il. 9. 626, οὐ γάρ μοι δοκέει … τελευτὴ … κρανέεσθαι.
κ.τ.λ.: 'but he who speaketh not, and withholdeth his mind and counsel, let him know that it is he, and he alone, who is robbing this company of their return.'
: only here in the sense of 'keeping back' (i.e. not uttering); in 327 ἀπέρυκεν means 'detained.'
: introducing the more probable alternative; cf. 4. 205.

: 'if we refrain from the battle-cry.' In
Il. 13. 525 ἐεργόμενοι πολέμοιο is used of the gods who are kept back from the fight.
: 'deprive of'; only here in act., the pass. in 785 and in Hesiod.

: σφέτερος is only twice used by Ap. in its proper sense (1. 530, 4. 1294). He uses it also (a) = ἑός, ὅς, as here; (b) = ἡμέτερος, 4. 1353; (c) = ὑμέτερος, 4. 1327. Hesiod has usages (a) and (c), Sc. 90, Op. 2.

div.p: The truth that 'swords and pistols are not the weapons of diplomacy' was early realized; cf. Eur. Phoen. 516, πᾶν γὰρ ἐξαιρεῖ λόγος )\Ο καὶ σίδηρος πολεμίων δράσειεν ἄν : Ter. Eun. 4. 7. 18, Omnia prius experiri, quam armis, sapientem decet. Qui scis, an, quae iubeam, sine vi faciat?

div.seg: : 'in seemly fashion'; cf. h. Hom. Merc. 138, αὐτὰρ ἐπεί τοι πάντα κατὰ χρέος ('as is meet') h)/nuse dai/mwn. Lehrs, wrongly, 'pro necessitate.'

: for the sing. verb after a parenthesis cf. 949: Thuc. 1. 42, ὧν ἐνθυμηθέντες, καὶ νεώτερός τις παρὰ πρεσβυτέρων μαθών, ἀξιούτω
κ.τ.λ.

: probably 'anything different'; cf.
Od. 14. 168, ἄλλα παρὲξ μεμνώμεθα 'let us turn our thoughts to other matters.' Others take παρέξ closely with ἔσκε, neque erat seorsum, qui aliud suaderet; so de M. "et il n'y avait pas de dissident qui proposât un autre plan de conduite."

: some variety of osier or willow, mentioned by Hippocrates (667, 47), and in a list of trees in Eupolis, Αἶγες fr. 14 (Kock). Hesych. explains πρόμαλος as μυρίκη (tamarisk) ἢ ἄγνος (willow, withy); cf. Et. Mag. 689, 41, παρὰ Ἀπολλωνίῳ πρόμαλοι, εἶδος ἀγρίας δρυός.

div.p: The Schol. says that the account of these curious rites is taken from the Νόμιμα Ἀσίας of Nymphodorus. Cf. Ael. V.H. 4. 1, Κόλχοι δὲ τοὺς νεκροὺς ἐν βύρσαις θάπτουσι, καὶ καταρράψαντες ἐκ τῶν δένδρων ἐξαρτῶσι: Sil. Ital. 13. 486, At gente in Scythica subfixa cadavera truncis Lenta dies sepelit, putri liquentia tabo.

div.seg:
: 'burying.' For this strange use of στέλλειν I can find no parallel. L. and S. cite υἱέα δ’ ὡς ἔστειλε in this sense from the Anth. (?) without fixing the reference. περιστέλλειν was used at times meaning 'to bury,' its first meaning being 'to dress the dead in funeral robes,' 'to lay out' as in
Od. 24. 293, οὐδέ ἑ μήτηρ Κλαῦσε περιστείλασα.

: the use of the dual shows that Ap. believed in Zenodotus' theory that in Hom. sometimes the dual and pl. are used indiscriminately; see Leaf on Il. 1. 567, 5. 487, etc. Merkel suggests that Ap. is imitating h. Hom. Ap. 487, ἱστία μἐν πρῶτον κάθετον λύσαντε βοείας , where the dual is clearly used for the pl. See also on 1. 384.

: 'howbeit the earth obtaineth rights equal to the air.' ἠέρι ἴσην is an instance of the comparatio compendiaria; cf.
Il. 17. 51, κόμαι Χαρίτεσσιν ὁμοῖαι. For ἔμμορεν see note to 4 supr.
: for the comparative denoting opposition (here to the male sex) v. Monro, H.G. 120.

: ἀντὶ τοῦ, οὗτος γὰρ ὁ τρόπος τοῦ νόμου. Schol. It is an echo of phrases like ἡ γὰρ δίκη ἐστὶ γερόντων,
Od. 24. 255.

div.p:
Cf.
Od. 7. 14,
kai\ to/t' *)odusseu\s w)=rto po/lind' i)/men: a)mfi\ d' *)aqh/nh
*pollh\n h)e/ra xeu=e fi/la frone/ous' *)odush=i
:
Aen. 1. 411,
At Venus obscuro gradientes aere saepsit
Et multo nebulae circum dea fudit amictu.

div.seg: : 'at the entrance' (to the courtyard), see note to 1.260.
: see note to 39 Ap. is imitating the description of the palace of Alcinous in Od. 7, and of the home of Calypso in Od. 5.

: 'capitals,' τορεν/μασι ἢ κιονοκράνοις. Schol. The line is quoted in Et. Mag. with the gloss γλυφὶς καὶ ἡ κεφαλὴ τοῦ κίονος. The word is only used here in this sense; cf. τρίγλυφος. For its ordinary meaning v. 282.

: sc. ἄμπελοι, 'cultivated vines'; cf.
Od. 5. 68, ἡ δ’ αὐτοῦ τετάνυστο περὶ σπείους γλαφυροῖο Ἡμερὶς ἡβώωσα, τεθήλει δὲ σταφυλῇσι.

div.p:
Cf.
Od. 5. 70, κρῆναι δ’ ἑξείης πίσυρες ῥέον ὕδατι λευκῷ . For πίσυρες see note to 1.671.

div.seg: : Ap. lengthens the υ in compounds of βλύω here and in 4. 788, 1417, but shortens it in 4. 1238. In 4. 1446 we have ἔβλυσε (from βλύζω) with short penult. Hom. has ἀποβλύζων ( Il. 9. 491).
: for the trans. use cf. h. Hom. Ap. 380, χῶρον ἔχουσ’ ἐρατὸν προρέειν καλλίρροον ὕδωρ : Theocr. 5. 124, Ἱμέρα … ῥείτω γάλα.
: the lengthening of the first syll. is un-Homeric; cf. 1. 925. Hom. always has υ short in the pres. and impf., but Ap. has it long in ἐδύετο, e.g. 1. 581.
: the Pleiads rise at the end of April, and set at the end of October.

: cf.
Il. 22. 151, προρέει εἰκυῖα … ἐξ ὕδατος κρυστάλλῳ .
: for the cogn. acc. cf. Pind. O. 8. 47, καπνὸν ἀμπνεῦσαι.
: 'of one piece.' In Hes. Op. 433, the αὐτόγυον ἄροτρον is contrasted with the πηκτὸν ἄροτρον in which the γύης 'plough-stock,' ἔλυμα 'share-beam,' and ἱστοβοεύς 'pole' are mortised together.

: father of Aeetes; πέπλασται ὁ μῦθος διὰ τὴν τοῦ θεοῦ τῶν ποδῶν χωλότητα· οὐ μέντοι πιθανῶς· μείζονα γὰρ εἶχεν δύναμιν τῶν Γιγάντων, δῑ ἧς αὐτοὺς ἐτρέψατο ἄν. ὁ μέντοι Ἀπολλώνιος αἰτίαν ἀποδέδωκε, δῑ ἧς ὁ Ἤφαιστος κατεσκεύασε τῷ Αἰήτῃ τούς τε χαλκώνυχας ταύρους καὶ τὸ ἄροτρον. ὅτι δὲ δυνατὸς ἧν Ἤφαιστος Ὄμηρος ἔδειξεν ἐπὶ Ξάνθου τοῦ ποταμοῦ. Schol. For the victory of Hephaestus over the giants see Apollod. 1. 6. 2.
: Phlegra, the scene of the conflict between the gods and giants, was identified with Pallene in Chalcidice and various other volcanic districts.
: 'the inner court'; τὸ μέσον τῆς αὐλῆς, ὄπου τῶν βυῶν αἱ στάσεις. μέσαυλον δὲ οἱ Ἀττικοὶ τὴν φέρουσαν εἴς τε τὴν ἀνδρωνῖτιν καὶ γυναικωνῖτιν. Schol. The former is the Homeric meaning.
: 'chambers.' In describing the Homeric house Monro (Od. App. v) says, "Any room except the μέγαρον may be called a θάλαμος or chamber."

: the whole length on either side: cf.
Od. 5. 439, νῆχε παρέξ 'was swimming along the shore.'
: 'crosswise,' see note to 1.1235. These loftier buildings were situated transversely to the αἴθουσα.

div.p: 'before he took Eidyia as lawful wife.'
div.seg:
: literally 'the knowing one' (cf. Ἴδμων, 1. 139 ). Hesiod calls her Ἰδυῖα,
Th. 958,
*ai)h/ths d' ui(o\s faesimbro/tou )heli/oio
*kou/rhn *)wkeanoi=o telh/entos potamoi=o
*gh=me qew=n, boulh=|sin *)idui=an kallipa/rh|on
. From her Medea may have inherited her skill.
: 'the very youngest,' ἅπ. λεγ. -- see note to 1.43.

: cf. 1236. This name is used not only for Absyrtus but also for the son of Helios, 4. 598, etc. The Colchian people call Absyrtus Phaethon, even as the Trojan people call Scamandrios, the son of Hector, Astyanax ( Il. 6. 402).

: 'her (i.e. Medea) the heroes beheld going from her chamber to the chamber of her sister in quest of her.' The passage is a harsh anacoluthon: the verb which should govern τὴν μετιοῦσαν, such as τέτμον or ἐνόησαν, is omitted after the parenthesis (250-52), and a fresh constr. begins in 253. For similar anacolutha v. 4. 435-42, 852.

div.p: 'For Hera kept her in her home, though seldom aforetime was she within the house, but she ministered in the temple of Hecate from morn till eve.' For θάμιζεν cf. 2. 451.

div.seg: : 'was quick to hear'; cf. Il. 17. 256, where Leaf says, "the power of hearing being regarded as something which goes out of a man is naturally called 'keen' when it penetrates to a long distance.'

: cf. Cat. 64. 319,
Ante pedes autem candentis mollia lanae
Vellera virgati custodibant calathisci.

: 'spindles,' cf. 4. 1062. Virg. may have had this passage before his mind in
Aen. 9. 476, excussi manibus radii, revolutaque pensa , though more immediately
Il. 22. 448, τῆς δ’ ἐλελίχθη γυῖα, χαμαὶ δέ οἱ ἔκπεσε κερκίς.
: the Schol. censures this use for ὑψόσε, but see on 1. 63. We have ἔκτοθι = ἔκτοσε (255) and τηλόθι = τηλόσε (261).

: this use of the impf. of μέλλω to denote what is destined is peculiar to epic poetry, cf.
Il. 5. 686,
e)pei\ ou)k a)/r' e)/mellon e)/gwge,
*nosth/sas oi)=ko/nde …
*eu)frane/ein a)/loxon
: Ap. 1. 1309, etc.

: imitated in
Aen. 5. 83, nec tecum Ausonium, quicunque est, quaerere Thybrim.
: = ὑμετέρην, as in 2. 332; see note to 1.1113.
: this form is only found here. For the plpf. expressing suddenness v. Goodwin, M.T. 32. Cf. 1. 1329.

: 'in great numbers'; cf.
Il. 3. 384, περὶ δὲ Τρῳαὶ ἅλις ἦσαν.

: for the causal sense cf. 4. 391, Anth. P. 7, 385, θυμὸν … ἔζεσας,
Aesch. Pr. 370, ἐξαναζέσει χόλον. Similar examples are προρέεσκε (225) and ἐπαΐσσων (1. 1254).
: cf. ἐξανίεσκον, 4. 622 . These forms, which are not Homeric, are modelled on ἀνίεσκε, Hes. Th. 157 .
: Ap. formed this new verb from the Homeric ὑποδράω 'to minister to' and ὑποδρηστῆρες 'servants.'
: 'clear,' διαφανοῦς. Schol.; cf. Eur. Or. 1376, πολιὸν αἰθέρ’ ἀμπτάμενος.
: 'tumultuous,' 'full of turmoil;' see note to 120 For the intrans. use of τέτρηχα see note to 1.1167. de M. wrongly renders, "portant avec lui le trouble de la passion."
: see note to 1.1265. Ap. is imitating Anacr. 3. 27, Τανύει δὲ καί με τύπτει Μέσον ἦπαρ, ὥσπερ οἶστρος· Ἀνὰ δ’ ἅλλεται καχάζων. For φορβάσιν see note to 2.89.
: cf. Call. fr. 46, βουσσόον, ὅντε μύωπα βοῶν καλέουσιν ἀμορβοί. The word had the double meaning of 'spur' and 'gadfly;' cf. Plat. Apol. 30e: Aesch. Pr. 675.

: 'lintel,' limen superius; cf. Theocr. 2. 60, θρόνα ταῦθ’ ὑπόμαξον Τᾶς τήνω φλιᾶς καθ’ ὑπέρτερον. In
Od. 17. 221 φλιαί means 'jambs.'
: 'fore-hall,' the vestibule to the μέγαρον, formed by the space covered by the αἴθουσα running along the inner side of the αὐλή.

div.p:
Imitated from
Il. 4. 116, ἐκ δ’ ἕλετ’ ἰὸν Ἀβλῆτα, πτερόεντα, μελαινέων ἕρμ’ ὀδυνάων.

div.seg:
: 'with quick glances'; cf.
Il. 9. 180, δενδίλλων ἐς ἕκαστον 'looking meaningly at each.' Doederlein refers it to *δένειν δονεῖν, to turn oneself about; Fick explains it as a redupl. form *δενδίλjω connected with Skt. A-dar to trouble oneself, take thought for; Curtius compares the redupl. with that in δέν‐δρἑv)ο‐ν beside δνῦς.

: 'stretching it'; cf.
Aen. 9. 623, intendit telum, diversaque bracchia ducens , etc.

: cf. Pind. P. 4. 328, ἡμιθέοισιν πόθον ἔνδαιεν Ἤρα :
Aen. 4. 2, vulnus alit venis et caeco carpitur igni : Cat. 64. 92 (of Ariadne),
non prius ex illo flagrantia declinavit
Lumina, quam cuncto concepit corpore flammam
Funditus atque imis exarsit tota medullis.

: the same comparison occurs in 1. 544, 4. 173; cf.
Il. 13. 330, φλογὶ εἴκελον ἀλκήν.
: cf. Aesch. Ag. 239, ἔβαλλ’ ἕκαστον ἀπ’ ὄμματος βέλει φιλοίκτῳ : ib. 743, μαλθακὸν ὀμυάτων βέλος, δηξίθυμον ἔρωτος ἄνθος. For ἀμαρύγματα see note to 2.42.
: 'in the direction of.' Here, as in 675, 1404, ὑπό c. acc. is used in a way that is not Homeric (Oswald).
: 'and in her breast her anxious heart throbbed wildly in its pangs.'
: πνοὴν ἔπεμπον ἢ μετεωρίζοντο. Schol.; cf. 688, 2. 81, 4. 1673.
: frequent in Hom. of a mind quick to perceive, so here of the heart 'sensitive,' 'responsive.'
: 'but her soul melted away in sweet sorrow.'
: = κατετήκετο, cf. 1131. In both passages L. and S. explain 'to overflow with.'

div.p:
'As a woman who laboureth with her hands, and whose craft is weaving, strews dry twigs around a smouldering firebrand, that she may kindle light by night beneath her roof when she must rise betimes; and a flame of wondrous power, roused from a tiny brand, consumeth the twigs -- even so did Love, merciless Love, crouching beneath her heart burn stealthily; and her soft cheeks did ever change their hue, now pale, now red, in her anguish of heart.' The simile of the toil-worn weaver is used again in 4. 1062 to illustrate Medea's fears. Homer employs a similar comparison in
Il. 12. 432,
a)ll' e)/xon, w(/ste ta/lanta gunh\ xernh=tis a)lhqh/s,
*)/hte staqmo\n e)/xousa kai\ ei)/rion a)mfi\s a)ne/lkei
*)isa/zous', i(/na paisi\n a)eike/a misqo\n a)/rhtai.
Virgil imitates all three passages in describing Vulcan speeding to his forge at early morn,
Aen. 8. 408,
cum femina primum
Cui tolerare colo vitam tenuique Minerva
Impositum, cinerem et sopitos suscitat ignes
Noctem addens operi
, etc. For the keeping a flame alive at night cf.
Od. 5. 488, ὡς δ’ ὅτε τις δαλὸν σποδιῇ ἐνέκρυψε μελαίνῃ … Σπέρμα πυρὸς σώζων κ.τ.λ.

div.seg:
: 'right early.' Ap. seems to have adopted this temporal sense of ἄγχι from
Od. 19. 301, ἐλεύσεται ἤδη Ἄγχι μάλα , where Eustath. so explains it, though most editors take it there in its usual local sense. Merkel's objection that ἄγχι 'foret mox non temperi' does not seem convincing: to rise 'soon' and to rise 'early' come to much the same thing.

: cf.
Aen. 4. 67,
est mollis flamma medullas
Interea, et tacitum vivit sub pectore vulnus.
: 'cruel'; cf. Virg. E. 8. 47, saevus Amor : Enn. Fab. 259, Medea, animo aegra, amore saevo saucia. L. and S. take οὖλος as ὅλος here and in 1078, explaining 'vigorous,' 'vehement.'

: ἅπ. λεγ. Prop. expresses the same change from blushing to paleness, 1. 15. 39, Quis te cogebat multos pallere colores? ; cf. Cat. 64. 100,
Quantos illa tulit languenti corde timores,
Quanto saepe magis fulgore expalluit auri.
: ταῖς πολυκηδείαις, τουτέστι ταῖς λύπαις. Schol.; elsewhere it means 'indifference,' e.g. 260 supr., 2. 219.
: δόρπον, the evening meal in Hom., is used loosely for food in later epic; cf. the Homeric σίτοιο ἠσὲ ποτῆτος.
: this form only here; the infin. ἀρέσαι in Hom. Cf. 901, 4. 373.

: 'has some mischance thwarted you in speeding your course?' Cf.
Il. 8. 408, αἰεὶ γάρ μυι ἔωθεν ἐνικλᾶν, ὅττικεν εἴπω. The dat. σωομένοις is on the analogy of verbs of opposition, e.g. δηριᾶσθαι. For the form σώομαι see on 2. 296, 1010. Schneider's ingenious suggestion, ἄνην for ἄτη, is based on Call. Jov. 90, αὐτὸς ἄνην ἐκόλουσας, ἐνέκλασσας δὲ μενοινήν.
ἄνω has long α.
: 'putting forward.' The gen. may be absolute or governed by πείθεσθαι, cf. Hdt. 1. 126, ἐμέο πείθεσθαι.
: 'for I marked it, when once I was whirled in my father the Sungod's car' (Way).

: the home of Circe, the Homeric Αἰαίη, was early identified with the Circeian promontory in Latium on the Tyrrhenian Sea; Hes. Th. 1011,
*ki/rkh d' *)heli/ou quga/thr *(uperioni/dao
*gei/nat' *)odussh=os talasi/fronos e)n filo/thti
*)/agrion h)de\ *lati=non …
*oi( d' h)=toi ma/la th=le muxw=| nh/swn i(era/wn
*pa=sin *gurshnoi=sin a)gakleitoi=sin a)/nasson.
Cf. 4. 850.
: 'the obstacles which have arisen in your path'; ἐν ποσίν = ἐμποδών.
: 'fearing for the safety of.' For the usual constr. of ὑποδ. v. 2. 821. Argus acts as spokesman, as in 2. 1122.
: sc. νῆα. For the wreck see 2. 1118.

: 'having fallen on some timbers' (when the vessel broke up). Ap. was thinking of Od. 12. 438 sqq. where Odysseus drops from a tree and catches hold of the δοῦρα of his vessel which have been vomited forth by Charybdis, and makes his way to land ἑζόμενος ἐπὶ τοῖσιν. In Ap. πεπτηῶτα (‐τας) is from πίπτω (not πτήσσω), as also πεπτηότες (‐τας), 4. 1263, 1298. He has πεπτηυῖα from πτήσσω 2. 535; but from πίπτω 4. 93, 1454. The reading ὑπὸ yields no sense, and was due to phrases like πῖπτον ὑπὸ δούρασι, 3. 1375 , and the Homeric ὑπὸ τεύχεσι πεπτηῶτες (of men lying in ambush),
Od. 14. 474. There seems to be a similar confusion of ἐπὶ and ὑπὸ in 4. 1263, τῇδ’ ὑπ’ ἐρημαίῃ πεπτηότας.

: cf.
Od. 5. 402, π(όχθει γὰρ μέγα κῦμα ποτὶ ξερὺν ἠπείροιο.
: detinebat. i.e. kept them on the island to befriend the sons of Phrixus. Such a use of ἀπερύκω (= ἐρύκω, 250) is unique. See on 174.
: 'the object of their quest,' see note to 33
: cf. Aesch. Ag. 773, οὐ γὰρ σ’ ἐπικεύσω (Musgrave).
: with ἱέμενος, "being fain with exceeding vehement spite" (Way).

div.p: 'he avows that the race of Aeolus shall not escape the grievous wrath and indignation of relentless Zeus, nor the awful pollution and retribution coming from Phrixus.' Cf. 2. 1194. For στεῦται see note to 2.1204.

div.seg: : in mentioning Colchian ships Ap. abandons the usual legend that the Argo was the first ship ever built.
: 'utterly'; see note to 2.283. The Schol. explains it by ἀθρόως, which may mean 'all at once.'
: here aor. act.: in 1147 infr. and in 2. 298 it is aor. pass.
: for this use of the neut. for the masc. cf. Theocr. 7. 4, εἴ τί περ ἐσθλὸν Χαῶν τῶν ἐπάνωθεν : Hor. S. 1. 6. 1, Lydorum quidquid Etruscos Incoluit fines.

: cf.
Od. 4. 81, πολλὰ παθὼν καὶ πόλλ’ ἐπαληθεις :
Aen. 1. 3, multum ille et terris iactatus et alto.

: the boundaries of the Sauromatae, who dwelt near the Sea of Azov, are given in Hdt. 4. 21. Their feuds with the Colchians are not recorded elsewhere. Diodorus (4. 45) mentions the legend that Circe (sister of Aeetes) was married to their king, and, after poisoning her husband, ruled her subjects in tyrannical fashion.

div.p: See on 2. 1160.

div.seg: : ἐπιχώομαι 'to be wroth at' is ἅπ. λεγ., though χώομαι is common.
: 'his heart surged high with passion.' See on 1. 944.

: cf.
Od. 1. 252, τὸν δ’ ἐπαλαστήσασα προσηύδα , where the Schol. says τὸ ἐπαλαστήσασα δηλοῖ τὸ ἐπὶ τοῖς λεχθεῖσιν ὡς ἀλάστοις καὶ δεινοῖς οὖσι δεινοπαθήσασα. Hom. also uses ἀλαστέω of the wrath which neither forgives nor forgets.

: 'for he deemed that it was on their account the Argonauts had come to his city'; cf. 4. 10. ἐώλπει shows metathesis of quantity for ἠόλπει; cf. ἐῴκει (189) for ἠοίκει. In Hom. ἔλπομαι often means 'to fancy.'

div.p:
Cf.
Il. 13. 474, ὀφθαλμὼ δ’ ἄρα υἱ πυρὶ λάμπετον.

'ere some one of you see the fleece and Phrixus to his sorrow.' For the form of threat cf.
Od. 17. 448, μὴ τάχα πικρὴν Αἴγυπτον καὶ Κύπριν ἴδηαι : Eur. Bacch. 351: Ar. Thesm. 853.

div.seg: : 'straightway accompanying them from Hellas you come hither, not to win the fleece, but to win my sceptre and royal state.' Aeetes, like Medea 775 infr., believes that the sons of Chalciope actually reached Greece and returned with the Argonauts. The lines have been variously misunderstood. Merkel keeps νέεσθαι in 376, apparently as an infin. of indignation, and so de M. renders, "Vous qui vous êtes empressés de partir de l'Hellade, et de venir ici, non pas pour la toison, mais pour ravir mon sceptre et mon autorité royale!"
: 'I would have cast you forth with but your feet left.'

div.p: 'such things have you falsely attributed even to the blessed gods.'
div.seg: : cf. Lucian Tox. 42, ὡς καὶ πολλὰ ἐπιψεύδοιο αὐτοῖς, 'so that you could attribute many things falsely to them.'
: 'bear with me in this emprise,' literally 'restrain thyself, I prithee (μοι eth. dat.), in the matter of, etc.' στόλῳ is dat. comm.

div.p:
Cf. Orph. Arg. 827, οὔτε νυ ληιστῆρες ἱκάνομεν, οὔτε τιν’ ἄλλην Γαῖαν ἐπιστρωφῶντες, ἐγείρομεν ὕβριος αἴσῃ Ἔργ’ ἄδικ’ ἀνθρώποισιν κ.τ.λ.:
Aen. 1. 527,
Non nos aut ferro Libycos populare Penates
Venimus, aut raptas ad litora vertere praedas.
For ἔολπας see note to 370

div.seg:
κ.τ.λ.: cf.
Od. 5. 99,
*zeu\s e)me\ h)nw/gei deu=r' e)lqe/men ou)k e)qe/lonta.
*ti/s d' a)\n e(kw\n tosso/nde diadra/moi a(lmuro\n u(/dwr;

div.p: 'we are ready to recompense thee speedily with our services in war.' πρόφρων c. inf. is very unusual.

div.seg: : 'wheedling him with soft words'; cf. σαίνοντες (1. 1145), Jebb on Soph. Ant. 1213.

κ.τ.λ.: cf.
Il. 14. 20,
w(=s o( ge/rwn w(/rmaine dai+zo/menos kata\ qumo\n
*dixqa/di' h)\ meq' o(/milon i)/oi …
*)=he met' *)atrei/dhn …
*(=wde de/ oi( frone/onti doa/ssato ke/rdion ei)=nai.
For πόρφυρεν see note to 1.461.
: 'or whether he should put their strength to the test.' For ὅγε see note to 1.308.

: cf.
Aen. 4. 287, Haec alternanti potior sententia visa est.

: Hom. has χέρηι, χέρηα, χέρηες, χέρηα (neut. pl.), which Monro, following Mahlow, explains on the analogy of the Aeolic πλέες (= πλείονες) for πλε‐εες, πλε‐jες‐ες (-- jες = Lat. ior). Ap. has also the usual epic forms χερείων, 2. 77, 3. 465, χερείους, 2. 1220.
: 'to take the goods of strangers:' cf. 591.
κ.τ.λ.: 'for in the case of valiant men I deal not grudgingly after the fashion of the king of Hellas (i.e. Pelias, 334) of whom ye speak.'

div.p: 'an ordeal which I myself compass with my hands, grievous though it be.'

div.seg: : cf. 2. 1268. The Schol. tells us that Antimachus in the Lyde had mentioned the bulls, the work of Hephaestus.
: for the acc., which is not Homeric, cf. 2. 87. We find an acc. with ἀμπνεῖν and ἐπιπνεῖν in 231, 1292, 1327.

: 'of four acres' (five, according to Pherecydes. Schol.), γύης meant primarily the plough-stock (see on 232), and was then used for a portion of ploughed land. Four of these was a good day's ploughing; cf. Od. 18. 374.

: Leaf, on Il. 13. 707, explains this as the headland or edge of the field where the plough turns on finishing the furrow. Curtius connects it, not with τέλος, but with Zend. karesh 'to plough,' Skt. kArS-man 'boundary.'

: a variation of the Homeric Δημήτερος ἀκτή. Δηώ = Δημήτηρ is first found in h. Hom. Cer. 47, πότνια Δηώ . ἀκτή was formerly connected with ἄγνυμι, but, as it is used in Hesiod of standing crops, it is now referred to ὰκ, seen in ἀκή, ἄκρος, acus, and explained of the spiky ears of corn.

div.p: 'the teeth of the dragon which grow into the form of armed men.' μεταλδήσκω is ἅπ. λεγ., μετά denoting the change in the process of growth. δέμας is adverbial, and the datives are used where we should expect a prep. c. acc.

div.seg:
: ased in the same two senses of 'harvesting' and 'slaughtering' in
Il. 19. 223, ἄμητος δ’ ὀλίγιστος, ἐπὴν κλίνῃσι τάλαντα Ζεύς.
: for the ellipse cf. εἰς Ἀίδαο, 2. 353.

: 'to accept the challenge'; cf.
Il. 7. 93, αἴδεσθεν μὲν ἀνήνασθαι, δεῖσαν δ’ ὑποδέχθαι.
: 'closely dost thou fence me within thy claim of right.'

div.p:
Cf. Cat. 64. 102,
Cum saevum cupiens contra contendere monstrum
Aut mortem oppeteret Theseus aut praemia laudis.

div.seg: : cf. Hes. Op. 703, τῆς δ’ αὖτε κακῆς (sc. γυναικός) ou) r(i/gion a)/llo.
: 'Go now to thy comrades,' ὅμιλος being used of the heroes as in 4. 183, etc. Way translates, "Come then to the gathering (at the ordeal)."
: never c. gen. in Hom.; cf. μαιμάω c. gen. 2. 269.
: Rzach points out that this is the only place where Ap. uses the forms in ‐αις, ‐αι in the weak aor. opt. except at the end of the line.

: cf.
Il. 3. 353, ὄφρα τις ἐρρίγῃσι καὶ ὀψιγόνων ἀνθρώπων Ξεινοδόκον κακὰ ῥέξαι.
κ.τ.λ.: 'for, in the meantime, he had made signs to his brethren that they should still remain there.' They were to enlist the sympathies of Chalciope on behalf of Jason.

div.p: Ap. is imitating the meeting of Nausicaa and Odysseus, Od. 6. 235; cf. 1. 1230.

div.seg: κ.τ.λ.: 'and the maiden, casting sidelong glances from beside her shining veil, gazed upon him'; cf. Cat. 64. 86, Hunc simul ac cupidc conspexit lumine virgo Regia , etc.
: i.e. from the side of the veil which hung around her face (see note to 1.760). Cf. Goldsmith, Deserted Village 29, "The bashful virgin's sidelong looks of love."
: 'with anguish smouldering in her heart'; cf. 762: Mosch. 4. 4, Ἔρως δ’ ἔσμυχ’ ἐπαμοιβά: Theocr. 3. 17, Ἔρως … Ὄς με κατασμύχων καὶ ἐς ὀστέον ἄχρις ἰάπτει.
: 'her soul, like a dream, fluttered haltingly in his footsteps as he went.'

: literally 'crawling' cf. 4. 1289. Its use here seems to involve, as Preston says, the notion of eager, yet unavailing and painful endeavour, which the ancients associated with dreams; cf.
Il. 22. 199, ὡς δ’ ἐν ὀνείρῳ Οὐ δύναται φεύγοντα διώκειν κ.τ.λ. :
Aen. 12. 908, Ac velut in somnis ... nequiquam avidos extendere cursus Velle videmur, et in mediis conatibus aegri Succidimus.

: cf.
Od. 11. 222, ψυχὴ δ’ ἠύτ’ ὄνειρος ἀποπταμενη πεπότηται.

: Couat (p. 310), "Nous retrouvons dans ce passage au milieu d'une éloquente peinture des premiers effets de la passion, les métaphores habituelles de l'Alexandrinisme. Aussi bien, Apollonius ne les oubliera pas, même dans les plus beaux endroits de ce drame. Il fera intervenir, non plus Eros seul, mais la troupe turbulente des Eros, et ramènera ainsi notre pensée d'abord séduite et touchée par son pathétique récit, vers les banalités de la littérature érotique. L'intention du poète est évidente; chacun des progrès de l'amour dans le cœur de Médée est signalé par une intervention d'Eros, etc." Cf. Val. Fl. 6. 457, volucrumque exercitus omnis Amorum : Claud. Epithal. Hon. 71, mille ... fratres ... gens mollis Amorum.

: ἐμφατικῶς αἱ προθέσεις. τὴν συνεχῶς ἀνειδωλοποιοῦσαν τῷ νῷ ἐμφαίνει, ὡς παρ’ Ὁμήρῳ "προπροκυλινδόμενος." Schol. See on 1013 infr. Virg. imitates this passage,
Aen. 4. 3,
Multa viri virtus animo multusque recursat
Gentis honos; haerent infixi pectore vultus
Verbaque.
: ἕεστο in 1225. For the connexion of these two forms with the original vεvεστο v. Curt., G.V. ii 147.

: cf.
Aen. 4. 83, Illum absens absentem auditque videtque.
Plato, Menex. 255, speaks of λόγοι ἔναυλοι, 'words which still ring in one's ears.'
: modal dat., see note to 346 For κηδοσύνη cf. 1. 277.

: cf. 635, Theocr. 23. 18, οὕτω δ’ ἀνενείκατο φωνήν. Buttmann shows that the use of this word in the Alex. poets was due to a misunderstanding of
Il. 19. 314, μνησάμενος δ’ ἀδινῶς ἀνενείκατο φώνησεν τε , where they took it to mean 'cried aloud,' though the meaning is rather 'drew a deep breath' or 'recovered himself.' In 4. 1748 we have the Homeric phrase ἀνενείκατο φώνησεν τε, so that Buttm. is wrong in saying that an accusative is
everywhere expressed with this verb by Ap., as there θεοπροπίας is gov. by πεμπάζων.
κ.τ.λ.: 'whether he be the greatest of heroes who goes to his doom, or one of a baser sort, let him perish!'

: 'unharmed.' This is the meaning in the Od.; in the Il. it means 'lifeless,' as in 2. 197. The agitation of Medea's mind is well portrayed in this sudden change of mood, when she hopes against hope that he may be saved, ὄφελλεν being properly used in a wish past realization.
: 'I would, in very truth, that this might come to pass.'
: Hecate, daughter of the Titan Perses; cf. Hes. Th. 409. Bacchylides (fr. 23, Jebb) makes her the daughter of Night, Ἑκατα δᾳδοφόρε, Νυκτὸς μελανοκόλπου θύγατερ.
κ.τ.λ.: ὅτι οὐκ ἐπιχαίρω ἐγὼ κακοῖς. ὁ δὲ λόγος ἐρωτικός. Schol. For ἐπαγαίομαι cf. 1262, and see on 1. 899.

: ἐτετάρακτο καὶ ἐν ἀγωνία ἦν. Schol. This plpf. form is derived by Buttman from εἴλω or εἰλέω 'to squeeze, press, oppress.' An impf. ἐόλει was restored by Boeckh for αἰόλλει in Pind. P. 4. 414, πῦρ δέ νιν οὺκ ἐόλει 'the flame did not trouble Jason.' Boeckh assumes a pres. ἐολέω (αἰολέὠ akin to εἰλέω. We find ἐόλητο again in Mosch. 1. 74, ἐόλητο θυμὸν … ὑποδμηθεὶς βελέεσσιν Κύπριδος.

div.p: 'Thou hast heard from me that a certain maiden useth magic drugs, inspired by Hecate.' For ἐννεσίῃσιν see note to 1.7.
'I fear that my mother would not undertake this for me,' i.e. that Chalciope will not consent to win Medea's aid.
div.seg: : the use of the opt. instead of the subj. is noticed by none of the editors. In Il. 10. 39 we find δειδω μὴ οὔ τίς τοι ὑπόσχηται τόδε ἔργον. The only exx. given in Kühner-Gerth of μή c. opt. after a primary tense are Soph. Aj. 279, δέδοικα μὴ … ἥκοι , and Hdt. 7. 103, ὅρα μὴ … εἰρημένος εἴη , which are now corrected to ἥκει (or ἥκῃ) and ᾖ. Probably ὑποστήῃ should be restored here.
: ὦ γλυκύτατε, προσφιλέστατε, ἐπεὶ καὶ ὁ πέπων μελίχρους. Schol.; cf. 1. 1337.
: 'sorry, in very truth, is our hope, when we have trusted to women for our return.' For μελέη see note to 1.1249.
: a curious use of this stock phrase; φίλος = ἑός, for σφ‐ίλος (sua, ὅς, suus).
: 'were I to tell you at length what hath passed, there would be no end to my tale nor to your questionings.'
: literally 'with these as a condition.' For the correction ὑπὸ cf. 1343.
: see note to 1.366. We also find the forms ὑπέστην 1. 412 , ὑπέστη, 2. 92 , ὑπέσταν, 4. 1389.

: Hom. has ἀνήνυστος,
Od. 16. 111, ἀνηνύστῳ ἐπὶ ἔργῳ . Cf. 4. 1307. Plato describes Penelope's web as ἀνήνυτον ἔργον,
Phaed. 84a.

: cf.
Il. 9. 30, δὴν δ’ ἄνεῳ ἦσαν τετιηότες υἷες Ἀχαιῶν. Ὀψὲ δὲ δὴ μετέειπε βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Διομήδης. In Hom. ἄνεῳ is usually regarded as the plural of an adjective ἄνεως 'silent' (ἀ‐αὔω); once, Od. 23. 93, it is used of one person, and there it is written ἄνεω and taken as an adv. Aristarch., Eustath., and Buttm. maintain that in all cases it is an adv. and is to be written ἄνεω.
: see note to 1.267. Cf. Il. 7. 161-199, where the Greeks are at first dismayed by the challenge of Hector, and then one after another offers himself as an opponent.

div.p: For the thought cf. 2. 332.

'Faithful to thy promise thou shouldst in truth prepare for the ordeal; but if thy soul hath no sure confidence in thy valour, then hasten not to the issue thyself, nor sit by and look round wistfully for one to take thy place, for I at least shall not hold back, since death will be the worst that I can suffer.'

div.seg: : 'I shall not hold back.' The Schol. explains by οὺκ ἀνέξομαι, 'I shall not suffer it'; but, while ἔχομαι may be used for ἀπέχομαι, it is doubtful if it is ever used for ἀνέχομαι (v. Jebb on Soph. Ant. 466).
: αἰζηοί· νεανίσκοι, οἱ τῷ αἵυατι ζέοντες, ἢ οἱ ἄγαν θερμοὶ καὶ θυμώδεις. Hesych. Benfey connects it with Skt. javijas 'younger.'

κ.τ.λ.: 'though there was not a vestige of the down of manhood as yet upon his cheeks'; cf. Call. Ap. 36, θηλείαις οὐδ’ ὅσσον ἐπὶ χνόος ἦλθε παρειαῖς. For οὐδ’ ὅσον see note to 1.290. ἐπανθιάω (= ἐπανθέω) is ἅπ. λεγ.; Apollonius, following Aratus who coins εὐδιάω, ὑπτιάω, φυλλιάω, etc., uses the new forms κατηφιάω (1. 461) , μεσημβριάω (2. 739) , καπνιάω (2. 131) , παρεδριάω (2. 1039).

: only here and in 2. 1086, though common in Hom., especially in the phrase οἱ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἀκὴν ἐγένοντο σιωπῇ. It may have been originally the acc. of a noun ἀκή (ἀ‐χαίνὠ 'silence'; cf. the glosses in Hesych. ἀκήν· ἡσυχίαν: ἀκὴν ἦγες· ἡσυχίαν ἦγες. For the forms ἀκέοις, etc. see note to 1.765.
: 'this, in truth, we may come to at the last'; i.e. to fare forth to do or die, as they proposed, was only a last desperate expedient.
: ἀντὶ τοῦ ἐδίδαξε. Schol.; see note to 1.724.

: 'streaming'; τὸ πολύχυτον· τὸ γὰρ νη καὶ στέρησιν σημαίνει καὶ ἐπίτασιν. Schol. The view that νη‐ could have an intensive force (ἐπίτασιν) is not borne out by the facts of the language, though it was believed by the Alex. writers, who invented this word which occurs in Call. fr. 313. See also on 2. 407.

div.p:
Cf. the description of the Massylian enchantress in
Aen. 4. 487 sqq.,
Haec se carminibus promittit solvere mentes
Quas velit, ast aliis duras immittere curas;
Sistere aquas fluviis et vertere sidera retro.

The eclipses of the sun and moon were attributed to magic, hence καθαίρεσις 'drawing down' was used for ἔκλειψις before the days of Democritus. This power was an especial gift of Thessalian witches; cf. Plato Gorg. 513, Hor. Epod. 5. 45, Virg. E. 8. 69.

div.seg: : = ὑμῖν αὐτοῖσιν, so σοί = σοὶ αὐτῷ, 350.

div.p:
For the portent cf.
Il. 8. 247,
au)ti/ka d' ai)eto\n h(=ke, teleio/taton petehnw=n,
*nebro\n e)/xont' o)nu/xessi, te/kos e)la/foio taxei/hs:
*pa\r de\ *dio\s bwmw=| perikalle/i+ ka/bbale nebro/n.
Virgil had our passage in mind in Aen. 6. 190, where he describes the sudden appearance of the two doves of Venus to guide Aeneas in his search for the golden branch. Apollonius introduces the dove appropriately, as it was sacred to the goddess of love; cf. Ov. Met. 15. 386, Armigerumque Iovis, Cythereiadasque columbas.

div.seg: : 'fell pierced by'; cf. 2. 831. It is first used by Apollonius.

div.p: 'nor is there a better interpretation thereof than to approach the maiden and entreat her, using all our subtlety.' For ὑποκρίνασθαι 'to interpret' cf. Od. 19. 535.

div.seg: : cf. Eur. Bacch. 713, τὸν θεὸν … Εὐχαῖσιν ἂν μετῆλθες.

: Ap. was thinking of
Od. 3. 118, κακὰ ῥάπτομεν ἀμφιέποντες Παντοίοισι δόλοισι , which probably means 'devised mischief, besetting them with every form of stratagem,' though M. and R. prefer to take ἀμφ., not with δόλοισι, but absolutely 'busying ourselves about them.' See on 2. 1158.
: an instance of the praesens propheticum.
: 'in the hands of'; cf. Soph. O.C. 1443, ταῦτα δ’ ἐν τῷ δαίμονι.
: emphatic, 'hers was yon gentle bird that narrowly escaped.'
: literally 'fled out from under,' as the dove flew out from under the swoop of the falcon.

: 'cajole,' cf.
Il. 5. 349, γυναῖκας ἀνάλκιδας ἠπεροπεύεις. Curtius derives it from Skt. apara 'different,' and vεπ, εἰπεῖν, literally 'to say one thing and think another.'
: 'murmured with bated voices.' They muttered, but none joined issue with Idas.

: cf.
Od. 4. 256, καὶ τότε δή μοι πάντα νόον κατέλεξεν Ἀχαιῶν.

: here, and in 1062, the best mss. have ἔαδεν, while in 1. 867 they have ἕαδεν. Editors have adhered to this in their texts, and Rzach says ἕαδεν is perf., ἔαδεν aor. As I can find no evidence of such an aor, as ἔαδεν (Ap. uses εὔαδε), and as the meaning is the same in all three passages, I read the Homeric perf. ἕαδεν in every case.
: leaving the marshy backwater of the Phasis ( ἕλος, 2. 1283 ) they were going now to fasten their vessel openly on the banks of the main channel of the river.

: 'crouching from the battle-cry,' as the birds cower under the foliage in
Il. 2. 312, στρουθοῖο νεοσσοὶ … πετάλοις ὑποπεπτηῶτες.
