: see note to 1.1362. For τυτθὸν ὑπέξ see 1. 1166.
: 'he avowed'; see notes to 337, 2. 1204. The long passage in orat. obl. which follows is un-Homeric and prosaic.
: = αὐτοῖς ἀνδράσιν 'crew and all'; cf. Polyb. 1. 20. 7, τὰς πρώτας συμβαλούσας ναῦς αὐτάνδρους ὰπέβαλον.

: this compound is only found here; cf. ἐκφλύξαι, 1. 275 . φλύω or φλύζω meant (1) to boil over, bubble up, (2) to bluster. Aeetes says, with savage humour, that when the Argonauts are roasting in their burning vessel they may 'sputter forth' their insolence. Cf. the use of ἐπιφλύειν, 1. 481.
: 'he never would have welcomed,' as we see he did, 2. 1147. ἄν is omitted with δέχθαι, see note to 1.197.
: so in Aen. 1. 301 Mercury is sent to Carthage to win a kindly welcome for the Trojans.

: 'that Phrixus might meet with a kindly host.' For προσκηδής cf.
Od. 21. 35, ἀρχὴν ξεινοσύνης προσκηδέος, though others explain it there 'bringing into alliance or kinship.'
: 'much less' nedum, a use peculiar to Ap., see note to 2.192.
: Ap. invents this form for ἐπιδρομαί 'incursions.'
: i.e. separately from Jason and his comrades.
: τιμωρίαν ἀποτίσειν. Schol., see note to 135

: ἅπ. λεγ. The dat. depends on ὀπηδούς as in h. Hom. Merc. 450, ἐγὼ Μούσῃσιν ὀπηδός . Linsenbarth and L. and S., however, say that ὁμιλαδόν here = δμοῦ c. dat., though elsewhere, as in Hom., it is an adv. = turmatim.
: see note to 1.8; ὅτι δὲ χρησμὸς ἦν Αἰήτῃ δεδομένος, ὑπὸ τῶν αὑτοῦ ἐγγόνων ἀπολέσθαι, καὶ Ἡρόδωρος ἐν τοῖς Ἀργοναύταις ἱστορεῖ. τούτου ἕνεκα καὶ τὴν ζεῦξιν τῶν ταύρων λέγει αὐτὸν ἐπινοῆσαι. Schol.

: Wellauer points out that Hom. never uses χρειώ elliptically for χρή, but always χρεώ, and that χρεώ is never used by him to stand for the infin. χρῆναι; so that in these two respects Apollonius differs from the Homeric usage.

div.p: 'wherefore he sent them, when they fain would go, on a long journey to the Achaean land to do their father's bidding.' Cf. 2. 1093 sqq.
'So he in his wrath disclosed his fell designs to the people of the land; and he bade them, with grievous threats, to watch the ship and the sailors that not one might escape destruction.'
div.seg:
: cf.
Il. 15. 97, οἷα Ζεὺς κακὰ ἔργα πιφαύσκεται.

: cf.
Od. 9. 194, αυτοῦ πὰρ νηί τε μένειν καὶ νῆα ἔρυσθαι.

κ.τ.λ.: 'but fear checked her purpose, lest haply she should try to persuade her unseasonably and all in vain, as she shrank from her father's pitiless wrath, or lest, if Medea yielded to her prayers, her deeds should be laid bare and brought to light.'

: imitated from
Od. 19. 390, μή ἑ λαβοῦσα Οὐλὴν ἀμφράσσαιτο καὶ ἀμφαδὰ ἔργα γένοιτο, where ἔργα is used in the same vague fashion, ἀμφαδά is clearly an adj. in our passage, and probably so in Od. l.c., though Ameis takes it there as an adverb.
: here in a causal sense = κατέπαυεν. Contrast Od. 9. 460.

: see note to 563; cf.
Od. 11. 364, ἠπεροπῆα τ’ ἔμεν καὶ ἐπίκλοπον.

: 'disquieted'; cf.
Od. 19. 517, ὀξεῖαι μελεδὼνες ὀδυρομένην ἐρέθουσιν. So Ariadne is faint with fear at the thought of Theseus facing the Minotaur, Cat. 64. 99.
: elsewhere Ap. always uses βουσί. Hom. has both forms.

div.p: '(She dreamt) that her parents set at nought the promise they had given, for it was not on her, their daughter, but on Jason himself that they had laid the ordeal of yoking the oxen; and so strife and disputation arose between her father and the strangers.'

div.seg: : used in Il. 23. 382 of a doubtful result of a race, a dead heat.
: see note to 1.366: we find ἐπέτρεπον, 1. 642.

: cf.
Il. 21. 417, μόγις δ’ ἐσαγείρατο θυμόν :
Od. 7. 283, θυμηγερέων : Ov. Met. 14. 352, ut primum valido mentem collegit ab aestu. See also on 1. 1233.

div.p:
Cf.
Aen. 4. 9, quae me suspensam insomnia terrent!

div.seg:
: 'my heart is in a flutter for the stranger'; cf.
Il. 3. 108, αἰεὶ δ’ ὁπλοτέρων ἀνδρῶν φρένες ἠερέθονται (i.e. are fickle). See on 1. 944.
: 'Medeae servanda erat virginitas, quia Hecates sacerdotio fungebatur' (Brunck); but, as de M. says, such a consideration would hardly occur to Medea's troubled mind.

div.p: 'Nevertheless, though I have banished shame from my heart, I will not yet essay aught without my sister, if haply she entreat me to aid them in their task through anguish for her sons; this would quench the aching that consumes my heart.'
div.seg:
: 'taking to myself a heart of shamelessness'; cf. Theogn. 89, καθαρὸν θέμενος νόον : Aesch. Pr. 163, τιθέμενος ἄγναμπτον νόον. These words are generally mistranslated, e.g.
Lehrs, 'deposito saevo animo': de M., 'laissant de côté toute intention cruelle.' The meaning is fixed by 4. 1669, θεμένη κακὸν νόον. Seaton takes αὐτοκασιγνήτης with both ἄνευθεν and πειρήσομαι, "I will no longer keep away from my sister, but will make trial of her to see whether, etc." comparing Il. 2. 27.

: ἀνυπόδητος. Schol. Rzach seems wrong in saying that Ap. models this form on the analogy of the Homeric ἀελλίπος ἀρτίπος, etc. In Soph. O.C. 349 we find νηλίπους (v. Jebb), and in Lyc. 635; in Theocr. 4. 56 ἀνάλιπος , where the Schol. cites a form ἦλιψ 'a shoe.'
: ἅπ. λεγ. for οἰοχίτων, μονοχίτων; cf. Eur. Hec. 933, λέχη δὲ φίλια μονόπεπλος λιποῦσα, Δωρὶς ὡς κόρα. For ἑανός see on 4. 169.

: there is one instance in Hom. also of the local ‐δε with persons.
Il. 24. 338, Πηλεϊωνάδ’ ἱκέσθαι.
: 'and again she shrank back within her chamber.' This intrans. use of ἀλεείνω is unique.

: μάταιοι. Schol.; cf.
Od. 3. 316, τηϋσίην ὁδόν. Düntzer connects it with ταΰς 'big,' so that its primary meaning would be 'over-big,' 'impracticable.' Ibycus, however, used the form αὔσιον (Et. Mag. 171, 7). In Bacchyl. 5. 81 we find μὴ ταΰσιον προΐει … ὀιστόν, and in h. Hom. Ap. 540 τηΰσιον ἔπος.

div.p:
Virgil imitates this in the death agonies of Dido,
Aen. 4. 690,
Ter sese attollens cubitoque adnixa levavit,
Ter revoluta toro est,
etc. See also on 683.

div.seg: : ὁ νοῦς, καθάπερ δὲ νύμφη ἐκδοθεῖσα ὑπὸ τῶν γονέων καὶ τῶν ἀδελφῶν εἰς γάμον ἀπολόμενον κατά τινα μοῖραν τὸν γήμαντα πρὶν ἐπ’ ἀλλήλοις τερφθῆναι διακαιομένη τὴν ψυχὴν ὑπὸ λύπης ἐν τῷ θαλάμῳκλαιει, αἰδουμένηκαὶ τῶν θεραπαινίδων τὴν ἐντροπήν, ἵνα μή τις αὐτὴν μωμήσηται προσιουσῶν γυναικῶν. Schol.

: 'love's devices.' "When fates relentless the dear youth remove; Untried the joys, the tender thefts of love" (Preston). There is no parallel to this use of δήνεσιν, which Herwerden regards as 'infelix veteris lacunae supplementum,' some word like ἥβης or εὐνῆς ( Od. 23. 346) having fallen out.
: cf. Epigr. 1046. 12 (Kaibel), γήραι ἐν ἀζαλέωι χήρηι περικείμενον εὐνῆι: Prop. 2. 9. 15, viduo ... toro.
: λοιδορήσωσι. Schol. Only found here and in 4. 1725. Hesych. στοβάζειν· κακολογεῖν. στόβος· λοιδορία. Cf. Lyc. 395, κόκκυγα κομπἀζοντα μαψαύρας στόβους.
: pedisequa. The fem. form only here; the masc. ἑπέτης in Pind. P. 5. 4, where wealth is described as πολύφιλον ἑπέταν.
: 'did she lightly regard' the tidings; see note to 1.149.
: cf. Eur. Hec. 655, δρύπτεταί τε παρειὰν δίαιμον ὄνυχα τιθεμένα σπαραγμοῖς. Hom. has ἀμφιδρυφὴς ἄλοχος (Il. 2. 700) , and ἀμφίδρυφοι παρειαί (Il. 11. 393).

: cf.
Od. 17. 103, δάκρυσι πεφυρμένη : Eur. Or. 1411, ὄμμα δακρύοις πεφυρμένοι.

: Doric for θεομορίη (= θεόμορος), cf. 974. We find θευμορίη (= θεοῦ μοῖρα. Hesych.) in Call. Epigr. 30. 4, χαλεπῇ δ’ ἤντεο θευμορίῃ. The notion that illness is specially sent by heaven is found in Hom., e.g. Od. 9. 411.

: 'would to heaven that I were not now beholding, etc.' This impers. use of ὄφελλε in a wish is unique. ὀφείλει impers. = oportet is found in Pind. N. 2. 6. Another very curious constr. occurs in Orph. Arg. 1164, ὤμοι ἐγών, ὄφελον με … ὀλέσθαι. Callimachus uses ὤφελε simply as an adverb in wishes, Epigr. 17. 1, ὤφελε μήδ’ ἐγένοντο θοαὶ νέες.

: this reminds one of the wish quoted by Cicero (e.g. Fam. vii 30) from some old poet "evolem Ubi nec Pclopidarum nomen nec facta aut famam audiam." Chalciope instils into Medea's mind the thought of flight from Colchis; so Anna fans the frantic passion of Dido in Aen. 4. 31 sqq.
: here ἐρυθαίνω is intrans., as probably in 1. 791; in 4. 474 it is trans.

: cf. Theocr. 9. 30, ἐπὶ γλώσσας ἄκρας : 25. 65, ἂψ δ’ ὄκνῳ ποτὶ χεῖλος ἐλάμβανε μῦθον ἰόντα. This line and 654 supr. are copied in Ov. Her. 4. 7,
Ter tecum conata loqui ter inutilis haesit
Lingua, ter in primo destitit ore sonus.

div.p: 'And often she wildly strove to make utterance with her sweet lips.'
div.seg:
: cf. 755; only here c. inf. 'to desire madly.' For ἀνὰ στόμα cf.
Il. 2. 250, τῶ οὐκ ἂν βασιλῆας ἀνὰ στόμ’ ἔχων ἀγορεύοις.
: literally 'she went no further with her voice,' i.e. the words did not pass her lips.

: ἀντὶτοῦἐθορύβουν. Schol. Here, and in 4. 1725, the mss. are strongly in favour of augmented iterative forms, contrary to the general rule. In Hom. we have one certain instance,
Od. 20. 7, αἳ μνηστῆρσιν ὲμισγέσκοντο , and παρεκέσκετο,
Od. 14. 521 , ἀνεμορμύρεσκε, 12. 238 , are probably sound. For Ἔρωτες see on 452.
: Hom. uses the simple κνώσσω 'to slumber.' Curtius connects it with νεύω, νυστάζω, con-niv-eo, rt. [κ]νυ.
: the dream is still vividly present.
: 'a flood of anguish surged within her soul.'
: σύν may be adverbial as in 707, 1175, 4. 1166, etc. L. and S. assume a new comp. συνδρήστειρα, and so apparently the Schol., καὶ συνεργὸς γενέσθαι.

div.p:
'I beseech thee by the blessed gods, by thyself, and by thy parents'; modelled on
Il. 22. 338, λίσσομ’ ὑπὲρ ψυχῆς καὶ γούνων σῶν τε τοκήων.

For the threat cf. 4. 385. Virgil imitates it,
Aen. 4. 385,
Et, cum frigida mors anima seduxerit artus,
Omnibus umbra locis adero; dabis, improbe, poenas.

div.seg: : 'let her head sink upon Medea's breast.'
: a constant Homeric phrase, in which οἷα is equivalent to ὅτι τοῖα.
: 'would that it were surely in my power to save thy sons.'
: ὅτι Κόλχων ὅρκος Οὐρανὸς καὶ Γῆ. Schol.
κ.τ.λ.: 'whatever power is mine thou shalt not be without it, if only thou askest what may be brought to pass.' For περ = γε v. L. and S., Monro. H.G. 353. For ἀντιόωσαν see on 1. 703.
: interim, 'Argus I left within the house while I came hither.'
: cf. Soph. Aj. 693, περιχαρὴς δ’ ἀνεπτόμαν.
: cf. Theocr. 20. 16, καὶ χρόα φοινίχθην ὑπὸ τὤλγεος ὡς ῥόδον ἕρσα.

: cf. 4. 1525. Ap. is imitating
Od. 9. 372, κὰδ δέ μιν ὕπνος ᾕρει.

: kinsmen, connexions by marriage (κηδεσταί), cf. 1274, 4. 91; Eur. Med. 990, κηδεμὼν τυράννων. In Hom., and nearly always in Attic, we find κηδεμών = curator, in which sense Ap. has κηδεμονεύς (1. 98, 271).
: Medea speaks of herself as the daughter of her elder sister Chalciope; so she calls Chalciope's sons her brothers (731).

: ἔν τισι φέρεται μετὰ τὸν "οἴσομαι εἰς Ἑκάτης θελκτήρια φάρμακα ταύρων" καὶ ἕτερος στίχος "οἰσομενη ξείνῳ, εἴπερ τόδε νεῖκος ὄρωρε," ἔν τισι δὲ οὐ φέρεται, ὡς καὶ ἐνταῦθα. Schol. Ruhnken was the first to advocate the introduction of the line as quoted by the Schol. Flor., though not in any MS., into the text, changing οἴσομαι into οἴχομαι. Brunck and Wellauer insert the line, with εἴσομαι in 738. Merkel and Seaton reject it altogether. Gerhard may be right in regarding the reading of our text as that of the second recension, and the reading of Brunck and Wellauer as that of the first recension.
: Chalciope, who now makes known to her sons that Medea will succour them.

: hanc ipsam (i.e. Medea). If this reading is sound, it is the most extraordinary of Ap.'s many vagaries in the use of pronouns. Merkel suggests as somewhat parallel Aristophanes'The scholar and critic, not the comic poet joining τόν to οὔτινα in Il. 14. 416. Samuelsson defends the text by 4. 1316, αὐτὸν δέ μιν ὰμφαδὸν οἶον … προσέειπον (Hom., however, has μιν αὐτόν), as the pronouns τόν, τήν, αὐτόν, αὐτήν, were not sufficiently distinguished by Ap.; he would even read τὰς δέ σφε (for σφι) in 4. 1410. In Plato we find the article τόν with ἐμέ, σέ, and also αὑτόν, but always for special emphasis.

div.p:
This beautiful description of night has been elaborated by Virgil,
Aen. 4. 522 sqq.,
Nox erat et placidum carpebant fessa soporem
Corpora per terras, silvaeque et saeva quierant
Aequora, etc.

div.seg:
: the hiatus after a diphthong in the thesis of the first foot without shortening of the syllable is very rare; cf.
Il. 1. 39, Σμινθεῦ· εἴ ποτέ τοι κ.τ.λ. (Monro, H.G. 380). Weil's objection that the wakeful sailors mar the perfect calm of the picture is hypercritical, and his conjecture νύσταλοι 'drowsy,' which is approved by de M., has nothing to recommend it. Cf. the watchfulness of the helmsman Palinurus in Aen. 5. 835 sqq.
: for the synizesis v. App. ii (h). This is one of the intensely human passages in Gr. literature.

: cf.
Od. 18. 201 (of the sleep sent by Athene to Penelope), ἦ με μάλ’ αἰνοπαθῆ μαλακὸν περὶ κῶμα κάλυψεν. In Il. 14. 358 νήδυμος ὜πνος says εὕδει Ζεύς, ἐπεὶ αὐτῷ ἐγὼ μαλακὸν περὶ κῶμα κάλυψα.
: cf. Varro Atac. ap. Sen. Controv. 16, Desierant latrare canes, urbesque silebant: Omnia noctis erant placida composta quiete.

div.p: Cf. Theocr. 2. 38, ἠνίδε σιγῇ μὲν πόντος, σιγῶντι δ’ ἀῆται, Ἁ δ’ ἐμὰ οὐ σιγῇ στέρνων ἔντοσθεν ἀνία.

From
Od. 15. 8, Τηλέμαχον δ’ οὐχ ὕπνος ἕλε γλυκύς, ἀλλ’ ἐνὶ θυμῷ Νύκτα δῑ ἀμβροσίην μελεδήματα πατρὸς ἔγειρεν. Cf.
Aen. 4. 529,
At non infelix animi Phoenissa (sc. somno posita erat), nec umquam
Solvitur in somnos, oculisve aut pectore noctem
Accipit.

div.seg: : a new form of this participle. We find the Homeric δειδιότες in 1329.

div.p:
'And as a sunbeam dances on the walls of a house, reflected from the water newly poured into a cauldron or perchance a pail; hither and thither it darts and flashes from the swift eddy--even so did the heart of the maiden throb and quiver within her breast.' Virgil borrows this in describing the perplexity of Aeneas,
Aen. 8. 19,
magno curarum fluctuat aestu;
Atque animum nunc huc celerem nunc dividit illuc,
In partesque rapit varias, perque omnia versat:
Sicut aquae tremulum labris ubi lumen aenis
Sole repercussum, aut radiantis imagine lunae,
Omnia pervolitat late loca iamque sub auras
Erigitur, summique ferit laquearia tecti.
Cf. Browning, Pippa Passes, "Aha, you foolhardy sunbeam--caught With a single splash from my ewer."
div.seg: : Knaack's ingenious conjecture δοκοῖς is based on Virgil's 'summi laquearia tecti.'
: the water has been freshly poured, and the eddies on the surface cause the dancing sunbeams.

div.p: "And the tears from her eyes were flowing for ruth, and through all her frame Like a smouldering fire her anguish burned, and coiled its flame Round every fine-strung nerve, and thrilled to her beating brain Where sharpest of all the pang strikes in, when the shafts of pain Are shot to the heart by the Loves that rest them never from harm" (Way).

div.seg: : the great tendon at the back of the neck supporting the head ( τοῦ τριχωτοῦ κρανίου … τὸ θ)πίσθιον [ἐστὶν] ἰνίον, Arist. H.A. 1. 7. 2 ), near the medulla oblongata, the chief centre of sensation. We often read of blows dealt there, e.g. Theocr. 25. 264, αὐχένος ἀρρήκτοιο παρ’ ἰνίον ἔφλασα προφθάς. For the physical particularization, which mars for us the beauty of the passage, cf. Cat. 64. 377, with Ellis' note.
: 'where the unwearying Loves implant their pangs within the soul.'
: ἐμπέσωσιν. Schol., but the verb is trans. as in 153; cf. 4. 113. Hesych. has a gloss ἐνισκίμψαντες· ἐνερείσαντες. For Ἔρωτες see on 452.

: 'she sat in doubt and indecision.' δοάσσατο occurs in Hom. in the set phrase δοάσσατο κέρδιον εἶναι, where the meaning is 'seemed,' and it, as well as δέατο, is referred by Buttman to δάω, δέδαα. Curt. thinks the root is διv 'shine.' Others connect it with δοvός, δοιός, rt. δεv, comparing dubitare. From the Homeric phrase ἐν δοιῇ εἶναι 'to be in doubt' was formed ἐνδοιάζω which occurs in Thucydides. Apollonius, as Buttman suggests, assumed a simple verb δοιάζω 'to doubt,' to which δοάσσατο here is to be referred; cf. 819, δοιάζεσκε βουλάς = διάνδιχα μερμήριξε: 955, δππότε δοῦπον δόασσαι 'when she thought (but was not sure) she heard a sound': 4. 576, δοιάζοντο λεύσσειν 'they thought they saw.' For ἐπιδοιάζω see note to 21
: 'am I now to be in this extreme of misery or in that?'; cf. Eur. Tro. 680, ἔνθα πημάτων κυρῶ.
: for Artemis as the bringer of sudden death to women cf. Od. 11. 172, Il. 6. 205, etc.

: Herwerden objects that the sons of Phrixus had never reached Greece, and says that ἱκέσθαι must mean 'set out,' which is impossible, or else we must read ἵεσθαι, in which the first syll. is elsewhere always long in epic. Medea, however, seems to think, like Aeetes (375), that they had reached Thessaly, and that the Argonauts had come in concert with them. The use of δεῦρο … κεῖθεν in 777 seems fatal to Herwerden's view.

div.p: Cf. 465. For νειόν see note to 1.687.

div.seg: : 'what crafty counsel of deliverance?' In Hom. ἐπίκλοπος is only used of persons.
: in 466 supr. Medea had used this word of Jason 'let him perish,' but now the die is cast, 'perish shame, perish honour!'
: ἐκεῖσε ἔνθα, cf. Call. Apoll. 112, χαῖρε ἄναξ, ὁ δὲ μῶμος ἵν’ δ( φθόνος ἔνθα νέοιτο.
: attracted into the mood of τεθναίην, cf. 1112.
: 'the roof-beam'; cf. the passages quoted on 1. 1065.
: φθαρτικά. Schol. Ap. is the first to use this adj. For the gen. θυμοῦ cf. 4. 921.

: ἐπικαταμωκήσονται. κυρίως δὲ τὸ τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς ἐπικλίνειν καταμωκώμενον. Schol. The cogn. acc. κερτομίας is very curious, literally 'will wink reproaches at me.' For ἐπιλλίζειν see on 1. 486. Merkel strangely suggests that the verb in our passage is not ἐπιλλίζω but ἐπι‐λίζω.
: 'by a fate of mystery' (Way). See on 1. 680.

div.p:
Cf.
Od. 4. 229, πλεῖστα φέρει ζείδωρος ἄρουρα Φάρμακα, πολλὰ μὲν ἐσθλὰ μεμιγμένα, πολλὰ δὲ λυγρά.

div.seg:
: cf.
Il. 9. 570, δεύοντο δὲ δάκρυσι κόλποι.

: 'in streams' (literally 'not in drops'), cf. ἄστακτος Eur. I.T. 1242 , ἀστακτί Soph. O.C. 1251 . In the other passage where ἀσταγής occurs, Soph. fr. 162, κρύσταλλον ἀσταγῆ, it means 'solid' (literally 'not dripping').

: = ὄφρα. This use as a final conjunction is peculiar to Alex. poets; cf. Anth. P. 9. 242, τόφρα … πλώσῃ ἐπ’ οἰκείης εἰς Ἀΐδην ἀκάτου. Hom. once has ὄφρα in the temporal sense of τόφρα,
Il. 15. 547.
: utpote; "jeune fille elle se souvenait des compagnes de son âge et de leur gaieté" (de M.).
: 'if she truly weighed each prospect in her mind': i.e. life appeared more fair than ever, if she were right in the estimate of the joys that were hers.

div.p: 'but he himself went back before them to the ship, separating from them.' For λιασθείς cf. 1. 94, 4. 306. de M., following the Lat. translators, renders "quant à lui, il retourna au vaisseau dont il était jusque alors resté éloigné," which might be defended by 1164 infr

Cf.
Aen. 4. 587, Regina especulis ut primum albescere lucem Vidit , etc.

Modelled on Il. 14. 170 sqq., ἀμβροσίῃ μὲν πρῶτον ἀπὸ χροὸς ἱμερόεντος Λύματα πάντα κάθηρεν, ἀλείψατο δὲ λίπ’ ἐλαίῳ Ἀμβροσίῳ ἑδανῷ … Ἀμφὶ δ’ ἄρ’ ἀμβρόσιον ἑανὸν ἕσαθ’ … Χρυσείῃς δ’ ἐνετῇσι κατὰ στῆθος περονᾶτο … Κρηδέμνῳ δ’ ἐφύπερθε καλύψατο δῖα θεάων Καλῷ νηγατέῳ.

div.seg: : Ap. extends to this perfect participle the Aeolic accentuation as a present which we find regularly in epic in ἀλαλήμενος (1. 1190), ἀκηχέμενος (4. 1260), πεπτάμενος (2. 405). See also on 1. 787.

: 'the troubles which beset her path, in number unspeakable, while others were fated to be added thereto hereafter.' For ἐν ποσίν cf. 314: Soph. Ant. 1327, τἀν ποσὶν κακά: Pind. P. 8. 32, τὸ δ’ ἐν ποσί μοι τράχον.
: 'mules.' Curtius connects it as 'mountain-beast' with ὄρος.

: cf. Sen. Med. 708,
quae fert opertis hieme perpetuâ iugis
Sparsus cruore Caucasus Promethei
: Prop. 1. 12. 10, num me deus obruit, an quae Lecta Prometheis dividit herba iugis? : Val. Fl. 7. 355 sqq.: Auson. 27. 9. 9, sicca inter rupes Scythicas stetit alitibus crux, Unde Prometheo de corpore sanguineus ros Adspergit cautes et dira aconita creat cos.

: i.e. 'Daughter' of Demeter, the name under which Persephone was worshipped in Attica; cf. Hdt. 8. 65, τῇ Μητρὶ καὶ τῇ Κούρῃ. The variant Δαῖραν, which may have come from the earlier recension, was a title of Demeter used especially in connexion with the Eleusinian Mysteries (cf. Lyc. 710). Some explain it as 'the knowing one,' others as 'the torch-bearer.' de M. would read κούρην, and refer it to Hecate herself, the only-begotten daughter of Perses (cf. 1035).
: cf. Il. 13. 323, χαλκῷ τε ῥηκτὸς μεγάλοισί τε χερμαδίοισιν.
: 'this plant first sprang up.' πρωτοφυές is ἅπ. λεγ.; cf. Anth. P. 4. 2, πρωτοφύτους κάλυκας.
: 'the blood divine'; cf. Il. 5. 339, ἄμβροτον αἷμα θεοῖο, Ἰχώρ, οἷός πέρ τε ῥέει μακάρεσσι θεοῖσιν· Οὐ γὰρ σῖτον ἔδουσ’ οὐ πίνουσ’ αἴθοπα οἶνον· Τούνεκ’ ἀναίμονές εἰσι καὶ ἀθάνατοι καλέονται.

: the saffron of the Corycian cave in Cilicia was famous; cf. Strab. 572, 34, τὸ Κωρύκιον ἄντρον ἐν ᾧ ἡ ὰρίστη κρόκος φύεται: Plin. N.H. 21. 17, prima nobilitas Corycio croco : Hor. Sat. 2. 4. 68, Corycioque croco sparsum.
: 'supported on,' 'waving on' a double stalk. In Et. Mag. 551, 48 we find καυλοῖσιν διδύμοισι μετῄορον, which, if not a misquotation, may be from the earlier recension.

div.p: 'the juice of this, like to the dark sap of a mountain-oak, she gathered in a Caspian shell, to use it as a drug.' For the constr., which Haupt (quoted by Ellis on Cat. 64. 238) shows to be peculiarly Alexandrian, cf. 1294: Theocr. 12. 8, σκιερὴν δ’ ὑπὸ φηγὸν Ἠελίου φρύγοντος ὁδοιπόρος ἔδραμον ὥς τις: Hor. A.P. 458, Hic ... Si veluti merulis intentus decidit auceps In puteum foveamve.

div.seg: : as the Caspian was supposed to be connected with the Ocean, the Schol. explains this of the large shells of Ocean.

: only here is the α long in thesis (cf. 1. 1305, 4. 374); it is always long in arsis. If, with Rzach and Gerhard, we adopt ἐνί, we have to lengthen the penult. of Κασπίῃ, a license possible in a proper name. In Hom. the first α of ἀμάω is long only in arsis, and the one apparent instance of its lengthening in the active in thesis, Od. 9. 135, εἰς ὥρας ἀμῷεν, is uncertain.

: Hecate; cf. Lyc. 1176, Πέρσεως δὲ παρθένος Βριμὼ Τρίμορφος (where Tzetz. connects the name with ἐμβριμάρμαι): Prop. 2. 2. 12: Stat. Silv. 2. 3. 38. For her functions as κουροτρόφυς cf. Hes. Th. 450, θῆκε δέ μιν Κρονίδης κουροτρόφον, οἳ μετ’ ἐκείνην Ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ἴδοντο φάος πολυδερκέος Ἠοῦς.
: noctivagam; an epithet applied to the Bacchants by Eur., Ion 718.
: for the local dat. cf. Il. 5. 546, ἄνδρεσσι ἄνακτα.

: cf.
Rom. and Jul. iv. 3, "shrieks like mandrakes' torn out of the earth."
: i.e. the Titan Prometheus (strictly he was only son of a Titan, Iapetus).

: cf. Val. Fl. 7. 368, gemit irritus (this favours αὔτως) ille Colchidos ora tuens :
Aen. 3. 39, gemitus lacrimabilis imo Auditur tumulo (when Aeneas plucks the myrtles and cornels from the grave of Polydorus).
: the penult. is lengthened at the end of the line, as in Od. 9. 398; elsewhere it is short in Hom., cf. Ap. 4. 1289.

div.p: Cf. Od. 6. 316 sqq., where Nausicaa drives homewards.

div.seg: : the wicker body of the car, tied on above the axle, πλέγμα τὸ ἐπὶ ἀμάξης. Hesych.
κ.τ.λ.: cf. 4. 940, h. Hom. Cer. 176, ὣς αἳ ἐπισχόμεναι ἑανῶν πτύχας ἱμεροέντων Ἤϊξαν κοίλην κατ’ ἀμαξιτόν: Cat. 64. 129, mollia nudatae tollentem tegmina surae.

div.p: This simile is from Od. 6. 102, Οἵη δ’ Ἄρτεμις εἶσι κατ’ οὔρεα ἰοχέαιρα Ἤ κατὰ Τηΰγετον … Τερπομένη κάπροισικαὶ ὠκείῃς ἐλάφοισιν· Τῇ δέ θ’ ἅμα νύμφαι, κοῦραι Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο, Ἀγρονόμοι παίζουσι, γέγηθε δέ τε φρένα Λητώ.

div.seg: : a river in Crete, on which was a town of the same name with a shrine of Eileithyia to whom the nymphs of the river (882) were sacred; cf. Od. 19. 188, Call. Dian. 15.
: see note to 2.696. Cf. Call. Dian. 110, Ἄρτεμι … χρύσεα μέν τοι Ἔντεα καὶ ζώνη, χρύσεον δ’ ἐζεύξαο δίφρον, Ἐν δ’ ἐβάλευ χρύσεια, θέα, κεμάδεσσι χαλινά.
: 'to take part in,' future participle, see note to 1.703. Cf. Od. 1. 25 (of Poseidon), ἀντιόων ταύρων τε καὶ ἀρνειῶν ἑκατόμβης.
: this compound is not found earlier.

div.p:
Cf.
Aen. 1. 499,
Exercet Diana choros, quam mille secutae
Hinc atque hinc glomerantur Oreades.
div.seg: : τὰς ἀκολούθους φησί. Schol. This form is only found here. ἀμορβός occurs in Call. Dian. 45, θυγατέρας Λητωΐδι πέμπεν ἀμορβούς, and Nicander uses ἀμορβεύειν = ἀκολουθεῖν.

div.p: For the different nymphs cf. 1. 1226.

div.seg: : 'whimper and fawn'; cf. Od. 16. 163, κύνες τε ἴδον καὶ οὐχ ὑλάοντο Κνυζηθμῷ δ’ … φόβηθεν: h. Hom. Ven. 70 sqq. See also on 1. 1145.

div.p: For the flashing eyes of Medea, descended from the Sun, cf. 4. 727.

div.seg:
κ.τ.λ.: neque sensi non accedendum esse alienigenas ad viros. For οὐδ’ ἐνόησα 'I did not bethink me' cf.
Od. 11. 62, οὐκ ἐνόησα Ἄψορρον καταβῆναι . μετά c. dat. after a verb of motion is found in 1. 648, ἀμειβομένη … ἐς αὐγὰς Ἠελίου ζωοῖσι μετ’ ἀνδράσιν. If correction were necessary, Samuelsson's ἔμμεναι is the best; cf. 1. 779, μετ’ ἀλλοδαποῖσιν ἐόντος Ἀνδράσι : Ov. Pont. 4. 10. 70, in mediis nec nos sensimus esse Getis. But ἴμεν is confirmed by 896, ἀλλ’ ἐπεὶ οὖν ἱκόμεσθα. Merkel's μήνιμα is supposed to mean 'neque memor fui simultatis susceptae cum peregrinis viris.' Schneider, putting a full stop after ἐνόησα and a note of interrogation after στρωφῶσιν, takes ἴμεν as pres. ind. 'peccavi imprudens. ut opinor, non incidemus in hostes?'
: quotidie, ἅπ. λεγ.; ἠμάτιαι in Il. 9. 72. For the new form ἀγέρονται (= ἀγείρονται) see on 1. 716.
: this form is only found here.
: 'having gathered.' The explanation of the Schol., ἀνακλιθεῖσαι, if not a mere mistake, may point to a variant κατὰ καλὰ τερείνης δ’ ἄνθεα ποίης in 898, as Weil suggests.
: 'when the wonted hour comes'; for the acc. see note to 1.278.
: συναρέσκω is used in a peculiar way by Ap. meaning 'to agree upon with another,' cf. 1100, 4. 373.
: προτρέπεται. Schol.; rather 'makes me to turn aside from the path of duty,' cf. παρατροπέων (946).
: here c. gen. as in Soph. El. 883, τίνος βροτῶν λόγον Τόνδ’ εἰσακούσασ’, but in 1. 766 c. ἀπό.

κ.τ.λ.: ὁ νοῦς, ἀγαθὸς μὲν καὶ ἐπιφανέντας καὶ ἀπιόντας εὖ σημειώσασθαι. Schol. This is the view taken by the Lat. translators, e.g. Shaw "peritus quidem advolantes interpretandi aves, peritus etiam eadem sentiendi aufugientibus." de M., who rejects this view as 'un contresens,' rightly renders "habile à tirer des présages des oiseaux qu'il apercevait, habile à conseiller ceux avec qui il allait." Lobeck, Phryn. 624, saw that ἰοῦσιν means iter facientibus. and compares h. Hom. Merc. 294 for the tmesis σὺν … φράσσασθαι.

div.p:
Cf. Ov. Met. 7. 84,
solito formosior Aesone natus
Illa luce fuit: posses ignoscere amanti.
An echo of Od. 11. 142, οὐδ’ ἑὸν υἱὸν Ἔτλη ἐσάντα ἰδεῖν οὐδὲ προτιμυθήσασθαι.

div.seg: : for the dat. cf. 1. 449, 2. 707; Hom. has the acc. with γηθέω, e.g. Il. 9. 77.
: 'for even now, I trow, he foresaw how everything would come to pass.' Cf. Od. 9. 338, ἤ τι ὀισάμενος 'having some foreboding.'

: 'cawing crows'; cf. Hes. Op. 747, μή τοι ἐφεζομενη κρώζῃ λακέρυζα κορώνη. The crow was a lucky omen in love affairs, cf. Nonn. Dion. 3. 119, ἐπαινήσεις δὲ κορώνην, Καὶ γαμίων καλεσεις με θεοπρόπον ὄρνιν Ἐρώτων: Ael. H.A. 3. 9.

div.p: Nonnus closely imitates this passage, Dion. 3. 102, καὶ πτερὰ σεισαμένη φιλοκέρτομον ἴαχε φωνήν.

div.seg: : 'declared'; in Hom. always 'upbraided,' 'censured.' Curtius explains it from ἐν and a reduplication of rt. ἰπ (ἴπτομαι 'hurt').

div.p: There is a clear reference to Call. Ap. 105, ὁ φθόνος Ἀπόλλωνος ἐπ’ οὔατι λάθριος εἶπεν Ὁὐκ ἄγαμαι τὸν ἀοιδόν, ὃς οὐδ’ ὅσα πόντος ἀείδεῑ κ.τ.λ., a passage which was written during the quarrel between the two poets (v. Introd. p. 7). Merkel and Bernhardy assume that our poet is here replying to Callimachus, but Ap. would hardly assign to himself the part of the noisy crow, and the lines have no point as a reply to what Call. had said. Linde holds that the passage refers to Call., but in quite a different way. His ingenious theory is that 927-48 (and probably 917-8) were added when the poem was revised at Rhodes. In the first edition there had been no actual mention of the withdrawal of Argus and Mopsus, it being tacitly assumed, and so Call. had censured their presence at the interview as a flaw in the poem. In consequence Ap. introduced these 20 lines, the strictures of Call. being put in the mouth of the crow, while Ap., in the person of Mopsus, merely smiles (μείδησε, 938), and, though he makes no direct answer to the crow, yet we are now distinctly told that Jason was alone when he met Medea.

div.seg: : Ap. keeps the aspirate in this word, borrowed from Trag., though he uses τούνεκα with Ionic psilosis.
, 'sweet'; in Hom. only used of taste, cf. 1. 456.
: cf. Il. 22. 128, παρθένος ἠίθεός τ’ ὀαρίζετον ἀλλήλοιιν.
: cf. Il. 23. 483, Αἶαν, νεῖκος ἄριστε, κακοφραδές.
: adspirant; cf. Nonn. Dion. 3. 121, ἤλιτον· ἀλλά με Κύπρις ἐπέπνεεν.

: "Cornix non humana quidem sed cornicina lingua Mopsum obiurgat, idque solus intelligit Mopsus" (Hoelzlin); cf.
Aen. 3. 360 (of Helenus), sentis Et volucrum linguas et praepetis omina pennae.
: συνεργὸς καὶ συμπράκτρια τῶν σῶν κινδύνων. Schol. Cf. Od. 6. 32 (of Athene), καί τοι ἐγὼ συνέριθος ἅμ’ ἕψομαι.
: statim, as in 4. 1591, a meaning not in the Lexicons; cf. αὐτοσχεδόν, παρασχεδόν.
: i.e. nothing but the coming of Jason.
κ.τ.λ.: 'of all the games wherewith she would make merry none pleased her long to play thereat.' For the sing. ἐφήνδανεν see note to 192 For ἑψιάασθαι see on 1. 459.
: i.e she broke off one game after another in her restlessness. See on 110 supr.
: the local gen. is rare in Ap. Besides αὐτοῦ we have νειοῖο 1056, χθονός 4. 1478.

: cf. Soph. fr. 58, ἅπαντα γάρ τοι τῷ φοβουμένῳ ψοφεῖ:
Aen. 2. 728, Nunc omnes terrent aurae; sonus excitat omnis Suspensum.
: the Ion. aor. θρέξασκον from τρέχω occurs in Il. 18. 599, 602.

: a comparison suggested by Il. 5. 5, δαῖε οἱ ἐκ κόρυθός τε καὶ ἀσπίδος ἀκάματον πῦρ, Ἀστέρ’ ὀπωρινῷ ἐναλίγκιον, ὅστε μάλιστα Λαμπρὸν παμφαίνῃσι λελουμένος Ὠκεανοῖο. Cf.
Aen. 8. 589, Qualis ubi Oceani perfusus Lucifer unda ... Extulit os sacrum.
: for the scorching power of Sirius cf. 2. 517.
: 'waked the pangs of a luckless love': cf. 4. 4.
: cf. 289; Il. 10. 93, οὐδ’ ἐμοὶ ἦτορ Ἔμπεδον, ἀλλ’ ἀλαλύκτημαι, κραδίη δ’ ἐμοὶ ἔξω Στηθέων ἐκθρώσκει.

: cf. 725, 4. 1525: Archil. 103, τοῖος γὰρ φιλότητος ἔρως ὑπὸ καρδίην ἐλυσθεὶς Πολλὴν κατ’ ἀχλὺν ὀμμάτων ἔχευε: Sapph. 2. 11, ὀππάτεσσι δ’ οὐδὲν ὅρημ’ ἐπιρρομβεῖσι δ’ ὰκουαί. L. and S. wrongly make ἤχλυσαν (or rather ἤχλυσεν) trans. here.
: cf. Ov. Met. 7. 78 (of Medea), et rubuere genae, totoque recanduit ore.

div.p:
Cf. Val. Fl. 7. 403,
haut secus in mediis noctis nemorisque tenebris
Inciderant ambo attoniti iuxtaque subibant,
Abietibus tacitis aut immotis cyparissis
Adsimiles, rabidus nondum quas miscuit auster
; Cat. 64. 106.

div.seg: : 'side by side.' Elsewhere always = παραυτίκα, see note to 1.383.
: 'to question,' a compound not in L. and S.

: cf. Aesch. Ag. 492, τερπνὸν τόδ’ ἐλθὸν φῶς ἐφήλωσεν φρένας. In Hes. Op. 373 we find φηλητής 'deceiver.' Curtius leaves it an open question whether these forms are to be connected with σφάλλω, or, as Fick conjectures, with the root bhal occurring in fallo.
: for this order of words in supplications cf. Eur. Alc. 275, μὴ πρός σε θεῶν: Ter. And. 3. 3. 6, per ego te deos oro.

div.p: Cf. the offer of Jason to Aeetes, 391 supr.

div.seg: : for the contracted form cf. h. Hom. 31. 18, κλῄσω μερόπων γένος ἀνδρῶν. Ap. also uses κληίζεται (4. 1153), κεκλήισται (4. 618), ἐκλήισται (4. 990).
: cf. Od. 8. 149, σκέδασον δ’ ἀπὸ κήδεα θυμοῦ.

: διὰ τούτων ἠθικῶς προκαλεῖται τὴν Μήδειαν εἰς τὸ ἀποπλεῦσαι σὺν αὐτῷ, παράδειγμα φέρων τὴν Ἀριάδνην. Schol. For the story of Theseus and Ariadne, daughter of Minos, v. Cat. 64. 50 sqq. According to the legend in Od. 11. 324 sqq. when they reached the island of Dia (Naxos) in their flight from Crete, Ariadne was slain by Artemis. Others say that she was deserted there by Theseus, who acted either faithlessly (Plut. Thes. 20, Ov. Her. 10), or under the compulsion of Dionysus (Diod. 4. 61, Paus. 1. 20). When thus abandoned, Dionysus took her to wife, placed her among the immortals, and set her marriage-crown among the stars; v. 4. 431, Hes. Th. 947, Ov. Met. 8. 175.

: i.e. not merely saved him, but even sailed away with him. Jason gives a version which suits his purpose. As the Schol. points out, the wrath of Minos against Theseus did not abate, and Jason suppresses the desertion of Ariadne.

: cf. Arat. 71, αὐτοῦ κἀκεῖνος στέφανος, τὸν ἀγαυὸν ἔθηκεν Σῆμ’ ἔμεναι Διόνυσος ἀποιχομένης Ἀριάδνης: Cat. 66. 60,
ne solum in lumine caeli
Ex Ariadneis aurea temporibus
Fixa corona foret.
For κλείουσι see note to 1.216.
: 'to judge from,' 'in accordance with'; cf. Il. 10. 68, ἐκ γενεῆς ὀνομάζων.
: ἅπ. λεγ. = Homeric ἐπητύς; see note to 2.987.

: 'with wondrous sweetness.' Here, and in 832, Ap. may be imitating one interpretation of this adj. in Il. 3. 385, 18. 25, where it is used of garments, viz. 'divine' (ἀμβρόσιος), though more probably it means 'fragrant' (εύώδης).
: for the enallage cf. 1. 355, 4. 170; h. Hom. Cer. 37, τόφρα οἱ ἐλπὶς ἔθελγε μέγαν νόον ἀχνυμένης περ.

div.p: Cf Val. Fl. 7. 433, nec quibus incipiat demens videt, ordine nec quo Quave tenus, prima cupiens effundere voce Omnia; sed nec prima pudor dat verba timenti : Aen. 4. 371.

div.seg: : ἐρωτικὴ ἡ ἐπαναδίπλωσις τῆς προθέσεως· ἐμφαίνει γὰρ μᾶλλον τὸ μετὰ σπουδῆς καὶ προχείρως γεγενῆσθαι τὴν δόσιν. Schol. It intensifies ἀφειδήσασα, 'eagerly and ungrudgingly.' In 4. 1234 προπρό means 'right to the very end,' 'completely.' Ap., who alone uses it, has it also as a prep. c. gen. = πρό, 453 supr.
: cf. Emped. fr. 138, χαλκῷ ἀπὸ ψυχὴν ἀρύσας.

: see note to 1.245. "Yea, now would she even have drawn forth all her soul from her breast, And had laid it with joy in his hands for her gift, had he made request, So wondrously now from the golden head of Aison's son Did Love out-lighten the witchery-flame; and her sweet eyes shone With the gleam that he stole therefrom, and her heart glowed through and through Melting for rapture away, from the lips of the rose as the dew At the sun's kiss melteth away, when the dayspring is kindled anew" (Way).
: the comp. ἀποστράπτω is not noticed by L. and S. For στράπτω (ἀστράπτω) see note to 1.544. We find ἀπαστράπτω in Arat. 430, and c. cogn. acc. in Opp. C. 3. 479, αἴγλην … ἀπαστράπτουσιν ὀπωπαί.
: 'captivated her flashing eyes'; cf. Ov. Am. 2. 19. 19, Tu quoque, quae nostros rapuisti nuper ocellos. For ἀμαρυγάς see note to 2.42.
: cf. Il. 23. 597, τοῖο δὲ θυμὸς Ἰάνθη, ὡς εἴ τε περὶ σταχν/εσσιν ἐέρση, where see Leaf's note.
: cf. Il. 13. 88, ὑπ’ ὀφρύσι δάκρυα λεῖβον.
: 'addressed'; cf. Od. 4. 647. The Schol. says that Soph. in his Κολχίδες introduced a dialogue in which Medea counselled Jason about the ordeal.
: ἅπ. λεγ., on the analogy of ἔμμορεν: 'waiting for the hour which divides the night in twain.' In Od. 14. 434 we find διεμοιρᾶτο with ε lengthened.

div.p: This digging of a trench and offering of sacrifice is modelled on Od. 10. 517 sqq., where Circe instructs Odysseus in the rites which he must perform before he has communion with the souls of the dead.

div.seg: : cf. Od. 10. 527, ἔνθ’ ὄιν ἀρνειὸν ῥέζειν θῆλύν τε μέλαιναν.

: 'lay it raw and entire on the fire.' ἀδαίετον 'undivided' is ἅπ. λεγ.; cf.
Aen. 6. 253, et solida imponit taurorum viscera flammis.
ὠμοθετῆσαι properly meant to lay raw slices cut from the carcass on the thighs which were wrapped in a double layer of fat (Od. 3. 456). As this sacrifice to the gods below was offered whole, the verb is very loosely used.

div.p: So Odysseus is commanded to make libation πρῶτα μελικρήτῳ, i.e. with a mixture of honey and milk; cf. Eur. I.T. 159, where the χοαί consist of milk and wine and honey (ξουθᾶν πόνημα μελισσᾶν). In 1199 infr. mention is made of the milk mixed with the honey. For σιμβλήια v. 1. 880, 2. 132.

div.seg: : cf. Soph. O.C. 490, ἀφέρπειν ἄστροφος (after offerings to the Eumenides): Theocr. 24. 93, ἂψ δὲ νέεσθαι Ἄστρεπτος: Ov. Fast. 6. 164, Quique sacris adsunt respicere illa vetat.
: 'lest haply thou cut short all things (i.e. ruin everything), and thou thyself return not duly to thy comrades.' Cf. Od. 8. 211, ἕο δ’ αὐτοῦ πάντα κολούει 'injures all his own interests.'
: 'soaking,' a verb elsewhere found only in Lycophron.
: 'that thou art equal to,' an intrans. use found in Plato (Legg. 773a) and late prose. Contrast Il. 12. 435, σταθμὸν … ἀνέλκει Ἰσάζουσα.
: i.e. not merely the spear, which was of primary importance for attack, but also the shield and sword.
: 'sprinkled.' The line is an echo of Od. 22. 184, σάκος εὐρὺ γέρον, πεπαλαγμένον ἄζῃ.
: i.e. the Sparti who would spring from the dragon's teeth.
: 'another thing, besides, that will help thee.' For παρέξ cf. 195.

: cf. Il. 13. 707, ἱεμένω κατὰ ὦλκα (*vόλκα, Fick). In 2. 396 ὁμώλακες = confines. The various forms αὖλαξ, ὦλαξ, and ἄλοξ are all connected with ὁλκός (141 supr.), sulcus, root *vελκ, suelq. Hesych. has ὄλοκες, from which Merkel conjectured ὄλοξιν in 1393 infr.

div.p: Pherecydes had told how Cadmus adopted a similar device, and how the Sparti, thinking they were attacked by one another, fought so fiercely among themselves that only five survived.

div.seg: : asperi. For a different use v. 4. 1442. This adj. is closely connected with κάρχαρος 'sharp,' 'sharp-toothed,' Lyc. 34, Τρίτωνος … κάρχαρος κύων (cf. Il. 10. 360, καρχαρόδοντε … κύνε). Curtius refers both words to the root kar 'to be hard or rough.'
: 'to rush straight to the onslaught'; see note to 2.950.
: 'as far as this (ordeal) is concerned'; cf. 1. 334.

: from this Brunck restored tepido for tepidos in Ov. Am. 3. 6. 68,
illa oculos in humum directa modestos
Spargebat tepido flebilis imbre sinus.

: this division of the ὅτ’ of the mss. is in accordance with the view of Aristophanes of Byzantium on Od. 5. 357, where see M. and R. On the ground that ὅτε cannot mean 'because,' and that ὅτι cannot be elided, Bekker has restored ὅ τε and ὅ τ’ in several passages in Homer, ὅ having the same force as in Od. 1. 382, ὃ θαρσαλέως ἀγόρευεν 'in that he spake boldly,' and τε generalising.
: a name familiar to her from the voyage of the sons of Phrixus; cf. 2. 1153.

: the mythical island-home of Circe in the far West,
cf. 4. 661, Od. 10. 135, 12. 3. Circe was said to be either the sister or daughter of Aeetes. The Schol. wrongly explains νῆσος ἐν τῷ Φάσιδί ἐστιν ἡ Αἰαία, ἐν ᾗ τὸ δέρας ἔκειτο, ὥς φησι Φερεκύδης, as this island cannot be referred to here.
: Pasiphae, mother of Ariadne, was the daughter of Helios, and so sister of Aeetes.
: subibat, 'stole over him.' ῥπέρχεσθαι and ὑφέρπειν are more common in this sense.

div.p:
So Aeneas says to Dido,
Aen. 4. 335, nec me meminisse pigebit Elissae Dum memor ipse mei.

Cf. Hdt. 7. 129, τὴν δὲ Θεσσαλίην λόγος ἐστὶ τὸ παλαιὸν εἶναι λίμνην, ὥστε γε συγκεκληιμένην πάντοθεν ὑπερμήκεσι ὄρεσι. τὰ μὲν γὰρ αὐτῆς πρὸς τὴν ἠῶ ἔχοντα τό τε Πήλιον ὄρος καὶ ἡ Ὄσσα ἀποκληίει … τὰ δὲ πρὸς βορέω ἀνέμου Ὄλυμπος, τὰ δὲ πρὸς ἑσπέρην Πίνδος, τὰ δὲ πρὸς μεσαμβρίην … ἡ Οθρυς· τὸ μέσον δὲ τούτων τῶν λεχθέντων ὀρέων ἡ Θεσσαλίη ἐστὶ ἐοῦσα κοίλη.
div.seg: : this passive use is rare; cf. Eur. fr. 1008, ἄροτος … ὄρεσι περίδρομος (of Messenia).
: 'with goodly pastures'; cf. Od. 15. 406, εὔβοτος, εὔμηλος, οἰνοπληθής, πολύπυρος.

: ὅτι Προμηθέως καὶ Πανδώρας υἱὸς Δευκαλίων Ἡσίοδος ἐν πρώτῳ Καταλόγων φησί, καὶ ὅτι Δευκαλίωνος καὶ Πύρρας Ἔλλην. ὅτι δὲ καὶ ὁ Δευκαλίων ἐβασίλευσε Θεσσαλίας Ἑλλάνικος ἐν πρώτῳ τῆς Δευκαλιωνείας φησίν. ὅτι δὲ καὶ ιβ θεῶν βωμὸν Δευκαλίων ἱδρύσατο Ἑλλάνικος ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ φησι συγγράμματι. Schol.

: this form occurs again in 1114; elsewhere Ap. always uses
Ἰωλκός. Hom. has Ἰαωλκός, e.g. Od. 11. 256. It was a city at the head of the Pagasaean Gulf, see note to 1.572.
: we must assume either an ellipse of ἔστι or a strange extension to Oratio Recta of the use of the infin. in Oratio Obliqua, e.g. Plat. Rep. 614b, ἀφικνεῖσθαι ἔφη εἰς τόπον ἐν ᾧ δύ’ εἶναι χάσματε.
: Minyas was the great-grandson of Sisyphus, who was son of Aeolus.

: i.e. from Haemonia (Thessaly); so the Schol. on 2. 1190 says, οἱ Ὀρχομένιοι ἄποικοί εἰσι Θεσσαλῶν. For an account of Orchomenus in Boeotia and the legends of its foundation v. Paus. 9. 34-8, where we have a description of the famous treasure-house of Minyas. The city was called after Orchomenus, the son of Minyas. It is mentioned as Ὀρχομενὸς Μινύειος in Il. 2. 511 and Od. 11. 284 (see the discussion by Schliemann, J.H.S. ii 122 sqq.).
: demulcens, καταμαλάττων. Schol. So Polybius uses καταψάω, e.g. 2. 13. 6, καταψήσαντες δὲ καὶ πραΰναντες τὸν Ἀσδρούβαν.
: οἰκτρῷ καὶ λυπηρῷ. Schol.: more probably 'earnest,' literally 'concentrated,' 'intense' (see note to 1.269).
: 'compacts,' cf. 1. 300; L. and S. 'ties of friendship or relationship.'
: 'wherefore, talk not to me of friendships made with a stranger.'

: 'rumour' which spreads in a mysterious fashion, and so in Hom. its authorship is attributed to the gods, e.g. Il. 2. 93, ὄσσα δεδήει … Διὸς ἄγγελος. Cf. the description of Fama in Aen. 4. 174 sqq. Curtius explains ὄσσα as ὄκγα, Skt. vakyam (vox). For the secondary meaning 'prophetic voice,' 'omen,' v. 1. 1087.
: attracted into the mood of ἔλθοι, cf. 788.
: cf. Od. 5. 419, μ’ ἐξαῦτις ἀναρπάξασα θύελλα.

: 'kinsmen.' This was the primary meaning of ἔται (for σvέται, from the pronom. stem sva); cf. sui = cognati, propinqui. In a wider sense it meant 'clansmen,' those belonging to the same φρατρία or φυλή, e.g. 1. 305.

div.p: 'and many a stalwart husband was delivered from doom by thee.' ἄδην is used absolutely in the sense of multi or omnino. σαοῦν here takes the ablatival gen. like σώζειν (e.g. Soph. Ph. 919, σῶσαι κακοῦ). In 2. 610 we have σώεσθαι c. ἐκ, as in Hom.; so ἐλαύνειν has the simple gen. in 3. 597, but the gen. c. prepp. in 4. 386, 1. 1107, etc. Cholevius, comparing Od. 5. 290, ἄδην (ἅδην) ἐλάαν κακότητος, takes κακότητος with ἄδην and explains "im Uebermasse des Unglücks" (in their excessive tribulation), but ἄδην in Od. l.c. is probably a real acc., see M. and R.

div.seg: : cf. Od. 3. 403, τῷ δ’ ἄλοχος δέσποινα λέχος πόρσυνε καὶ εὐνήν, where πόρσυνε = ηὺτρέπιζε. It was then used generally of the wife 'sharing' her husband's bed, e.g. Od. 7. 347, πὰρ δὲ γυνὴ δέσποινα λέχος πόρσυνε καὶ εὐνήν. See M. and R. on these passages, and Ellis on Cat. 64. 163.
: see note to 1.646. Ap. is imitating Od. 4. 179, οὐδέ κεν ὑμέας Αλλο διέκρινεν φιλέοντέ τε τερπομένω τε, Πρίν γ’ ὅτε δὴ θανάτοιο μέλαν νέφος ἀμφεκάλυψεν.

div.p: 'nevertheless she shuddered to see the awful deeds which she must do.' ἀίδηλα seems here to have its Hom. meaning 'ruinous' (see note to 1.102), though it may mean 'dark' (i.e. with uncertain issue), and so Way renders "deeds whose end was beyond her ken."

div.seg:
: ἐδέετο, ἔχρῃζεν, ἀπῄτει· ἢ ὅτι ἐνελείπετο ὁ τῆς ἡμέρας καιρός. Schol. There are thus two interpretations: (1) 'the time of day demanded that she should return'; (2) 'the time of day was failing for her to return (so that
she should return).' Seaton (Cl. Rev. iv 117) defends the latter, referring to the absolute use of δεύομαι in Il. 20. 122, μηδέ τι θυμῷ Δευέσθω, but the constr. is unique in either sense. Samuelsson defends his conj. ἐδύετο by Od. 13. 33, τῷ κατέδυ φάος ἠελίοιο Δόρπον ἐποίχεσθαι, taking ἤματος ὥρη either as = ἦμαρ, or = tempus opportunum, solitum (v. 899). We have ἦμαρ ἔδυ in 1407.
: i.e. without any conscious effort of will.
κ.τ.λ.: "But rapt in a trance of thoughts back-drifting she heard not a word" (Way). παλ. is used by Polybius of reverses of fortune.
κ.τ.λ.: 'brooding on the direful deed in which she was a sharer by her own counsels.' In 4. 435 ἐπεξυνώσατο means 'gave a share of,' 'communicated.' For πορφύρουσα see note to 1.461.
: 'where he left them when he parted from them'; cf. 827 supr., 1. 94, 4. 306.
: nursing his wrath, biting his lips to keep back an outburst of passion: cf. Ar. Nub. 1369, ὅμως δὲ τὸν θυμὸν δακὼν ἔφην. For the cause of the wrath of Idas v. 556 sqq.
: for the form cf. εἰκαθεῖν, διωκαθεῖν, ἀμυναθεῖν.
: as a rule Ap. uses the simple gen. with μέλεσθαι, e.g. 1. 967, but we find ἀμφί τι 2. 376, ἀμφί τινος 4. 491.
: cf. 1. 640, where he is sent as herald to Hypsipyle.
: 'they journeyed not in vain'; cf. Il. 16. 737, οὐδ’ ἁλίωσε βέλος: Od. 2. 273, οὔτοι ἔπειθ’ ἁλίη ὁδὸς ἔσσεται.
: 'the terrible teeth for the ordeal which was to come.'
: Βοιωτικοῦ. Schol. The Ἄονες, sprung from Aon, a son of Poseidon, are mentioned amongst the oldest dwellers in Boeotia, Paus. 9. 5. 1, Strab. 344, 40.

: Κόριννα τὸν Ὤγυγον Βοιωτοῦ υἱὸν εἶπεν. Schol. Thebes is called ὠγυγία πόλις in Aesch. Th. 308, where Verrall says: "the word clearly means very ancient, something like our 'pre-historic' ... It was explained of course by reference to a hero Ὤγυγος, but is probably of foreign, possibly of Phoenician, origin."

: Europa, sister of Cadmus, was carried off by Zeus to Crete. After a fruitless search for her, Cadmus consulted the oracle at Delphi which bade him desist from the search, follow a certain cow, and found a city where the cow would sink down exhausted. Thus Thebes was founded. Wishing to sacrifice the cow to Athene he sent to draw water from the well of Ares, but his messengers were slain by the dragon at the well. Cadmus then slew the dragon and sowed its teeth at the bidding of Athene. The warriors who sprang up
attacked each other, and only five survived to become the founders of the Theban race (Apollod. 3. 1. 1: Paus. 9. 5. 1, etc.: Hygin. Fab. 178).
: cf. 1. 87. For the dat. cf. Il. 13. 450, Μίνωα … Κρήτῃ ἐπίουρον.

: cf. Eur. Phoen. 638, Κάδμος ἔμολε τάνδε γᾶν | Τύριος, ᾧ τετρασκελὴς | μόσχος ἀδάματος πέσημα | δίκε τελεσφόρον διδοῦσα | χρησμόν, οὑ κατοικίσαι | πεδία νιν τὸ θέσφατον | πυροφόρ’ Ἀόνων ἔχρη. For προηγήτειρα cf. Bacch. 1159.

div.p: The goddess gave half the teeth to Aeetes, half to Cadmus.

div.seg: : this form = γηγενῆ is not found elsewhere.
: 'founded'; only here of peoples, elsewhere of temples, e.g. 2. 807. Hom. has the act. εἷσα of planting a colony, Od. 6. 8.

div.p: 'from as many as were left when the War God had mown them with his spear'; see note to 1179 For ἀμώοντος cf. 418.

div.seg: : = εἴ περ καί 'even granting that,' Od. 9. 35.
: 'was sinking beneath the darkened earth,' ὑπὸ τὸν ὁρίζοντα. Schol. In Il. 6. 19 γαῖαν ἐδύτην means 'went beneath the earth' i.e. died.
: τὰς ἐσχατιὰς ὡς ὑπερκειμἑνας τῆς οἰκουμένης. Schol.
: cf. Od. 1. 22, Αἰθίοπας … Οἱ μὲν δυσομένου Ὑπερίονος, οἱ δ’ ἀνιόντος.
: the active is used in 1. 452, κλίνοντος ἠελίοιο, though it is not so used in any previous poet.
: 'with all things needful.' The form χρήεσσι = χρέεσι is only found here.

div.p: Coleridge mistranslates, "and Argus went with him bringing a ewe and milk from the flock, which things he took from the ship itself." Jason went alone to perform the rites: Argus had already gone to the flock and brought him the ewe and the milk, while the other things needful for the sacrifice Jason took from the ship itself.

div.seg: : 'out of the beaten track,' cf. Il. 20. 137, κιόντες Ἐκ πάτου.
: "where under the unscreened sky the clear meads spread" (Way); cf. Theocr. 26. 5, ἐν καθαρῷ λειμῶνι. For ὑπεύδιος see note to 1.584. For εἱαμενῇσιν see note to 2.795.

: οἰκτρᾶς, λυπηρᾶς διὰ τὴν ἀπόλειψιν. Schol., cf. 1104. Merkel and Buttm. explain ἀδινός here as = ἡδύς. More probably it means 'frequent.' "in memory of many a night of love" (Coleridge). For the stay of the heroes at Lemnos v. 1. 608 sqq.
: τῶν κρυφίων. Schol. κευθμός = κευθμών is found in Il. 13. 28.
: for the notion that the gods actually came in person to receive the sacrifice cf. 880.

: 'twined'; cf. Il. 11. 36, τῇ δ’ ἐπὶ μὲν Γοργὼ … ἐστεφάνωτο. As evidence that Hecate was wreathed with snakes and oaken shoots the Schol. quotes a chorus from the Ῥιζοτόμοι of Soph. (fr. 480, Dindorf), Ἡλιε δέσποτα | καὶ πῦρ ἱερόν, τῆς εἰνοδίας | Ἑκάτης ἔγχος, τῷ δῑ Ὀλύμπου | πολλὴ φέρεται καὶ γῆς, καίουσ’ | ἱερὰς τριόδους στεφανωσαμένη | δρυσὶ καὶ πλεκτοῖς | ὠμῶν σπείραισι δρακόντων. Here belongs Varro Atac. fr. 8, Cuius ut aspexit torta caput angue revinctum.
: infernae canes (Hor. S. 1. 8. 35) ; cf. Lucian Philopseud. 22, 24, where these hounds are described as ἐλεφάντων ὑψηλότεροι, καὶ μέλανες καὶ λάσιοι, πιναρᾷ καὶ αὐχμώσῃ τῇ λάχνῃ.

: 'at her tread'; cf. Sen. Oed. 569,
Latravit Hecates turba, ter valles cavae
Sonuere maestum, tota succusso solo
Pulsata tellus
:
Aen. 6. 256,
Sub pedibus mugire solum, et iuga coepta moveri
Silvarum, visaeque canes ululare per umbram
Adventante dea.

: imitated in
Aen. 4. 168, summoque ulularunt vertice nymphae , though the meaning there is probably different (v. Conington).
: 'river-nymphs'; cf. Nic. Al. 128, ποταμηίσι νύμφαις (used of 'water of the river').
: Ἀμαράντιοι ἔθνος βάρβαρον ὑπὲρ Κόλχων ἐν τῇ ἠπείρῳ, ὅθεν αἱ τοῦ Φάσιδος πηγαὶ ἐξερεύγονται. ἢ ὄρος Κολχικὸν καλούμενον Ἀμαράντιον, ὅθεν ὁ Φᾶσις καταφέρεται. Schol.; see on 2. 399.
: 'but, for all that, his feet bore him away without one backward turn'; v. 1039. Cf. Il. 6. 496, ἄλοχος δὲ φίλη οἶκόνδε βεβήκει Ἐντροπαλιζομένη.

: as the sun had sunk behind the Aethiopian heights (1192),
so now the snowy Caucasus receives the first ray of dawn; cf. 162 supr. For ἠριγενής see note to 2.450.

: ὅτι οὐκ ἦν ἁλυσιδωτός, ἀλλὰ σταδιαῖος. ἀπὸ τῆς στάσεως ἐσχημάτισται. τινὲς δὲ στάδιον τὸν εὐπαγῆ, ὃν καὶ Καλλίμαχος λέγει "στάδιον δ’ ὑφέεστο χιτῶνα." Schol. This θώρηξ was made of stiff plates of metal, as opposed to the ἁλυσιδωτὸς θώρηξ, lorica annulata, chain-armour. The epithet στατός was also applied to it (v. schol. Ar. Pax 1227), because this stiff cuirass could stand by itself. Callimachus (fr. 59) uses στάδιος χιτών in the sense of ὀρθοστάδιος, i. e. the ungirdled tunic falling straight from the neck to the feet.
: cf. Hor. C. 3. 4. 53, Typhoeus et validus Mimas. In Eur. Ion 216 the Chorus speak of this giant as slain by the thunderbolt of Zeus, τὸν δάϊον Μίμαντα πυρὶ καταιθολοῖ (sc. Ζεύς).

: probably the same as τετράφαλος, 2. 920 (where see note). Buttm., arguing from the verb φαληριάω (κῦμα φαληριόων), maintained that φάληρος was either one of the names for the plume of a hclmet or an epithet of it, so that τετραφάληρος means 'with four-fold plume.'
: 'the round gleaming orb'; cf. Il. 23. 455, περίτροχον ἠύτε μήνη: ib. 22. 134, χαλκὸς ἐλάμπετο εἴκελος αὐγῇ … ἠελίου ὰνιόντος.
: cf. the shield of Ajax, Il. 7. 220.
: 'resistless,' from the stem μαιμαχ (μαιμάω, μαιμάσσὠ. Some explain it as a redupl. form from ἄμαχος.
: v. 1. 1290. Heracles remained to search for Hylas.
: in Hom. ῥυτήρ means 'the trace,' but later it was used for 'the reins,' e.g. Soph. O.C. 900, σπεύδειν ὰπὺ ῥυτῆρος , immissis habenis.

: Pindar (N. 5. 37) speaks of Poseidon journeying from Aegae in Achaia to the Isthmian festival, Ποσειδάωνα … ὃς Αἰγᾶθεν ποτὶ κλειτὰν θαμὰ νίσσεται Ἰσθμόν κ.τ.λ. The festival was held in the τέμενος Ποσειδάνιον.

: see note to 1.102. The temple of Poseidon was at the extreme
point of the peninsula.
: a marsh near Argos, where Heracles slew the hydra. For the amours of Poseidon with Amymome at Lerna v. Prop. 3. 18. 47.

: the ὜αντες were aboriginal inhabitants of Boeotia expelled by the Cadmeans (Strab. 345. 5; 363, 38). Onchestus was named after the son of Poseidon. For the temple and grove cf. Il. 2. 506, Ὀγχηστόν θ’ ἱερὸν Ποσιδήιον, ἀγλαὸν ἄλσος. Strabo (354, 31) says that the temple had no grove, οἱ δὲ ποιηταὶ κοσμοῦσιν, ἀλση καλοῦντες τὰ ἱερὰ πάντα κἂν ᾖ ψιλά. Pausanias, however, mentions the grove (9. 26. 3), ἐπ’ ἐμοῦ δὲ ναός τε καὶ ἄγαλμα Ποσειδῶνος ἐλείπετο καὶ τὸ ἄλσος ὃ δὴ καὶ Ὄμηρος ἐπῄνεσε.

: an island in the Saronic Gulf. Strabo (321, 24) mentions thelegend that Poseidon received Calaurea from Leto in exchange for Delos. It was in the temple at Calaurea that Demosthenes took refuge from Antipater, and ended his life by poison.

: τὴν Θεσσαλίαν Πέτραν. χωρίον δέ ἐστιν ἐν ᾧ Ποσειδῶνος ἄγεται ἀγών, ὡς ἀπὸ τοῦ τόπου Πετραῖον καλεῖσθαι. Schol. Pindar, P. 4. 138, applies to Poseidon the epithet Πετραῖος 'Cleaver of the Rock,' which is explained either of his opening a passage for the Peneius through the rock, or creating the first horse which leaped forth from a rock in Thessaly or Attica.
: Geraestus was a town and promontory in Euboea. For the famous temple there cf. Od. 3. 177, ἐς δὲ Γεραιστὸν Ἐννύχιαι κατάγοντο· Ποσειδάωνι δὲ ταύρων Πόλλ’ ἐπὶ μῆρ’ ἔθεμεν.
: 'sprinkled around,' ἅπ. λεγ. For μυδήνας see note to 1042
: 'but, just as it was, it remained hard and unbroken in their stout hands.'
: the first syll. is short in Od. 11. 575. αἰὲν ἀαγές; Ap. lengthens it on the false analogy of ἀθάνατος and ἀκάματος.
: it had become dry, and so was well-seasoned and hard in their hands.
: the 'butt-end' of the spear. Leaf, on Il. 13. 443, distinguishes it from σαυρωτήρ, the spike at the butt-end.

div.p:
This simile is drawn from Hom., who describes Paris going forth from Troy to battle, Il. 6. 506, ὡς δ’ ὅτε τις στατὸς ἵππος ἀκοστήσας ἐπὶ φάτνῃ, Δεσμὸν ἀπορρήξας θείῃ πεδίοιο κροαίνων, Εἰωθὼς λούεσθαι ἐυρρεῖος ποταμοῖο, Κυδιόων· ὑψοῦ δὲ κάρη ἔχει, ἀμφὶ δὲ χαῖται Ὤμοις ἀίσσονται· ὁ δ’ ἀγλαΐηφι πεποιθώς, Ῥίμφα ἑ γοῦνα φέρει μετά τ’ ἤθεα καὶ νομὸν ἵππων. Cf.
Aen. 11. 492 (of Turnus),
qualis ubi abruptis fugit praesepia vinclis
Tandem liber equus ...
Emicat arrectisque fremit cervicibus alte,
Luxurians, luduntque iubae per colla per armos.

div.seg: : like Polydeuces before his contest with Amycus, 2. 45.

div.p: "Thou hadst said that adown through the murky welkin the leaping flash Of the tempest-levin was gleaming and flickering once and again From the clouds that are bringing hard after their burden of blackest rain" (Way).

div.seg: : 'to flash,' ἅπ. λεγ. The simple verb occurs in 4. 1442 and Il. 2. 450, παιφάσσουσα ('dazzling') διέσσυτο λαὸν Ἀχαιῶν. It is a redupl. form (cf. δαιδάλλω) from a secondary variation of the root φα, φαίνω.
: as distinct from ὑετός, ὄμβρος was 'thunder rain': cf. Il. 10. 6, Hdt. 8. 12. For ὅτε c. subj. see note to 1.76.
: τὰ ζυγά, ἐφ’ ὧν οἱ ἐρέται κάθηνται. Schol. In Hom. it is a disputed point whether κληῖδες means 'benches' or 'thole-pins' (which Ap. calls σκαλμοί, 1. 379, 392).

div.p: 'It (i.e. the plain) lay over opposite the city, as far in front thereof as the goal which the chariot must gain is from the starting-place, what time a chieftain dies and his kinsmen ordain contests for prizes for those on foot and for those in chariots.'

div.seg: : τῆς ἀφετηρίας. Schol., Lat. carceres; cf. Ar. Eq. 1159, ἄφες ἀπὸ βαλβίδων.

: the goal, meta. In Hom. νύσσα means (1) the turning-post, καμπτήρ, Il. 23. 332; (2) the post at the other end from which they started, which served also as the winning-post, Od. 8. 121. Our poet means that the plain was as far from the city as the pillar at one end of the hippodrome was from that at the other. The plain was on the side of the river opposite to the city, v. 2. 1268.
: for funeral games cf. 1. 1060, 1304; Od. 24. 88, ὅτε κέν ποτ’ ἀποφθιμένου βασιλῆος Ζώννυνταί τε νέοι καὶ ἐπεντύνονται ἄεθλα.

div.p:
Cf. Ov. Met. 7. 101,
Conveniunt populi sacrum Mavortis in arvum,
Consistuntque iugis: medio rex ipse resedit.

div.seg: : 'winding'; cf. Hes. Th. 791, δίνῃς ἀργυρέῃς εἱλιγμένος εἰς ἅλα πίπτει.
: imitated in Orph. Arg. 545, νηὸς ἀποπροθορόντες. The compound is only found in these two passages.

: the body of Jason was not encased in a στάδιος θώρηξ like that of Aectes, so that partly he resembled the naked War God Ares, and partly Apollo 'of the golden brand.' For χρυσάορος v. Leaf on Il. 5. 509.

: τὰ μεγάλα καὶ ἀναρίθμητα. Schol.; cf. 4. 158, νήριτος ὀδμή: Hes. Op. 509, πᾶσα βοᾷ τότε νήριτος ὕλη. Curtius refers it to the root ἀρ (ἀριθμός). Others explain 'certain,' (e.g. Lehrs and de M.), following the old deriv. from νή and ἐρίζειν.
: 'stalls,' ἡ βούστασις. Schol. This form occurs only here; βόαυλος in Theocr., and βοαύλιον in Orph. Arg.

: both εἰλυμένος and ἐλυσθείς are used by Ap. in two distinct senses: (1) rolled up, huddled, crouching; (2) enfolded, enwrapped. The former is the meaning in 281, 296, and 1. 1034; the latter here and in 1313, 1. 254. Buttmann distinguished two verbs, ἐλύω to push or compress, and εἰλύω to envelop (wrap). In Hom. εἰλυμἑνος is from the latter, ἐλυσθείς from the former. We see that Ap. recognized no such distinction.

κ.τ.λ.: 'awaits their onset, as an ocean reef awaits the onset of the billows lashed to fury by the hurricane's resistless might.' Cf. Il. 15. 618, ἴσχον γὰρ πυργηδὸν ἀρηρότες, ἠύτε πέτρη Ἠλίβατος, μεγάλη, πολιῆς ἁλὸς ἐγγὺς ἐοῦσα· Ἤ τε μενει λιγέων ἀνέμων λαιψηρὰ κέλευθα, Κύματά τε τροφόεντα, τά τε προσερεύγεται αὐτήν:
Aen. 10. 693,
Ille, velut rupes vastum quae prodit in aequor
Obvia ventorum furiis, expostaque ponto,
Vim cunctam atque minas perfert caelique marisque,
Ipsa immota manens
: Tennyson, Will, "Who seems a promontory of rock, That, compass'd round with turbulent sound, In middle ocean meets the surging shock, Tempest-buffeted, citadel-crown'd."

div.p: 'As when the brazier's bellows of stout hide now send quick tongues of flame through the holes of the smelting-furnace, kindling a devouring fire, and, again, cease from their blast; and a fierce roar arises from the fire in its upward rush: even so did these two bulls bellow, breathing forth quick blasts of flame from their mouths, and the deadly glow played round him with lightning flash.' Cf. Il. 18. 470, φῦσαι δ’ ἐν χοάνοισιν ἐείκοσι πᾶσαι ἐφύσων, Παντοίην εὔπρηστον ἀυτμὴν ἐξανιεῖσαι, Ἄλλοτε μὲν σπεύδοντι παρέμμεναι, ἄλλοτε δ’ αὖτε, Ὄππως Ἤφαιστός τ’ ἐθέλοι καὶ ἔργον ἄνυτο. The χόανος was the smelting-furnace from which the metal was run; cf. Hes. Th. 862, ἀτμῇ θεσπεσίῃ καὶ ἐτήκετο, κασσίτερος ὣς Τέχνῃ ὑπ’ αἰζηῶν ὑπό τ’ εὐτρήτου χοάνοιο Θαλφθείς, ἠὲ σίδηρος κ.τ.λ. For ἐύρρινοι cf. Virg. G. 4. 171 (of the Cyclopes), taurinis follibus auras Accipiunt redduntque.

div.seg: : this word has excited much suspicion, but I believe it to be sound. Ap. combines the two notions of the quick puffs of the bellows and the quick flashes of flame which follow, and expresses them by a compound which is ἅπ. λεγ., though the simple verb is common. The Schol. says, μαρμαίρουσι: κυρίως καίουσι· μετενήνοχε δὲ τὴν φωνὴν ἐπὶ τῆς σφοδροτάτης φυσήσεως ἐνεργούσης ἔσωθεν. Ruhnken's ἀναμορμύρουσιν 'roar' anticipates and spoils the effect of 1302. For Merkel's ἀναμαιμάουσιν cf. Il. 20. 490.
: sc. πυρός. Merkel's αὖ τοῦ is more ingenious than convincing.

: cf. Ov. Met. 7. 104,
Ecce adamanteis vulcanum naribus efflant
Aeripedes tauri; tactaeque vaporibus herbae
Ardent: utque solent pleni resonare camini,
Aut ubi terrena silices fornace soluti
Concipiunt ignem liquidarum adspergine aquarum:
Pectora sic intus clausas volventia flammas,
Gutturaque usta sonant.
: neuter here, but masc. in Eur. Supp. 208.

: 'yoke-collar,' Lat. subiugium; cf. Aesch. Pr. 463, ἔζευξα … ἐν ζυγοῖσι κνώδαλα Ζεύγλαισι δουλεύοντα.
Leaf, on Il. 17. 440, 19. 406, explains ζεύγλη as the 'yoke-cushion' i.e. a circular pad wrapped round the yoke to keep it from chafing the horses' necks. The epithet χαλκείῃ shows that Ap. attached no such meaning to it.
: ἐπὶ τὰ γόνατα. Schol. Flor. It is generally used of a crouching posture, cf. ὸκλαδόν (122), but the meaning here is fixed by γούνασιν ἐν προτέροισι (1313).
: 'with a swift thrust of his foot against its hoof.'

div.p: 'he brought it to its knees as it charged, smitten with one quick movement.' For βεβολημένον see note to 1.262.

div.seg: κ.τ.λ.; 'moving hither and thither, now on this side, now on that, he kept them down where they had fallen on their fore-knees. The flame enveloped him in a moment.'
: see note to 1291 For διὰ φλογός (where Oswald says the sense of διά fades into that of ἐν) cf. 4. 874, σπαίροντα διὰ φλογός.
: 'for it had been told them beforehand so to do.'
κ.τ.λ.: 'lifting up and placing the pole between them he fastened it by its sharp tip to the yoke.'

: the point of the pole to which the yoke was booked or tied; cf. Poll. 1. 252, τὸ δὲ μετὰ τὸν γύην ἱστοβοεύς, τὸ δὲ τέλος αὐτοῦ τὸ μετὰ τὸν ζυγὸν κορώνη. For the complicated way in which the ζογόν and ἱστοβοεύς were fastened together v. Helbig, Hom. Epos 147 sqq.; Leaf on Il. 24. 268 sqq. (Vol. ii, App. M).
: 'took up'; cf. Il. 18, 476, γέντο δὲ χειρὶ Ῥαιστῆρα. Fick explains it as γενθ‐το, from rt. gandh, but it is for γέμ‐το (ἀπόγεμε· ἄφελκε, Hesych.).

: 'goad' (literally 'thorn'); cf. Anth. P. 6. 41, βούπληκτρον ἄκαιναν. Our Schol. gives us the only information we have about the word: ἀντὶ τοῦ κέντρω·| ἄκαινα δέ ἐστι μέτρον δεκάπουν Θεσσαλῶν εὕρεμα· ἢ ῥάβδος ποιμενικὴ παρὰ Πελασγοῖς ηὑρημένη, περὶ ἧς Καλλίυαχός φησιν "ἀμφότερον, κέντρον τε βοῶν καὶ μέτρον ἀρούρης." We find a form acna or acnua used of a measure of land 10 feet square in Varro R.R. 1. 10 (Keil).
: 'blustering' (βύζω); cf. Od. 10. 20, βυκτάων ἀνέμων κατέδησε κέλευθα.
: 'and the rough fallow was broken up behind them.' Cf. Hes. Sc. 286, οἱ δ’ ἀροτῆρες Ηρεικον χθόνα δῖαν.

: if genuine, this must mean the plough-share, culter aratri, on which the ploughman pressed his foot to drive it deeper into the earth. In the only references we have to the word (Favorinus, s.v. λήϊον; Bast, Commentatio Palaeographica, p. 872 n.) the meaning given is δρέπανον, falx messoria, not culter aratri. Samuelsson explains his ingenious correction λαιῷ of the ploughman pressing with the left foot on the back part of the plough as illustrated in Baumeister, Denkm. i Tab. i, 13a. 13b. He regards the vulg. βαθμόν as a gloss to provide an object for ἐπιπιέσας, as βαθμός may have been a name for the part of the plough 'inter stivam et burim.' Pierson and Brunck explain βαθ. ἐπιπ. 'forti pede gradum premens,' 'fortiter pedem figens.'

: sc. καιρόν. cf. Hom. βουλυτόνδε,
Hor. C. 3. 6. 42, sol ubi ... iuga demeret Bobus fatigatis. The opposite phrase for dawn occurs in Hes. Op. 581, ἠὼς … πολλοῖσί τ’ ἐπὶ ζνγὰ βουσὶ τιθησιν.
: 'while he saw the furrows still void of earthborn men.'
: the very helmet from which he had sown the dragon's teeth.
: the phrase γούνατα κάμπτειν (γνάμπτειν) usually means 'to sink down to rest,' e.g. 1. 1174, Il. 7. 118; here the meaning is that Jason bent his knees to test their suppleness (cf. 1263).
: cf. Il. 13. 471. ἀλλ’ ἔμεν’, ὡς ὅτε τις σῦς οὔρεσιν ἀλκὶ πεποιθὼς … Ὀφθαλμὼ δ’ ἄρα οἱ πυρὶ λάμπετον· αὐτὰρ ὀδόντας Θήγει, ἀλέξασθαι μεμαὼς κύνας ἠδὲ καὶ ἄνδρας.

: cf. Hes. Sc. 389, ἀφρὸς δὲ περὶ στόμα μαστιχόωντι (κάπρᾠ Λείβεται:
Aen. 1. 324, spumantis apri . ῥεῖ: this correction is necessary, as the impf. is not used by Hom. or Ap. in similes. If ῥέε is kept, it must refer to Jason. For the contracted form ῥεῖ cf. πνεῖ, 2. 229.

: horruit; cf. Il. 13. 339, ἔφριξεν δὲ μάχη φθισίμβροτος ἐγχείῃσι:
Aen. 7. 525,
atraque late
Horrescit strictis seges ensibus, aeraque fulgent
Sole lacessita, et lumen sub nubila iactant
: 11. 601, ferreus hastis Horret ager.

: cf. Il. 13. 147, ἔγνεσιν ἀμφιγύοισιν, where four interpretations have been given: (1) having a γυῖον, a limb (of iron), at each end--the λόγχη and σαυρωτήρ; (2) having a λόγχη curved (γυ) on both sides; (3) bending to either side, elastic (so Leaf); (4) wielded with both hands. See also on ἀμφιγυήεις, 37 supr. In Soph. Tr. 505 ἀμφίγυοι means 'valiant rivals' (Jebb).

div.p:
Cf. Il. 5. 302 sqq., 12. 445 sqq.; Ov. Met. 7. 140,
Ille, gravem medios silicem iaculatus in hostes,
A se depulsum Martem convertit in ipsos.
Medea advises this stratagem, 1057 supr.

div.seg: : this name, which is usually a subst., is here an epithet of Ares as in Il. 17. 210, Ἄρης Δεινὸς Ἐνυάλιος. For its meaning and connexion with Ἐνυώ see the exhaustive article by Jessen in Pauly-Wissowa, Real-Encycl.
: δίσκον. Schol. In Il. 23. 826 σόλος αὐτοχύωνος is used of the mass of metal hurled in one of the contests.

div.p:
Cf.
Aen. 12. 896,
saxum circumspicit ingens ...
Vix illud lecti bis sex cervice subirent
Qualia nunc hominum producit corpora tellus.
Ille manu raptum trepida torquebat in hostem.
Both Ap. and Virg. are indebted to Hom., Il. 5. 302, 20. 285.
Cf. Il. 2. 394, Ἀργεῖοι δὲ μέγ’ ἴαχον, ὡς ὕτε κῦμα κ.τ.λ.

Οὗτος καὶ οἱ ἑξῆς στίχοι εἰλημμένοι εἰσὶ παρ’ Εὐμήλου, παρ’ ᾧ φησι Μήδεια πρὸς Ἴδμονα. Σοφοκλῆς δὲ ἐν Κολχίσι πεποίηκε τὸν ἄγγελον τοῦ Αἰήτου πυθομένου περὶ τῶν προειρημένων "ἦ βλαστὸς οὐκ ἔβλαστεν οὑπιχώριος;" λέγοντα "καὶ κάρτα φρίξας εὐλόφῳ σφηκώματι Χαλκηλάτοις ὅπλοισι μητρὸς ἐξέδυ." ταῦτα δὲ Ἀπολλώνιος παραγέγραφεν. Schol.
Cf. Il. 4. 75, οἷον δ’ ἀστέρα ἧκε Κρόνου πάϊς ἀγκυλομήτεω, )\Η ναύτῃσι τέρας ἠὲ στρατῷ εὐρέϊ λαῶν, Λαμπρόν· τοῦ δέ τε πολλοὶ ἀπὸ σπινθῆρες ἵενται· Τῷ εἰκυῖ’ ἤιξεν ἐπὶ χθόνα Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη.

div.seg: : this word has been suspected, but it is defended by the fact that Val. Fl. (7. 619) mentions those whose heads only were above the ground, 'necdum humeri videre diem.' Ap. is distinguishing different stages of growth: (1) those who had risen half way, (2) those who were beginning to rise, (3) those who had risen completely. The use of καί before ἄχρις is as superfluous as in 1385, where we might apply the criticism of the Schol. on 1. 604, περιττὸς ὁ καὶ σύνδεσμος.
: 'concerning boundaries.' For this use of ἀμφί cf. 1. 747, ἀμφὶ βουσὶν μάρναντο: Il. 3. 70, ἀμφ’ Ἑλένῃ μάχεσθαι. Some take it here in a local sense, e.g. de M. 'aux frontières.'

: 'the owner of a farm.' The subst. γεωμόρος always means a landowner (big or small). In 4. 1453, γειομόροι μύρμηκες, and in 1. 1214, βοὸς γεωμόρου, the adj. means 'earth-cleaving,' and it is possible that a husbandman is here called an 'earth-cleaver.'
: i.e. foemen may cut it down before he has time to reap it. Ellis in his note on Cat. 64. 353, praecerpens messor aristas , wrongly explains προταμεῖν here of 'cutting in front of him.'
: 'and does not wait till harvest-time for it to be ripened by the rays of the sun.' ὡραίη is used like ὥρα ἔτους for the reaping season; cf. ἀναγκαίη = ἀνάγκη, Ἀθηναία = Αθηνᾶ, σεληναίη = σελήνη.

: 'channels,' 'runnels'; cf.
Il. 21. 259, ἀμάρης ἐξ ἔχματα βάλλων. They served to diffuse the water for irrigating the fields.
: Ap. alone uses the passive, cf. 4. 564. πλήθω is sometimes trans. in late Greek.

: 'biting it with their teeth.' The pleonasm is merely apparent, as ὀδάξ and ὀδούς are prob. from different roots. Cf. 4. 18, κουρὶξ Ἑλκομένη πλοκάμους . Ap. may have regarded these as justifiable extensions of the curious Homeric λὰξ ποδί.

is from
Il. 2. 418, πρηνέες ἐν κονίῃσιν ὀδὰξ λαζοίατο γαῖαν . Some needlessly try to take ὀδοῦσιν of the dragon's teeth, 'biting the clods broken for the dragon's teeth,' which is suggested by the ending of 1336, βῶλον ὀδόντας. Brunck adopts ὀκλάξ, the conjecture of Abresch, but, even granting that ὀκλάξ can be used for γνύξ (as in 1308), it is inconsistent with πρηνεῖς in the following line. Lehrs accepts Hermann's ἀρούρης, regarding ὀδοῦσιν as a gloss on ὀδάξ, but such a familiar word would not require a gloss. For Merkel's ὔλοξιν see on 1054; he keeps ὀδοῦσιν in his text.

: 'rough,' see note to 1.1167. As βῶλος elsewhere in the poem is always fem., we must, with Merkel, consider this as an
instance of the Schema Atticum, cf. 3. 21. Masculine forms of participles as well as adjectives can be used as feminine in epic, e.g. Hes. fr. 703, δαϊζομένοιο πόληος. For the varying gender of βῶλος in late Greek v. L. and S.

: cf.
Il. 11. 425, ὁ δ’ ἐν κονίῃσι πεσὼν ἕλε γαῖαν ἀγοστῷ .
: 'like sea-monsters in form.' δομή for δέμας is found in Lycophron.

: διύγροις. Schol., either 'wet with blood,' or 'damp with the death-agony.' As πλαδαρός is also used of flesh in the sense of 'flabby' (cf. πλαδόωσαν, 2. 662 n), the meaning may be that they were weighed down by their heads which hung forward limply, cf. Ov. Met. 10. 195, Ipsa sibi est oneri cervix, humeroque recumbit.

div.p:
Cf.
Il. 8. 306,
*mh/kwn d' w(\s e(te/rwse ka/rh ba/len, h(/t' e)ni\ kh/pw|,
*karpw=| briqome/nh, noti/h|si te ei)arinh=|sin:
(\*ws e(te/rws' h)/muse ka/rh ph/lhki barunqe/n
:
Aen. 9. 435,
Purpureus veluti cum flos succisus aratro
Languescit moriens; lassove papavera collo
Demisere caput, pluvia cum forte gravantur
:
Ov. Met. 10. 190,
Ut si quis violas, riguove papaver in horto,
Liliaque infringat, fulvis haerentia virgis;
Marcida demittant subito caput illa gravatum,
etc.

div.seg: : 'the labours of gardening folk.' So in Od. 10. 98 vineyards or gardens are called ἔργα ἀνδρῶν. Others explain πόνος as the toil or vexation caused to the gardeners by the devastation. ἀλωεύς as a common noun is first found in Aratus; in Hom. it is a proper name.
: τὸν δεσπότην. Schol., see note to 1.575.
: 'in what way he could the more quickly thwart them.'

list.head: Summary
list.item: Invocation of the Muse (1-5)
Distress of Medea, who bids farewell to her home (6-33)
Flight of Medea: exultation of Titania (34-65)
Medea comes to the Argonauts (66-91)
Jason welcomes Medea (92-108)
Jason takes the fleece by the magic agency of Medea (109-182)
The Argonauts begin their return (183-211)
The Colchians pursue them (212-235)
They land at the mouth of the Halys (236-252)
Argus sets forth the plan of their voyage (253-293)
They enter the Ister (294-302)
The Colchians pursue them through the Ister to the Adriatic (303-337)
Truce between the Argonauts and Colchians (338-349)
Medea reproaches Jason; they plot the murder of Absyrtus (350-444)
Imprecations on Eros (445-451)
Murder of Absyrtus (452-481)
On the advice of Peleus the heroes press on; the Colchians cease pursuing and settle in Illyria (482-521)
The Hylleans receive the heroes hospitably (522-551)
The will of Zeus is revealed that they must be cleansed from their bloodguiltiness (552-591)
They enter the Eridanus (592-626)
They pass into the Rhodanus, and reach the sea at the Stoechades (627-658)
Arrival at Aeaea: Circe purifies Jason and Medea (659-717)
Medea tells her tale to Circe, who spurns her from her house (718-752)
Hera persuades Thetis to save the Argo from Scylla and Charybdis (753-832)
Thetis visits Peleus, and reveals the will of Hera (833-884)
The Argonauts pass by the isle of the Sirens; the Nereids save them from the Planctae (885-981)
They come to Phaeacia; others of the Colchians arrive and demand back Medea, who implores Arete and the heroes (982-1067)
Alcinous, on his wife's entreaty, decides that Medea shall not be given up if she be already wedded to Jason (1068-1109)
Arete brings these tidings to Jason; consummation of the marriage (1110-1169)
Alcinous declares his decision to the Colchians, who are allowed to settle among the Phaeacians; departure of the Argonauts (1170-1227)
They are driven by a tempest within the Syrtes; despair of the heroes (1228-1304)
The Libyan goddesses take pity on them, and send a wondrous portent (1305-1379)
They bear the Argo on their shoulders over the desert to Lake Tritonis, where the Hesperides show them a spring (1380-1460)
Search for Heracles who has carried off the golden apples: death of Canthus (1461-1501)
Death of Mopsus (1502-1536)
Triton shows them the outlet of the lake, and guides the Argo seaward (1537-1622)
They sail towards Crete (1623-1637)
They are repelled by Talos, who is slain by Medea's magic wiles (1638-1693)
Phoebus appears to save them at the isle of Anaphe (1694-1730)
The dream of Euphemus: its interpretation by Jason (1731-1764)
Arrival at Aegina (1765-1772)
End of the voyage (1773-1781).

div.p: For the invocation cf. 3. 1.

div.seg: : cf. Od. 1. 10, θεά, θύγατερ Διός, εἰπὲ καὶ ἡμῖν.

κ.τ.λ.: 'for, of a truth, my
mind within me is in a whirl of dumb perplexity, as I ponder whether I shall say that it was the anguish of her luckless infatuation, or that it was unworthy panic, through which she left the tribes of the Colchians.'
: by hypallage for ἄτης πῆμα δυσιμέρου. As in 3. 961, δυσίμερος refers to Medea's luckless love, cf. δυσέρως. L. and S. wrongly explain it as 'unlovely,' 'hateful.'
: cf. Il. 9. 2, φύζα, φόβου κρυόεντος ἑταίρη. Aristarchus defines φύζα as ἡ μετὰ δειλίας φυγή.
: cf. ἀεικὴς φύξις, 748 infra. The Schol. explains it by κακώσεως φυγήν, i.e. a flight from ill-treatment, and this meaning is adopted by de M. and others.
: cf. h. Hom. Merc. 66, ὁρμαίνων δόλον αἰπὺν ἐνὶ φρέσιν.
: the thought that Jason had come safely through the ordeal was galling to him.
: 'he weened that these things had not been accomplished without his daughters' aid'; see note to 3.370.
: see note to 2.696. For the timidity of deer cf. Il. 4. 243, 21. 29, 22. 1.
: cf. Il. 15. 606, βαθέης ἐν τάρφεσιν ὕλης.
: 'that the help which she had given to Jason was not hidden from Aeetes, and that she would soon fill to the full the measure of calamity.'
: συνίστορας, συνειδυίας. Schol.; see note to 2.872.
: cf. 1. 879: Sapph. 2. 11, ἐπιρρόμβεισι (ἐπιβρόμεισι, Bergk) δ’ ἀκουαί: Cat. 51. 10, sonitu suopte Tintinant aures.

: 'she clutched at her throat'; see note to 3.106. For λευκανίης cf. 2. 192. It is here used, not for the gullet, but for the throat generally, a meaning which some assign in Il. 22. 325 (v. Leaf). In Hom. the form λαυκανίη is the best attested, but in 2. 192 our mss. agree in λευκανίηνδε. There Beck adopted λαυκανίηνδε, which had been suggested by Brunck. Here L has λαυκανίης. Merkel and Seaton strangely read λευκανίηνδε but λαυκανίης.
: for the pleonasm see on 3. 1393. The Schol. explains τουρίξ by κατὰ κόρρης, κατὰ κεφαλῆς, but it is connected with κουρά, κείρω.
: 'moaned'; cf. Soph. Tr. 904 (of Deianira), βρυχᾶτο μὲν βωμοῖσι προσπιπτουσ’. It is used in Hom. of the death-cry of wounded men, and of the moaning of the waves.
: 'fluttering.' The Schol. takes it in a proleptic sense, οἷον κοῦφος· ἐκουφίσθη τοῦ προτέρου λογισμοῦ, ταχέως μετέπεσεν αὐτῆς ἡ ψυχή, εἰς ἱλαρότητα μετετράπη.

: 'she poured back at once all the drugs from her bosom into the casket.' The whole passage very closely resembles 3. 806 sqq. Preston interprets quite differently, "Drawn from her casket, in her breast she placed The magic hoard of drugs," i.e. took them with her in her flight as her most precious possession. The order of words is against this.

: so in Soph. Ph. 533 Philoctetes says, ἴωμεν, ὦ παῖ, προσκύσαντε τὴν ἔσω Ἄοικον εἰσοίκησιν. Cf.
Aen. 2. 490, amplexaeque tenent postes atque oscula figunt : 4. 659 (of Dido), os impressa toro.
: 'my prayer is that thou mayest fare well while I go far hence.' For the dat. cf. Jebb on Soph. O.T. 596, νῦν πᾶσι χαίρω.

: cf.
Aen. 4. 657,
Felix, heu nimium felix, si litora tantum
Nunquam Dardaniae tetigissent nostra carinae
: Cat. 64. 171,
Iuppiter omnipotens, utinam ne tempore primo
Gnosia Cecropiae tetigissent litora puppes.

: 'stealing forth from,' λάθρα διεξελθοῦσα τοῦ δόμου, ἀποδράσασα, φυγοῦσα. Schol. The word occurs again in Nonnus (quoted on 1531 infr.). Schellert (De Ap. Rh. Comparationibus p. 41) says it means abducta, "Cardo tum similitudinis in eo vertitur, quod eodem tristi animo et timore quo puella in servitium abducta Medea affecta est e domo egrediens"; but the point of the comparison is the secrecy of the flight of the two unhappy maidens.
: with ὑπὸ χεῖρας. Way wrongly renders, "shrinking in horror from slavery Under the cruel hands of a mistress, forth does she flee."

div.p: For bolts yielding to the charm of magic cf. Macbeth 4. 1, "Open, locks, Whoever knocks!"

div.seg: : = ἐπῳδαῖς; cf. 59. Carmina is used in the same way, e.g. Aen. 4. 487.

: τὸ ἀπολῆγον τοῦ χιτῶνος, ὃ ἡμεῖς ᾤαν λέγομεν. τὸ γὰρ πρότερον ὑπὲρ τοῦ μὴ τρίβεσθαι δέρμα προβάτου προσέρραπτο. Schol. Cf. Anth. P. 6. 287, τὰν μίαν αἱ τρισσαὶ πέζαν ὑφηνάμεθα. In 1258 infr. πέζα is used of a strand or coastline; Hom. uses it of the end of a pole, Il. 24. 272, ἐπὶ π(υμῷ Πέζῃ ἐπὶ πρώτῃ.
: 'spacious,' literally 'with broad dancing-places.' It is improbable that it is a poetical equivalent of εὐρύχωρος, which was the view of the Schol. on Od. 4. 635.
: this may mean either 'noxious' (χαλεπὰς καὶ κακάς. Schol.), or more probably 'tough,' 'hard to uproot' (δυσχερῶς ἀνασπωμένας. Schol.). de M., "racines, dont la puissance est irrésistible."
: = Σελήνη. The Sun and Moon were the children of Hyperion, the Titan, and Thia; cf. Hes. Th. 371. Ennius uses Titanis, and Ovid Titania, for Diana.
: this adj. combines the two notions of 'wandering' and 'distraught.'
: 'exulted over her'; cf. Soph. Aj. 961, οἱ δ’ οὖν γελώντων κἀπιχαιρόντων κακοῖς.

: Latmus was a mountain in Caria, where the Moon kissed the sleeping Endymion; cf. Ov. A. A. 3. 83, Latmius Endymion non est tibi, Luna, rubori. Strabo (543, 17) mentions the cave, πρὸς τῷ Λάτμῳ δείκνυται τάφος Ἐνδυμίωνος ἔν τινι σπηλαίῳ.
: only here in the sense of ἀλύω or ἀλύσσω 'to roam distraught'; elsewhere it means 'to flee from.'
: cf. δαιομένη, 3. 661: Call. Epigr. 49. 3, Πάμφιλον … ἔρωτι δεδαυμένον, Ap. 49, ἠιθέου ὑπ’ ἔρωτι κεκαυμένος: Hor. C. 2. 4. 7, arsit virgine rapta.

div.p:
'Full often, I ween, have I come down from heaven, remembering my love for him, through thy cunning
incantations, that thou mightest be able in the blackness of the night to follow at thy ease the magic arts so dear to thee.' For the power of witchcraft over the Moon see note to 3.533; Ov. Her. 6. 84,
Illa (sc. Medea) reluctantem curru deducere Lunam
Nititur, et tenebris abdere Solis equos.

div.seg: : 'to take upon thyself a burden of bitter woe.'
: ἐπιτεταμένως, μεγάλως. Schol.; cf. Il. 11. 10, ἤυσε … ὄρθια: h. Hom. Cer. 20, ἰάχησε δ’ ἄρ’ ὄρθια φωνῇ.
: 'divined' that it was the voice of M.
: 'on the opposite shore'; cf. 2. 392, 4. 848. Ap. seems to be the only writer who uses the full expression; elsewhere we find only περαίη, sc. γῆ, χώρα (v. 1. 1112).
: cf. Od. 12. 442, ἧκα δ’ ἐγὼ καθύπερθε πόδας.
: sc. χερσί; cf. Od. 10. 264, αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ ἀμφοτέρῃσι λαβὼν ἐλλίσσετο γούνων.
: here only as an adj.; in Hom. it is an adv. opposed to κρύβδην; cf. ἀμφαδά, 3. 615.
: the middle form only here, though common in Hom.

div.p:
The Schol. says that the author of the Ναυπακτικά (rather Ναυπάκτια, the form found in Paus.; v. Introd. p. 20) represented Medea as bringing the fleece with her in her flight from her father's house where it lay. Aphrodite sent
deep sleep on Aeetes. who was plotting with the Colchians to burn the Argo, and the heroes escaped from his palace followed by Medea.

div.seg: : = μεμπτήν. The Homeric form is ὀνοστός. For κηδεμόνων see note to 3.732.
: cf. Soph. Ph. 1324, Ζῆνα δ’ ὅρκιον καλῶ. Pausanias (5. 24. 2) mentions a statue of Ζεὺς Ὄρκιος in the βουλευτήριον at Olympia, with a thunderbolt in either hand.

: 'goddess of marriage rites'; Ζυγία· ἡ Ηρα. Ζύγιος· Ζεύς. Hesych. Cf. Musaeus 274, ἦν γάμος, ἀλλ’ ἀχόρευτος· ἔην λέχος, ἀλλ’ ἄτερ ὕμνων· Οὐ Ζυγίην Ἤρην τις ἐπευφήμησεν ἀοιδός. Juno had a temple under the
name Iuga or Iugalis in the Forum at Rome.
: cf. Il. 19. 242, αὐτίκ’ ἔπειθ’ ἅμα μῦθος ἔην, τετέλεστο δὲ ἔργον: Ter. Andr. 381, dictum factum invenerit : Ov. Met. 4. 549, res dicta secuta est.

div.p: "In the hour when men from their eyes the fetters of slumber cast, Even huntsmen, which put their trust in their hounds, nor ever waste In slumber the end of the night, but the light of the sun they prevent, Lest, ere they be forth, he efface the track of the beasts, and the scent Of the quarry, with stainless-gleaming shafts down-smiting thereon, Even then with the maid from the galley forth stepped Aison's son" (Way).

div.seg: : here 'huntsmen' (ἀγρευταί); cf. the gloss in Hesych. ἀγρόται· θηρευταί, referring primarily to Od. 16. 218, οἰωνοὶ … οἷσί τε τέκνα Ἀγρόται ἐξείλοντο, though there the word may have its usual meaning 'rustics.' Ap. uses ἀγρότις 'huntress,' 2. 509; cf. Anth. P. 6. 13, ἀγρότα Πάν, 6. 111, κούρᾳ … ἀγροτίδι (i.e. Artemis).
: τὸν καιρὸν τὸν πλησίον καὶ ἐγγὺς τῆς ἡμέρας, ὥσπερ λυκόφωτα. Schol. The word is ἅπ. λεγ.
: here ἐνσκίμπτειν has the force of incumbere, and βολῇσιν is instr. dat.: elsewhere in Ap. it is equivalent to infigere, 3. 153, 765.

: 'at the spot which men call the resting-place of the ram'; ὅπου πρῶτον τὸν Φρίξον κομίσας ὁ κριὸς ἀνεπαύσατο. Schol. For the legend see note to 2.653. For the constr. cf. 1. 216, 237; Pind. N. 9. 41, ἔνθα Ῥέας πόρον ἄνθρωποι καλέοισιν: Il.
11. 757, Ἀλεισίου ἔνθα κολώνη Κέκληται, 'where is the hill called the hill of A.'
: 'suffered them (i.e. Jason and Medea) to go apart.'
