Od. 6. 263, καλὸς δὲ λιμὴν ἑκάτερθε πόληος), and adds ἱστορικῶς Ἀπολλώνιος ἀμφιλαφῆ τὸν λιμένα φησὶ … ἱστορεῖ δὲ περὶ τοῦ λιμένος τῶν Φαιάκων Ἀπολλωνίδης ἐν τῷ Περίπλῳ τῆς Εὐρώπης. Way wrongly renders 'forest-mantled.' For other uses of ἀμφιλαφής see on 1366, 2. 733.
: the fertility of Corcyra was famous, cf. Xen. Hell. 6. 2. 6, Κέρκυραν … ἐξειργασμένην μὲν παγκάλως καὶ πεφυτευμένην.
: i.e. the sea facing the Ceraunian Mts. (v. 519).

: cf. 2. 708. Ap. is imitating Arat. 637, Ἄρτεμις ἱλήκοι· προτέρων λόγος, οἵ μιν ἔφαντο κ.τ.λ. The story of the mutilation of Uranus by Kronos is told in Hes. Th. 180 sqq. Kronos was instigated by Gaea, wife of Uranus, who was wroth that her children were confined in Tartarus by their father Uranus. In the case of the Sicilian city Drepanum we also have the legend that the sickle of Kronos was buried there: v. Serv. on Aen. 3. 707, Tzetz. on Lyc. 869.

: Demeter; cf. 3. 413. The Schol. says that Aristotle in the Κερκυραίων πολιτεία told how Demeter got from Hephaestus a sickle (δρεπάνη) to teach the Titans reaping, and afterwards buried it on the coast of Corcyra. The constant washing of the waves on the coast gave to the island the form of a sickle.

: 'teeming'; πολύν, δαψιλῆ· Φιλητᾶς ἐν Ἀτάκτοις γλώσσαις ἀπέδωκε ὄμπνιον στάχυν τὸν εὔχυλον καὶ τρόφιμον. Κυρηναίων δέ τινες τὸν πλούσιον καὶ εὐδαίμονα ὄμπνιον καλοῦσιν. Schol.
It is from the same root as ἄφενος, opes. Hesych. cites Ὄμπνια as an epithet of Demeter = alma Ceres.
: the nurse of Dionysus; v. 1131 sqq. The island was called Μάκρις after her (v.n. 540) before it received the name of Δρεπάνη. The Homeric name is Σχερίη, Od. 5. 34. etc.

div.p: According to the Schol. Acusilaus and Alcaeus also said that the Phaeacians were sprung from the drops of blood which fell from the mutilated Uranus. In Od. 7. 56 Alcinous is descended from Poseidon.

div.seg: : Flangini notices the contrast between this hearty welcome of strangers by the Phaeacians and their character in the Od., where Athene says to Odysseus (7. 32), οὐ γὰρ ξείνους οἵδε μάλ’ ἀνθρώπους ἀνέχονται, Οὐδ’ ἀγαπαζόμενοι φιλέουσ’ ὅς κ’ ἄλλοθεν ἔλθῃ.
κ.τ.λ.: cf. Arat. 196, φαίης κεν ἀνιάζειν ἐπὶ παιδί.

κ.τ.λ.: 'like as if they had set foot in the heart of Thessaly.'
For the constr. cf. Il. 11. 467, τῷ ἰκέλη. ὡς εἴ ἑ βιῴατο μοῦνον ἐόντα. For Αἱμονίῃ cf. 2. 504.
: these words are repeated from the second line of the poem. The other Colchian force. which had pursued the Argo up the Ister, settled in Illyria after the death of Absyrtus (v. 507 sqq.).

: ἐξαίρετον. Schol., 'to take her from the heroes and bring her back to her father's house.' In Hom. ἔξαιτος means 'choice,' e.g. Od. 2. 307, ἐξαίτους ἐρέτας, and is explained either from αἴνυμαι or αἰτέω, or as a syncop. form of ἐξαίρετος.
: 'or threatened else that they would engage in grievous conflict with ruthless might, both now, and afterwards when Aeetes came.'

: adveniente Aeete (Beck); a strange expression. The meaning may be 'joining their forces with the expedition which A.
would lead thither'; for κέλευθος 'expedition' cf. Aesch. Ag. 126, ἀγρεῖ Πριάμου πόλιν ἅδε κέλευθος. This is Seaton's view.
: so Odysseus entreats Nausicaa, Od. 6. 149, γουνοῦμαί σε, ἅνασσα.

div.p: ᾧ: for ἐμῷ; see note to 2.132.

div.seg: κ.τ.λ.: 'whose minds are swift to rush to folly through thoughtless waywardness.' For the thought cf. Soph. Ant. 1023, ἀνθρώποισι γὰρ Τοῖς πᾶσι κοινόν ἐστι τοὐξαμαρτάνειν: Pind. P. 4. 139, ἐντὶ μὲν θνατῶν φρένες ὠκύτεραι | κέρδος αἰνῆσαι πρὸ δίκας δόλιον.
: see note to 3.467. Medea was priestess of Hecate.
: for this constr. in oaths cf. Il. 10. 330, ἴστω Ζεὺς … μὴ μὲν τοῖς ἵπποισιν ἀνὴρ ἐποχήσεται ἄλλος.

div.p: Cf. Od. 6. 180, σοὶ δὲ θεοὶ τόσα δοῖεν ὅσα φρεσὶ’, σῇσι μενοινᾷς, Ἄνδρα τε καὶ οἶκον καὶ ὁμοφροσύνην ὀπάσειαν.

div.seg: : this emendation seems right, but Merkel, I think, construes it wrongly. He says the constr. is ἀτύζομαι ἀμφ’ ὑμῶν καὶ ἀμφ’ ὧν ἔκαμον ἀέθλοις ὑμετέροις, but it is rather ἀτύζομαι ὑμῶν καὶ ὧν ἔκαμον ἀμφ’ ἀέθλοις ὑμετέροις, 'it is on account of you and of my service in your ordeals that I am now in an agony of fear.' For the simple gen. with ἀτύζομαι, cf. 2. 635, εἷο … ατύζομαι: Eur. Tro. 810, πώλων ἀτυζόμενος. That ἀμφί is not to be separated from ἀέθλοις is shown by 733 supr., ὅσα τ’ ἀμφὶ θοοῖς ἐμόγησαν ἀέθλοις. In 1354 G has ὧν ἕνεκα μεν for ὧν ἔκαμεν. Those who keep οὕνεκεν try to explain it as pleonastic after ἀμφί like χάριν ἕνεκά τινος, etc. Wellauer takes οὕνεκεν as a conj. 'quoniam,' and, removing the stop after ἀτύζομαι, regards the whole sentence as a protasis, the apodosis beginning in 1042.

: sc. ἐμέ. The constr. is not clear: the acc. and inf. may depend on νέμεσιν, 'the wrath of the gods at my being sent back into the hands of Aeetes to perish by painful sufferings'; cf. Il. 3. 156, οὐ νέμεσις Τρῶας … ἄλγεα πάσχειν, or we may repeat δείσατε "craignez de me remettre" (de M.).

div.p: οὐ γὰρ ναός μοί ἐστι βοηθὸς οὔτε πύργος οὔτε ἄλλος οὐδὲ εἷς, ἀλλ’ ὑμεῖς μοι ἀσφάλεια πᾶσα. Schol.

div.seg: : 'I throw myself upon the protection of'; in Il. 5. 879 it seems to mean 'to attack,' but see Leaf.
: here in the Homeric sense 'cruel' (see note to 2.1028).
: see note to 387 The gen. is used with σχέτλιος 'wretched,' e.g. Eur. Hec. 783, ὦ σχετλία τῶν πόνων.
: 'cut off,' i.e. isolated from the rest of the Colchians.
: 'if Medea should meet with an unjust decision.' Alcinous was to decide between the Colchians and the Argonauts (v. 1010).

: φθειρομένοις καὶ καταπονουμένοις, ἢ καὶ προσδιατρίβουσιν. Schol. The latter meaning seems correct here, the weariness being the weariness of delay and inaction: cf. Hesych. στρεύγομαι· διατρίβω. See also on 384. de M. renders "pendant que leur assemblée s'agitait ainsi, survint la nuit."
: "that putteth to sleep the labours of men" (Way). In Aesch. Pr. 895, Pers. 153 εὐνάτειρα is equivalent to ἄκοιτις.
: see note to 3.255. For the simile cf. 3. 291 and the passages quoted there.
: στάζει, παρ’ δ καὶ ὁ σταλαγμός. Schol. σταλάσσω is the classical form.
: cf. Il. 5. 399, ὀδύνῃσι πεπαρμένος: Hes. Op. 203, πεπαρμένη ἀμφ’ ὀνύχεσσι.
: 'flowing'; v. M. and R. on Od. 4. 705, θαλερὴ δέ οἱ ἔσχετο φωνή.
: for φίλε, to avoid hiatus, as in Il. 4. 189, etc.
: cf. Od. 4. 538, ἔμοιγε κατεκλάσθη φίλον ἦτορ.

κ.τ.λ.: 'and thereupon, essaying to cure one evil by another (as oft we do when we have gone astray), she fled from the pitiless wrath of her imperious sire.' σχεδόθεν is not used elsewhere in this sense.
: the expression is proverbial; cf. Hdt. 3. 53, μὴ τῷ κακῷ τὸ κακὸν ἰῶ: Soph. Aj. 362, μὴ κακὸν κακῷ διδοὺς Ἄκος πλέον τὸ πῆμα τῆς ἄτης τίθει.

: from ‐ζέω 'quick to
anger,' 'touchy'; v. M. and R. on Od. 7. 307, δύσζηλοι γάρ τ’ εἰμὲν ἐπὶ χθονὶ φῦλ’ ἀνθρώπων.

: for the constr. cf. Il. 10. 52, κακὰ μήσατ’ Ἀχαιούς. In 1. 735 Antiope is said to be the daughter of the river-god Asopus; here the poet follows the other legend that she was the daughter of Nycteus (Apollod. 3. 5. 5). When she was with child by Zeus, she fled from her father's wrath to Sicyon. Nycteus died in despair, having charged his brother Lycus to recover her. Her sons, Zethus and Amphion, afterwards avenged the wrongs inflicted on her by Dirce, wife of Lycus.

: daughter of Acrisius. An oracle had declared that her son would slay Acrisius, and so he immured her in a tower of bronze, where, however, Zeus visited her in the form of a shower of gold, and she became mother of Perseus. Acrisius then exposed both
Danae and Perseus in an ark (λάρναξ) on the open sea, but they floated safely to Seriphus. The most beautiful of the fragments of Simonides is the Lament of Danae beginning Ὄτε λάρνακι δαιδαλέᾳ ἄνεμος τέτμε πνέων.
: 'lately and not far away from this land.'

: a king of Epirus notorious for his fiendish cruelty; cf.
Od. 18. 84, Ἔχετον βασιλῆα, βροτῶν δηλήμονα πάντων κ.τ.λ. He blinded his daughter Metope, or Amphissa, for yielding to her lover Aichmodicus. Moreover, he gave her barleycorns of bronze, promising to restore her sight if she could grind them into flour (Eustath. p. 1839).
: cf. Od. 15. 533, ὑμετέρου δ’ οὐκ ἔστι γένος βασιλεύτερον ἄλλο.
: for the rare causal sense cf. Eur. Supp. 153, σφ’ ἀδελφὸς χρημάτων νοσφίζεται.
: 'for Alcinous (she said) is going to declare to the Colchians this judgment.' For the sudden change to the ind. cf. 440.
: ἀπὸ τοῦ ὜λλου τοῦ ἐκ Μελίτης καὶ Ἡρακλέους. Schol.; cf. 524, 538.
: 'to be sacrificed at the altar'; cf. Theocr. 16. 26, θεοῖς ἐπιβώμια ῥέζειν.

: 'hallowed,' an epithet only applied to places, and generally explained as ἄγαν θεῖος (v. Buttm. Lexil.). Goebel regards it as a strengthened form of ἀγαθός. Leaf (on Il. 1. 252) proposes ἀγάθεος (from ἄγαν) with the first syll. lengthened metrically.

: 'whose care was for honey';
elsewhere this adj. is always used of things 'sweet to the mind.' For Aristaeus and the bees cf. Virg. G. 4. 282 sqq. He was also said to have been the first to extract oil from olives.
: Rzach regards this aor. as an Alex. innovation, but we find εὑράμενος (εὑρόμενος, Fischer) in Hes. fr. 3.

: the Abantes were the oldest dwellers in Euboea (Strab. 382, 19); cf. Il. 2. 536, οἳ δ’ Εὔβοιαν ἔχον μένεα πνείοντες Ἄβαντες. According to Aristotle they were Thracians who passed over to Euboea from the Phocian town of Abae.

: when his mother Semele was slain by the levin-brand of Zeus; cf. the opening of Eur. Bacch.
Hence Dionysus was called πυριγενής (Strab. 537, 30) and ignigena (Ov. Met. 4. 12).

div.p: Cf. Od. 7. 335, where Arete bids her handmaids δέμνῑ ὑπ’ αἰθούσῃ θέμεναι καὶ ῥήγεα καλὰ Πορφύρε’ ἐμβαλέειν, στορέσαι τ’ ἐφύπερθε τάπητας.

div.seg: : which they had brought from Colchis.
: this same word is used of the tufts of the golden fleece in Pind. P. 4. 231.

div.p: For the classification of nymphs cf. 1. 1223.

div.seg: : 'grove-nymphs'; cf. 1. 1066. It is found only in these two passages.
: 'they (i.e. the nymphs) made Jason and Medea one.'
: 'at the entrance to the bridal chamber'; see note to 1.260.

div.p: For the pessimistic thought cf. Call. fr. 418, ἐπεὶ θεὸς οὐδὲ γελάσσαι Ἀκλαυτὶ μερόπεσσιν ὀιζυροῖσιν ἔδωκε: Lucr. 4. 1133, medio de fonte leporum Surgit amari aliquit quod in ipsis floribus angat : Ov. Met. 7. 453, usque adeo nulla est sincera voluptas Sollicitique aliquid laetis intervenit. For ἀλλὰ γάρ see note to 1.772. Ap. first uses δυηπαθής (δυήπαθος, h. Hom. Merc. 486); cf. δυηπαθίη, 1395 infr.

div.seg: : 'get a firm footing on'; "may tread full-footed the path of delight" (Way). There is a different use of ὅλῳ ποδί explained by Suidas ὅλῃ δυνάμει, with which we may compare Quint. 12. 9. 18, omni pede standum est.

div.p: Our poet had in mind the opening of Od. 8, =Ἠμος δ’ ἠριγένεια φάνη ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠὼς Ὤρνυτ’ ἄρ’ ἐξ εὐνῆς ἱερὸν μένος Ἀλκινόοιο κ.τ.λ.

div.seg: : cf. h. Hom. Cer. 13, γαῖα τε πᾶσ’ ἐγέλασσε καὶ ἁλμυρὸν οἶδμα θαλάσσης : Aesch. Pr. 90: Lucr. 1. 8.
: cf. 1. 1281, διαγλαύσσουσι δ’ ἀταρποί, Καὶ πεδία δροσόεντα φαεινῇ λάμπεται αἴγλῃ.

: for the form cf. 1. 925. It is not noticed by L. and S. The Schol. says it was a peninsula running out from the mainland of Epirus opposite to Corcyra, called Macridia from having been colonized from Euboea, the old name of which was Macris (Strab. 382. 6). More probably it is the projecting neck of land on which the mod. Corfu is situated.
: used παρατατικῶς (i.e. as an impf.) as is shown by the following verbs; see note to 865
: the symbol of authority borne by kings and chiefs (e.g. Od. 3. 412), by speakers in the assembly (Il. 1. 234), by judges (Il. 18. 505), etc.
: in Hom, always used of persons.

: 'by the
authority of which the people had righteous judgments given them throughout the city.' In Il. 16. 387 σκολιὰς κρίνωσι θέμιστας occurs in a couplet probably spurious. Leaf says, "the phrase κρίνειν θέμιστας (for δίκας) is not Homeric in expression or thought; to H. the θέμιστες are rather laws or principles than judgments to be given." See on 347 supr. For the use of διακρίνω cf. Theocr. 25. 46, διὰ δὲ κρίνουσι θέμιστας: Hes. Op. 35, διακρινώμεθα νεῖκος ('let us get the dispute settled') Ἰθείῃσι δίκῃς.
: 'for Hera had spread abroad tidings that erred not.'
: 'yet unworked,' and so fit for sabrifice; cf. the Homeric ἤκεστος and Tac. Germ. 10, equi nullo mortali opere contacti.

: 'with
which the newly wedded are furnished.' L. and S. take the verb as middle, but it is passive as in 1. 235, ὅσσαπερ ἐντύνονται … νῆες.

: 'glistering'; a constant epithet of raiment in Hom. It has been connected with σίαλος 'fat,' or with svigala 'clear,' 'bright'; while some refer it to rt. γαλ 'to shine' (v. n. 427), with σι as an intensive prefix.

: i.e. marking time with his foot for the chant and dance. κρότος ποδῶν was generally used of dancing. e.g. Eur. Tro. 546. In Od. 8. 264 the youths dancing to the lyre of the minstrel Demodocus πέπληγον … χυρὸν θεῖον ποσίν:
Aen. 6. 644, pars pedibus plaudunt choreas et carmina dicunt.
: sc. Orpheus, 'whene'er he touched on wedlock, they lifted up their voices in a tuneful marriage song.' Merkel remarks that the description is that of a χορὸς κύκλιος.
: Merkel adopts φᾶσθαι, the form found in L, taking it not from φημί but from φάω = φαινω, πιφαύσκω.
: the words of wisdom which Alcinous had spoken to her during the night.

div.p: 'and he, according as he had declared at first the decree of unswerving justice (v. 1104), and already the consummation of the marriage had been noised abroad, even so he observed his promise steadfastly to the end.'

div.seg: : 'he remained true to the inviolable oath by which he had bound himself.' ἔχεν is intrans., cf. Od. 19. 494, έξω, ὡς ὅτε τις στερεὴ λίθος.

: 'when the Colchians perceived that their opposition would be in vain' ἠλέματος is the form generally used by Alex. poets for the Homeric ἠλεός. αντιοωντες might also mean their entreaties (see note to 1.703), and so Way renders "in vain they besought him to swerve."
: the threats of Aeetes are described in 230 sqq.
: 'they induced the Phaeacians to receive them as comrades.' The Schol. explains συνήμονας as συνήθεις, ἑταίρους, παρὰ τὸ ἧσθαι; but it is connected with συνίημι. Cf. συνημοσύνας, 3. 1105.

: this powerful clan were supreme at Corinth from c. 750 b.c. They were driven out by Cypselus c. 657 b.c. (Hdt. 5. 92, Paus. 2. 4, etc.). When they lett Corinth they settled in different parts of Greece and even in Italy.
: Hom., speaking in his own person, calls the city Κόρινθος, while the Homeric heroes call it Ἐφύρη (v. Lehrs, Aristarch. 228).
: "une île plus lointaine" (de M.), but περαίην can hardly mean this. The meaning should be 'an island opposite (to Corcyra),' adversam msulam (Shaw); see note to 1.923.
: the Abantes of Euboea (v.n. 1135) were suppored to have settled near the Cerauman Mts, and to have founded a town Ἀβοντία or Ἀυαντία (Steph. Byz. s.v. Ἀβαντις).
: on the coast of Epirus, nearly opposite to Brundusium. Pliny (N.H. 3. 23) calls it 'oppidum a Colchis conditum.'

div.p: 'Howbeit these things came to pass after a long lapse of time.' Τίμαιος δέ φησι μετὰ ἔτη ἑξακόσια τῶν Τρωικῶν Χερσικράτη, ἀπόγονον τῶν Βακχιαδῶν, κατῳκηκέναι τὴν νῆσον. Schol. For ἄδην cf. 276.

div.seg: : see note to 2.507. The Schol. seems wrong in saying διὰ τὸ κατὰ νόμον γενέσθαι τὴν κρίσιν τοῦ Ἀλκινόου, διὰ τοῦτο Νομίου Ἀπόλλωνος ἱερὸν ἱδρύσασθαι τὴν Μήδειαν.

: the
Ambracian Gulf is an arm of the lonian (or Sicilian) Sea, between Epirus and Acarnania (Polyb. 4. 63).

: Strabo (398, 4) mentions how the Curetes (who came originally from Chalcis in Euboea) had been driven out of Aetolia into Acarnania. For the strife between the Curetes and Actolians v. Il. 9. 529 sqq.

: 'and the narrow islets which come next in order, amongst others the Echinades.' The Echinades were called after the ἐχῖνος or 'sea-urchin' from their sharp out-lines; cf. Strab. 393, 43, Thuc. 2. 102. etc.
: the Greater and Lesser Syrtis, and the dangers of the navigation there, are fully described in Strab. 708, 20 sqq. Cf. also Luc. Phars. 9. 300 sqq.
: literally 'weedstrewn thickets of the deep.' Ap. forms μνιόεις from μνίον, alga, a late Gr. word (φῦκος in Hom.). Distinguish τάρφεα 'thickets' (cf. 13) from ταρφέα 'often' (1195).
: 'and over them the sea-foam flows with noiseless swell.' For κωφή cf. 153. The form ἐπιβλύω is only found here; see on 788, 3. 223.

: πῦν τὸ πολὺ καὶ δαψιλὲς ἠερόεν λέγομεν. Schol. This meaning is required by 1246. The sandy waste extended indefinitely like the vast expanse of air. One meaning given by Hesych. for ἠέριον is μέγα. Diodorus (1. 33) uses ἀέριος in a similar way, θῖνας ἄμμου ἔχοντας μέγεθος ἀέριον. For other uses of ἠέριος v.n. 267, 1. 580. Some take it here as 'misty,' and Way blends the two views
in his rendering "into haziest distance stretcheth the land."
: 'moves,' literally 'soars,' used by zeugma with ἑρπετόν.

: ''twas there then that the flood-tide--for oftentimes the streaming waves fall back from the land, and again with angry onset hurl themselves on the beach--in a moment drove them far in on the shore, and but little of the keel was left in the water.'
: "the long low backs of the land" (Way).
: 'unbroken.' διηνεκής is used as an epithet of νῶτον in its literal sense in Il. 7. 321, νώτοισι διηνεκέεσσι, 'with slices cut the whole length of the chine.'
: i.e. the same course as on the outward voyage through the Symplegades.

: cf. Il. 17. 321, Ἀργεῖοι δέ κε κῦδος ἕλον καὶ ὑπὲρ Διὸς αἶσαν. Similarly ὑπὲρ μόρον, 1. 1030. Leaf (on Il. 16. 780) points out that these phrases are never used of anything which is actually said to have happened, but always of the future or unrealized possibilities in the past; v. M. and R. on Od. 1. 34.

div.p: Cf. Hector's words, Il. 22. 304, μὴ μὰν ασπουδί γε καὶ ακλειῶς ἀπολοίμην, Ἀλλὰ μέγα ῥέξας τι καὶ ἐσσομένοισι πυθέσθαι.

div.seg: : 'so dreary is the coast-line of this vast continent which unfolds itself before our eyes.'
: 'limitless,' μέγα καὶ ἐπὶ πόλυ διῆκον (Suid.). Cf. Call. fr. 111, ἔνθ’ ἀνέμων μεγάλων κῦμα διωλύγιον. It is a Platonic word of unknown derivation.

: 'fallen on this desolation.' Here, as in 3. 321, ἐπί seems to have been
corrupted into ὑπό. For the use of ὑπό Oswald compares 1524, ὑπὸ χροΐ δύετο κῶμα, which is not parallel at all. The only possible meaning which could be extracted out of ὑπό here would be 'under the power of,' 'into the clutches of.' For the enallage of cases ἄμμι … πεπτηότας see on 3. 1009.
: 'from the land'; even though the wind blew off the shore, it would not help them to get away.
: see note to 2.283. It seems to refer to the mass of water, though Merkel explains it by ματαίως, meaning, I presume, 'uselessly' from the point of view of refloating the Argo.
: 'torn into spray runs up on the foamwhitened sand.' L. and S. wrongly take ὕδωρ as acc. ἐπιτροχάω is used differently in 1606.
: 'while still far from the land.' The vessel would have been broken to pieces in the shoals, had not the flood-tide carried it up on the shore.
: in 1241 and 2. 576 the penult. is long; here it is short, as in Od. 9. 486 (which Ap. is imitating), τὴν δ’ αἶψ’ ἤπειρόνδε παλιρρόθιον φέρε κῦμα Πλημμυρὶς ἐκ πόντοιο, θέμωσε δὲ χέρσον ἱκέσθαι.
κ.τ.λ.: 'and the sea-water, not deep enough to float the vessel, merely washes about it, barely rising above the ground.' For ὅσσον see note to 2.112.
: cf. Lat. abscidere spem. The metaph. use of ἀποκόπτειν is common in late Gr.

: φαίνοιεν seems an impossible form of 3 sing. opt., and, so far as I know, lacks any analogy. Merkel says that it may derive some support from Il. 14. 241, where for ἐπισχοίης A and C have ὲπίσχοιες, which is said to have been defended by Herodian (v. Heyne ad loc.; Kühner-Blass 214).

: 'was frozen'; cf. Il.
17. 112, ἦτορ παχνοῦται: Ov. Her. 15. 112, astrictum frigore pectus.
χλόος: see note to 2.1216.
: cf. Liv. 21. 40, effigies immo, umbrae hominum.

: Virg. imitates this,
G. 1. 324, ruit arduus aether, Et pluvia ingenti sata laeta boumque labores Diluit.
ἔργα βοῶν is from Hes. Op. 46; Hom. uses ἔργα ἀνθρώπων in a similar passage, Il. 16. 390, χαράδραι … στενάχουσι ῥέουσαι Ἐξ ὀρέων ἐπὶ κάρ, μινύθει δέ τε ἔργ’ ἀνθρώπων.

div.p:
With this enumeration of prodigies cf. Tibull. 2. 5. 75, Et simulacra deum lacrimas fudisse tepentes, Fataque vocales praemonuisse boves, Ipsum etiam Solem defectum lumine vidit Iungere pallentes nubilus annus equos: Virg. G. 1. 478,
pecudesque locutae
Infandum ....
Et maestum inlacrimat templis ebur, aeraque sudant.
The Schol. refers to the portents before the battle of Chaeronea (Plut. Demosth. 19).

div.seg: : cf. 3. 866. Ap. had in mind Il. 24. 12, δινεύεσκ’ ἀλύων παρὰ θῖν’ ἁλός.
: = ἀλλήλους; cf. Hes. Sc. 403, ἀλλήλοις κοτέοντες ἐπὶ σφέας ὁρμήσωσι. See on 2. 128.

div.p: 'and they went forth on different ways, one further than another, to choose a resting-place.'

div.seg: κ.τ.λ.: so in 2. 861 after the death of Tiphys the heroes εντυπὰς εὐκήλως εἰλυμένοι οὔτε τι σίτου Μνώοντ’ οὔτε ποτοῖο.

: cf. Il. 19. 346, ὁ δ’ ἄκμηνος καὶ ἄπαστος. ἄκμηνος occurs four times in Il. 19, and Schol. A explains it ἄγευστος, παρὰ τὴν υκμήν. οὕτω δὲ τὴν ἀσιτίαν Αἰολεῖς λέγουσι. Both it and ἄπαστος are used of food and drink; cf. Il. 19. 320, άκμηνον πόσιος καὶ ἐδητύος, Od. 4. 788, άπαστος ἐδητύος ἠδὲ ποτῆτος.
: the Phaeacian handmaids given by Arete to Medea (v. 1221).

div.p:
"This simile is perfectly original, and highly beautiful and expressive. The
fears, the tenderness, and unavailing cries of the Phaeacian virgins (who found themselves sent from the ease, the plenty, and indulgence of a palace in Phaeacia, to perish by hunger in that Libyan desert) are well expressed by the helpless state of the young and unfledged birds falling out of the parent nest in a rock, in the absence of the mother" (Preston).

div.seg: : Πακτωλὸς ποταμὸς Λυδίας, ὁ νῦν Χρυσορρόας λεγόμενος. Schol. It was famous for its gold dust (ψῆγμα χρυσοῦ), Strab. 535, 4.

: Il. 2. 459, ὥς τ’ ὀρνίθων πετεηνῶν ἕθνεα πολλά, Χηνῶν ἢ γεράνων ἢ κύκνων δουλιχοδείρων, Ἀσίῳ ἐν λειμῶνι, Καϋστρίου ἀμφὶ ῥέεθρα, Ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα ποτῶνται ἀγαλλόμενα πτερύγεσσιν, Κλαγγηδὸν προκαθιζόντων, σμαραγεῖ δέ τε λειμών:
Aen. 7. 700, Ceu quondam nivei liquida inter nubila cycni ... longa canoros Dant per colla modos; sonat amnis et Asia longe Pulsa palus. In our passage there may be a further reference to the death-song of the swan, cf. Aesch. Ag. 1444, κύκνου δίκην Τὸν ὕστατον μέλψασα θανάσιμον γόον Κεῖται.
: = ὰνώνυμοι, cf. 2. 982. Merkel takes it here in the sense recognized by the Schol. on Il. 13. 227, νωνύμνους· τινὲς ἀθρηνήτους· ὕμνον γὰρ καὶ Ἀνακρέων τὸν θρῆνόν φησιν.
: the form ἡρῷσσα for ἡρωίνη is found in Anth. P. 6. 225, Ἡρῷσσαι Λιβύων ὄρος ἄκριτον αἵτε νέμεσθε.
: 'guardian deities,' praesides; cf. Aesch. Ag. 519, ἐμὸν τιμάορον Ἑρμῆν. The Schol. quotes from Call., δέσποιναι Λιβύης ἡρωίδες, αἳ Νασαμώνων Αὖλιν καὶ δολιχὰς θῖνας ἐπιβλέπετε.
κ.τ.λ.: πρῶτος Στησίχορος ἔφη σὺν ὅπλοις ἐκ τῆς τοῦ Διὸς κεφαλῆς ἀναπηδῆσαι τὴν Ἀθηνᾶν. Schol. For the legend v. Pind. O. 7. 35 sqq., h. Hom. Minerv.
: 'met with her, and bathed her in the waters.' Cf. Call. Jov. 15, ἔνθα σ’ ἐπεὶ μήτηρ μεγάλων ἀπεθήκατο κόλπων, Αὐτίκα δίζητο ῥόον ὕδατος, ᾧ κε τόκοιο Λύματυ χυτλώσαιτο, τεὸν δ’ ἐνὶ χρῶτα λοέσσαι.
: 'noon,' see note to 1.603. The short penult. is only found in Alex. writers; cf. Call. Cer. 39, τῷ δ’ ὕπο ταὶ νύμφαι ποτὶ τὤνδιον ἑψιόωντο,

: 'lonely.' Triton is called οἰοπόλος δαίμων, Pind. P. 4. 49. Our Schol. wrongly explains it by
ἐπιαηλίδες, and so Hoelzlin and Shaw translate pecorariae deae, but the meaning is fixed by ἐρημονόμοι, 1333.
: indigites, see note to 2.504; cf. Soph. Aj. 201, χθονίων ἀπ’ Ἐρεχθειδῶν. For the usual meaning v. 987.
: Hom. uses θεὸς αὐδήεσσα of Calypso and Circe who speak with the speech of mortals.
: in Hom. Amphitrite is not a goddess, but, at most, a personification of the sea. As a goddess and wife of Poseidon she appears first in Hes. Th. 243, 930.
: 'unyokes.' In Il. 5. 731 Hera is represented as yoking her chariot, ὑπὸ δὲ ζυγὸν ἤγαγεν Ἤρη Ἴππους ὠκύποδας.
: ἔδει εἰπεῖν ὑμετέρᾳ (see note to 3.186). λέγει δὲ τῇ νηί. φέρει γὰρ αὐτοὺς ἐν τῷ κύτει, ὡς ἐν γαστρὶ μήτηρ. Schol.
: cf. Tac. Ann. 2. 6, lato utero (navium), and the use of uterus of the Trojan Horse, Aen. 2. 38.
κ.τ.λ.: 'they straightway vanished where they stood, as their voice died away.' For παρας χεδόν see note to 1.354.
: "in the multitude of counsellors there is safety." Cf. Il. 10. 224 sqq., Plaut. Mil. 3. 3. 12, nemo solus satis sapit.
: 'his mate'; cf. Soph. Ph. 1436, ὡς λέοντε συννόμω.
: οἱ βουκόλοι. Schol. Ap. is the first to use this word.

κ.τ.λ.: 'but the voice had no terrors for them (i.e. the Argonauts),
being the voice of their comrade calling on his friends.'
: the place where the vessel lay.
: for this rare simple form cf. Pind. P. 4. 202, μίγα κωκυτῷ. Ap. has ἄμμιγα c. dat., 1. 573, etc.

: τοῖς δέρμασιν. ἔνθεν καὶ στερφῶσαι. Ἴβυκος δὲ στερφωτῆρα στρατὸν εἴρηκε τὸν ἔχοντα δέρματα. ὅθεν καὶ παρ’ Αἰσχύλῳ (fr. 377) ἀξιοῦσι γράφειν μελανοστέρφων γένος, οὐχ, ὥς τινες, μελανοστέρνων. Schol. For this
Libyan dress cf. Hdt. 4. 189, αἰγέας περιβάλλονται ψιλὰς περὶ τὴν ἐσθῆτα θυσανωτὰς αἱ Λίβυσσαι κεχριμένας ἐρευθεδάνῳ.
: cf. Il. 2. 20 (of Ὄνειρος visiting Agamemnon), στῆ δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπὲρ κεφαλῆς.
: cf. the symbolic appearance of the four white steeds, the portent of war, in Aen. 3. 537 sqq.

: ἀντὶ τοῦ ποικίλος ἢ μέγας ἢ ἀμφοτέρωθεν θριξὶ στεγαζόμενος. Schol. The last of these explanations is that generally received, and so the line means 'its hair flowing on both sides, with arching neck and golden mane.' To explain it by μέγας is to make it a weak repetition of πελώριος. For other uses of ἀμφιλαφής see on 983, 2. 733.
: 'unyielding,' from rt. στεμφ (στεμβω, stamp); cf. Il. 2. 344, ἔχων ἀστεμφέα βουλήν.
: 'for he will not plunge beneath the dry land' (as he might beneath the waves).

: ὑπηρέτης. Schol.; see note to 1.22. Cf. Call. Dian. 186, εἰπὲ θεά, σὺ μὲν ἄμμιν, ἐγὼ δ’ ἑτέροισιν ἀείσω: Theocr. 22. 116, εἰπὲ θεά, σὺ γὰρ οἶσθα, ἐγὼ δ’ ἑτέρων ὑποφήτης Φθέγξομαι:
Aen. 7. 645, et meministis enim, divae, et memorare potestis.
: Ap. is the first to use this compound.
: cf. 1031. With this apostrophe to the heroes Ellis compares the self-interpellation in Cat. 64. 116.

div.p:
Cf. Pind. P. 4. 25, δώδεκα δὲ πρότερον | ἁμέρας ἐξ Ὠκεανοῦ φέρομεν νώτων ὕπερ γαίας ἐρήμων | εἰνάλιον δόρυ. According to another version the Argonauts bore their vessel on their shoulders
when passing from the Ister into the Adriatic (Justin. Histor. 32. 3).

div.seg: : for the unusual dat. with φέρειν cf. 3. 392.
: cf. Theocr. 2. 82, ὡς ἴδον, ὡς ἐμάνην: Virg. E. 8. 41, ut vidi, ut perii . See Leaf on Il. 14. 294. The meaning here is 'when .. then.' In 1. 269 ὡς … ὧς means 'as .. so.'
: ἅπ. λεγ., "rushing, like unto hounds in the wild hunt's frenzy-burst" (Way).
: 'for parching thirst crowned their woes and sufferings.' For δυηπαθίῃ cf. 1165.

: the dragon which guarded the golden apples of the Hesperides by the orders of Hera. He was the son of Gaea (so χθόνιος, 1398), or of Phorcys and Ceto (Hes. Th. 333). The apples were given by Gaea to Hera on her marriage with Zeus.

: 'in the home of Atlas.' The same form of expression occurs in Aesch. Eum. 673, Πέλοπος ἐν τόποις, Pers. 786, ἐς τὸν Ἑλλήνων τόπον. Cf. Hes. Th. 517, Ἄτλας δ’ οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἔχει κρατερῆς ὑπ’ ὰνάγκης Πείρασιν ἐν γαίης, πρόπαρ Ἑσπερίδων λιγυφώνων Ἑστηώς. Virg. ( Aen. 4. 481) represents the garden of the Hesperides as a templum (τέμενος),
Ultimus Aethiopum locus est, ubi maxumus Atlas
Axem humero torquet ...
Hinc mihi Massylae gentis monstrata sacerdos,
Hesperidum templi custos, epulasque draconi
Quae dabat et sacros servabat in arbore ramos.

: cf. Eur. H.F. 394, ὑμνῳδούς τε κόρας ἤλυθεν (sc. Ἡρακλῆς) ἑσπέριον ἐς αὐλάν: Hipp. 742, Ἑσπερίδων ἀοιδῶν. This is the only place where Ap. lengthens the α of ἀείδω. There is also one example in Hom., Od. 17. 519.
: hodie, 'on this very day' referring to χθιζόν in 1397; see note to 252

: 'lay
stretched along by the trunk of the apple-tree.'
: cf. Quint. Smyr. 8. 320 (of the convulsive writhings of one mortally wounded), ὃς δ’ ἔτι ποσσὶν Ὀρθὸς ὰνεσκαίρεσκεν.

κ.τ.λ.: 'and as the arrows had left in its blood the venom of the Lernaean hydra, the flies clustering on the festering wounds were being withered (by the poison).' The arrows of Heracles were dipped in the black gall of the hydra, which haunted the marsh of Lerna near Argos; cf. Soph. Tr. 573, μελαγχόλους Ἔβαψεν ἰοὺς θρέμμα Λερναίας ὕδρας.

: this seems to mean that the flies were withered up by the poison, or else that their poisoned bodies were shrivelled by the sun's strong rays. Merkel says, "τερσαίνοντο nisi forte propria locutio de apricantibus eius modi bestiolis fuit explicatum non habet:
temptaveram ταργαίνοντο, h.e. ἐταράσσοντο, πορσαίνοντο, h.e. ἐσπούδαζυν."
κ.τ.λ.: 'as they (the heroes) eagerly drew near, the Hesperides were straightway turned into dust and earth where they stood.' For κιόντων see note to 692
: = νοήσατο; cf. Theogn. 1298, νωσάμενος; Hdt. 1. 68, ἐννώσας.
: on the analogy of κέρα; we also find τέραα (Od. 12. 394), τέρεα (Hdt. 8. 37), τέρα^ (Nic. Th. 186).
: 'tried to win their favour for the heroes by his prayers.' This constr. of παρηγορέω is without parallel. For Samuelsson's conj. see on 3. 741.
: 'nymphs of the desert'; see note to 1322

: with αἰθομένην, 'which
parches us with fierce intensity'; see note to 1.513. Lehrs takes ἄμοτον with λωφήσομεν 'omnino restinguamus.'
: 'shoots'; cf. Il 21. 38. First the grass appeared, then tall shoots above the grass, and then the young trees (ἔρνεα) reared their branches.

div.p: Sometimes we find four Hesperides mentioned, Aegle, Erytheia, Hestia, and Arethusà; Diod. (4. 27) mentions seven.
sqq.
div.seg: : 'and from those trees their forms were made manifest in the full likeness of what they had been aforetime--a prodigy most strange.'

div.p: 'Verily it was to prove himself a great succour in your distress that he (Heracles) came hither.'

div.seg: : the force of καί is that he too, like the Argonauts, sought water.
: 'his throat rough and parched with thirst'; cf. Virg. G. 3. 434, asperque siti : Il. 21. 541, δίψῃ καρχαλέοι … θεῦγον. See on 3. 1058.
: 'rushed wildly,' ἐνθουσιωδῶς ἐφέρετο. Schol. Cf. μεταπαιφάσσεσθαι, 3. 1266, where see note.
: cf. 1546. The simple ἐρέω occurs in 1. 1354.

div.p: 'this, by his own device, or rather on the prompting of some god, he smote at the base with his heel.' For ἢ καί cf. 205. For ἐννεσίῃσιν see note to 1.7. In Call. Jov. 30 Rhea smites a mountain and makes water gush forth.

div.seg: : 'stooping, with head bent down.' This line is twice imitated by Nicander: Alex. 495, ἢν δέ τις αὐαλέῃ πεπιεσμένος αὐχένα δίψῃ Ἐχ ποταμοῦ ταυρηδὸν ἐπιπροπεσὼν ποτὸν ἴσχῃ: Ther. 340, αὐτὰρ ὅγ’ ἠύτε ταῦρος ὑπὲρ ποταμοῖο νενευκὼς Χανδὸν ἀμέτρητον δέχεται ποτόν.

div.p:
'As when the ants who turn up the earth run to and fro in busy haste around a narrow cleft, or when flies lighting round a tiny drop
of sweet honey press towards it in a greedy swarm, so, etc.'

div.seg: : Virgil borrowed the comparison of the ants but gave it a different development in Aen. 4. 402 sqq.
: cf. Il. 2. 469, ἠύτε μυιάων ἀδινάων ἔθνεα πολλά, Αἵ τε κατὰ σταθμὸν ποιμνήιον ἠλάσκουσιν Ὤρῃ ἐν εἰαρινῇ, ὅτε τε γλάγος ἄγγεα δεύει: 17. 570 sqq.

div.p: 'He spake: and, as they held converse, those who were fitted for such a quest separated themselves from the other heroes, and sped away, one on this side, another on that, to search for Heracles.'
div.seg: : i.e. by fleetness, or keenness of vision.

: ἐκεκάλυπτο. Schol., 'had been effaced'; the literal meaning must be that the tracks had the sand rolled on them (ἐπαλινδέω) by the wind. This compound is only found here; ἐπαλίνδομαι in Nic. Th. 266.
: v. 1. 77 sqq., where his death in Libya is foreshadowed.
: Heracles and Polyphemus were left behind by the Argonauts in Mysia (1. 1240 sqq.). For their diverse fortunes v. 1. 1345 sqq.
: v. 1. 1323. The Schol. tells us, on the authority of Nymphodorus, that Polyphemus died fighting there.
: the white poplar, the black being called αἴγειρος. Pausanias (5. 14. 3) connects the name with Ἀχέρων, as it was brought from the underworld by Heracles. In Attic it was called λεύκη.
: 'deemed that he saw'; see note to 1.718.

κ.τ.λ.: 'as, on the day of the new moon, one sees, or thinks that he sees, the moon in a veil of mist.' For νέῳ cf. ἕνη καὶ νέα. In Plat. Legg. 849 we find μηνὸς τῇ νέᾳ (sc. ἡμέρᾳ). Virg. borrowed this simile,
Aen. 6. 452 (where Aeneas sees dimly the shade of Dido), agnovitque per umbram Obscuram, qualem primo qui surgere mense Aut videt aut vidisse putat per nubila lunam. Cf. Milton, P. L. 1. 783, "Whose midnight revels ... some belated peasant sees, Or dreams he sees."
: 'that now no other who went in quest should overtake him.'
: 'shepherd,' ὁ ἀπὸ τῆς ἐπαύλεως, ὁ ἀγροῖκος. ἔστι δὲ παρὰ τὴν αὖλιν τὸ ὄνομα. Schol., cf. Soph. fr. 445, ἑωθινὸς γὰρ πρίν τιν’ αὐλιτῶν ὁρᾶν. ὅ …

: 'who, warding thee off in defence of his flock, whilst thou wouldst carry it off for thy needy comrades, slew thee with the cast of a stone.' This use of τόφρα c. opt. meaning 'while' seems to be unique. In Alex. Greek we sometimes find τόφρα used in various senses of ὄφρα (see note to 3.807), but there is no instance of ὄφρα c. opt. in this sense. Merkel cites as similar uses of the opt. 4. 1720, ὅσσα … ἐφοπλίσσειαν, and Il. 5. 303, ὃ οὐ δύο γ’ ἄνδρε φέροιεν (which he mistranslates ferre voluissent), but these are not parallel, as they are both the ordinary potential opt. with ἄν or κε omitted (see note to 1.480).

: ὰντὶ τοῦ Δελφικοῦ. οἱ γὰρ Δελφοὶ τὸ πρῶτον Λυκωρεῖς ἐκάλοῦντο ἀπό τινος κώμης Λυκωρείας.
Schol. Λυκώρεια was the ancient name for the highest peak of Parnassus. Brunck supposes that there is a special reference to the legend recounted in Anton. Lib. Met. 30 that the child which the nymph Acacallis bore to Apollo was nurtured by wolves (λύκοι).

: = κύημα; cf. Aesch. Eum. 659, τροφὸς δὲ κύματος vεοσπόρου: Eur. fr. 107, γέμουσαν κύματος θεοσπόρον. The Schol. says, Ἀλέξανδρος ἐν πρώτῳ Κρητικῶν τῇ Ἀκακαλλίδι συνελθεῖν φησι τὸν Ἑρμῆν καὶ τὸν Ἀπόλλωνα, καὶ ἐκ μὲν Ἀπόλλωνος γενέσθαι Νάξον, ἐκ δὲ Ἐρμοῦ Κύδωνα, ἀφ’ οὗ ἡ πόλις Κυδωνία καλεῖται ἐν Κρήτῃ. The offspring of Acacallis, daughter of Minos, are mentioned also in Paus. 8. 53. 2.
: the Garamantes, a pastoral tribe in Libya, took their name from him; cf. Hdt. 4. 174, where the Nasamones are also referred to.
: 'flocks.' The noun ῥήν (which L. and S. mark as fem.) was formed by Alex. writers from the Homeric πολύρρηνος, πολύρρηνες. See on 1. 49.
: Ap. originated this form for ἀποτροπή; cf. ὑποτροπίη, 1. 1052. For the thought cf. 1. 1035.
: 'too sluggish to injure.' For this use of the positive cf. Pind. I. 6. 44, βραχὺς ἐξικέσθαι: Xen. Cyr. 4. 5. 15. ὀλίγοι ὡς ἐγκρατεῖς εἶναι: Hor. C. 1. 35. 28, ferre iugum pariter dolosi.

div.p: 'the path to Death is not one cubit long.' For πήχυιον cf. 1. 379, 3. 1207.

div.seg: : the healer of the gods in Hom. (Il. 5. 401, etc.).

: this name of Perseus is found also in Euphorion (fr. 16).
It is noted in Hesych. and Et. Mag.
: we have the form καλέσκετο in Il. 15. 338.
: a new form = νεότομος in Trag.

div.p: Cf. 2. 1211 sqq., where the dragon which guarded the golden fleece is said to be sprung from the blood of the stricken Typhoeus.

div.seg:
: cf. Ov. Met. 4. 616,
Cumque super Libycas victor (sc. Perseus) penderet arenas,
Gorgonei capitis guttae cecidere cruentae:
Quas humus exceptas varios animavit in angues;
Unde frequens illa est, infestaque terra colubris
; Milton P. L. x 526, "not so thick swarmed once the soil Bedropt with blood of Gorgon." Lucan gives an elaborate version, Phars. 9. 619-99.

: 'trod upon.' Lucan imitates this description, 9. 737 sqq.,
Signiferum iuvenem Tyrrheni sanguinis Aulum
Torta caput retro dipsas calcata momordit.
Vix dolor aut sensus dentis fuit ...
Ecce subit virus tacitum carpitque medullas.
: ταρσὸν ποδός is treated as a compound 'foot-sole'; contrast Il. 11. 377, ταρσὸν δεξιτεροῖο ποδός.
: the tibia, the great bone of the leg.
: the cluster of muscles in the leg, the calf; cf. Il. 16. 314, πρυμνὸν σκέλος ἔνθα πάχιστος Μυὼν ἀνθρώπου πέλεται.
: 'also.' For the pleonastic use cf. Od. 6. 84, ἅμα τῇγε (Nausicaa) καὶ ἀμφίπολοι κίον ἄλλαι.
: 'for no overwhelming pain was torturing him.' This rare use of ἕνεκα for οὕνεκα is found in Call. fr. 287, h. Hom. Ven. 199.

: the deadness, or numbness, such as followed the drinking of
hemlock as described in Plat. Phaed. 117.
: an epithet of ὕπνες in Od. 20. 56.
: cf. Il. 5. 696, κατὰ δ’ ὀφθαλμῶν κέχυτ’ ἀχλύς. To this passage is to be referred Varro Atac. fr. 10, semianimesque micant oculi, lucemque requirunt.
: 'he grew coìd with the chill of death, in utter helplessness.'

: 'the dank hair fell away from the skin'; cf. μυδῶν σῶμα, Soph. Ant. 410. The falling of the hair from poisoned bodies is described later in Nonn. Dion. 4. 364, ψαφαρὴ δὲ κατ’ αὐχένος ἔρρεε χαίτη Αὐτομάτη πλαδαροῖο διειλυσθεῖσα καρήνου.
: 'mattocks'; cf. Hes. Op. 468, Theocr. 16. 32. Hom. has μάκελλαν, Il. 21. 259.

: 'they gave a share of their locks,' i.e. cut off their locks and laid them on the corpse. For this custom cf. Il. 23. 135, θριξὶ δὲ πάντα νέκυν καταείνυσαν, ἃς ἐπέβαλλον, Κειρόμενοι,
where Leaf says, "A part cut straight from the living body represents the whole man, who thus offers himself as an escort to the shades."
: 'honoured with all due rites.' εὖ ἔχειν is used by Hom., but not the idiom εὖ ἔχειν c. gen. common in later Gr.
: ἅπ. λεγ., 'they guessed at the channels so as to come forth, etc.' Cf. 1570.

: Hector awaiting Achilles is compared to a serpent, Il. 22. 93, ὡς δὲ δράκων ἐπὶ χειῇ ὀρέστερος ἄνδρα μένῃσιν. The comparison of the tortuous movement of a serpent had been already used by Hesiod (ap. Strab. 364, 13) of a river, καί τε δῑ Ὀρχομενοῦ εἱλιγμένος εἶσι, δράκων ὥς.

: 'sparks,' ἅπ. λεγ. σπινθήρ is the usual form; σπινθαρίς occurs in h. Hom. Apoll. 442. Cf.
Aen. 2. 210 (of the snakes which attack Laocoon), Ardentesque oculos suffecti sanguine et igni, Sibila lambebant linguis vibrantibus ora.
: 'fissure,' ἡ κατὰ τὴν γῆν ῥῆξις. Schol.; cf. Il. 23. 420.
: one of the two mentioned in 529 supr. Cf. Hdt. 4. 179, where Triton asks Jason for the tripod, promising to show him the right course.
: our poet closely follows Pind. P. 4. 20, Τριτωνίδος ἐν προχοαῖς | λίμνας θεῷ ἀνερι vειδομένῳ γαῖαν διδόντι | ξείνια πρῴραθεν Εὔφημος καταβὰς | δέξατο.

: cf. Hes. Th. 931, ἐκ δ’
Ἀμφιτρίτης καὶ ἐρικτύπου Ἐννοσιγαίου Τρίτων εὐρυβίης γένετο. Diodorus (4. 56) rationalizes the story by making Triton a king of Libya, who succoured the heroes.
κ.τ.λ.: 'for I have now no gift surpassing great to bestow on those who come hither.' For ἐγγυαλίξαι see note to 1.245.
: μαίομαι c. acc. = quaero (cf. Od. 13. 367); c. gen. = appeto, as in 1275.
: for the lengthening of the first svll. v. App. II (g). It is imitated in Dion. P. 253.

: Ποσειδῶνος υἱὸς καὶ Κελαινοῦς τῆς Ἄτλαντος, βασιλεὺς δὲ Κυρήνης. Schol. He is mentioned in Call. Ap. 91. Triton takes the same name in Pind. P. 4. 32, φάτο δ’ Εὐρύπυλος Γαιαόχου παῖς ἀφθίτου … ἔμυεναι.
: Varro Atac. (fr. 19) translates this by 'feta feris Libye.'

: 'stretched out his hands towards the clod'; cf. Pind. l.c., χειρί vοι χεῖρ’ ἀντερείσαις δέξατο (sc. Εὔφαμος) βώλακα δαιμονίαν. ὑπερέσχεθε seems to be used very loosely here; contrast Il. 24. 374, τις … ἐμεῖο θεῶν ὑπερέσχεθε χεῖρα 'held his hand over me (to protect me).' ὑποέσχεθε is possible.
: as son of Poseidon (v. 1. 180) he welcomes Poseidon's son.

: this reading seems undoubtedly right, though wrongly explained by the Schol. as an island off Crete. Ἀπίς is a form only found here for the usual Ἀπία, the old name for the Peloponnesus (v.n. 263). The vulg. Ἀτθίδα 'Attica' is meaningless, as they were making for the Peloponnesus (v. 1570, 1577).
: πέλαγος πρὸ τῆς Κρήτης. αὕτη γὰρ Μίνωος ἦν βασιλεία. Schol.; cf. 2. 299.
: 'deep to the very edge'; cf. Od. 5. 413, ἀγχιβαθὴς δὲ θάλασσα.
: μελανέω is the form used by Alex. writers; μελάνω occurs in Il. 7. 64, μελάνει … πόντος (where see Leaf). Ap. also uses μελαίνουαι, 569 supr.

: 'but on either side white breakers bristle, clearly to be seen.' de M. takes ῥηγμῖνες in the sense of rugged coasts, "de blanches falaises se hérissent, éclatantes à la vue"; cf. 2. 348. In Hom. ῥηγμίν combines the two meanings of 'surf' and 'shore.'

div.p: 'now that sea, fading in mist, extends above Crete to the sacred land of Pelops.'
div.seg: : ἅπ. λεγ.; cf. ἠέριος, 1239, etc. L. and S. explain 'exposed to the air,' which seems pointless.

: they are
to hug the coast until it turns north and runs out in the headland of Phycus, the most northerly point on the Libyan coast, 2800 stadia south of Taenarus in the Peloponnesus; cf. Strab. 710, 24.

: 'where the land winds sloping round in another direction.' From this elbow of land (ἀγκών, 1583) they would sail north through the open sea to Greece. The adv. περιρρήδην is ἅπ. λεγ.; for the adj. περιρρηδής see note to 1.431. Erotianus in his Glossary explains περιρρηδές in Hippocrates by ἑκατέρωθεν ἐγκεκλιμένον μηνοειδῶς.
κ.τ.λ.: 'let there be no grieving at your hard lot, that limbs endued with lusty youth should have to toil.'
: ἅπ. λεγ. Ap. has several new compounds with ἐπιπρο (‐έχομαι, 4. 524, ‐θέω 1. 582, ‐μολεῖν 3. 665, ‐πίπτω 4. 1449, ‐φαίνομαι 3. 917, ‐φέρω 4. 1519).

: 'taking-up'; cf. 1376. Hdt. (4. 179) says that Triton set the tripod in his temple, having prophesied to the Argonauts that, when one of their descendants bore it away, a hundred cities of Hellenes should be established about Lake Tritonis.
: 'was seen' (εἴδω). The Schol. explains it by ὥρμησεν, as if from εἶμι.
: 'to speak words of good omen' as he took the victim in his hands; cf. Aesch. Pers. 620, χοαῖσι … ὕμνους ἐπευφημεῖτε. For a different use see note to 295
: cf. Hor. C.S. 15, sive tu Lucina probas vocari, Seu Genitalis.

: 'children of the foam.' Curtius explains ὕδνη as sunja, fem. of sunus 'son' (rt. su 'to beget').
Leaf (on Il. 20. 207) says, "It is possible that ‐υδν‐ may be the same as the stem υδα‐τ for υδ n-τ (G. Meyer Gr. 335). The word will then mean 'daughter of the salt-water,' the patronymic force residing only in the noun-termination ‐η."
: i.e. in his true form as the sea-god Triton; he had appeared αἰζηῷ ἐναλίγκιος (1551).

κ.τ.λ.: 'As when a man leads a swift steed into the wide circle of the racecourse, holding the docile creature by the flowing mane, running lightly on; and it follows, its neck arched high with haughty grace; and in its mouth the foam-flecked bit rings in answer as it champs it from side to side--even so did he, grasping the stern-post of the curved Argo, guide it on ward to the sea.'

: Oswald says that ἐπί denotes the cause, as with χλιδᾶν, ἀγάλλεσθαι, etc., but
when we compare the description of the horse in 3. 1261, κυδιόων ὀρθοῖσιν ἐπ’ οὔασιν αὐχέν’ ἀείρει, it seems more probable that here ἐπ’ αὐχένι ἀερθείς = ἐπ’ αὐχένι ἀερθέντι, ἐπί denoting the attendant circumstance.
: a present found often in late epic. In Od. 4. 826 ἕσπεται is a v.l. for ἔρχεται, accepted by Wolf and Spitzner.
: probably 'white with foam,' though it may mean 'polished.'

: cf.
Aen. 7. 279, fulvum mandunt sub dentibus aurum. The verb occurs elsewhere only in Call. Del. 322.

div.p: 'but beneath his flanks there extended the tail of a sea-monster, forking to this side and to that.'
div.seg: : this adj. is found in Anth. P. 6. 32 meaning 'two-horned'; it is here used of the bifurcation at the end of the tail of a fish. For the short final syll. cf. ἀντιπέραιαν, 521; Meineke, Del. Anthol. p. 212, quotes other instances, δείλαιαν, χλωρά, λαιψηράν, etc.

: 'tail' (ἕλκω); used as a subst. by Nicander also, Th. 123, 225.
The variant ἀλκαίη is interesting: the Schol. says, ἀλκαία λέγεται ἡ τοῦ λέοντος οὐρὰ ἀπὸ τοῦ δῑ αὐτῆς εἰς ἀλκὴν τρέπεσθαι … Καλλίμαχος δὲ κακῶς ἐπὶ τῶν μυιῶν τέθεικεν "ἀλκαίας ἀφύσσα." … ἐν δὲ τῇ Κωμικῇ λέξει οὐ μόνον ἡ τοῦ λέοντος οὐρὰ ἀλκαία, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἵππου καὶ βοὸς καὶ τῶν ἐμφερῶν, ὅσα ὥσπερ ἀλεξητηρίῳ τῇ οὐρᾷ χρῆται. In Opp. Hal. 5. 264 we have ἀλκαίη used of the tail of a sea-monster. Wellauer suggests that ἀλκαίη was the reading in the first recension, and was altered in the second to avoid the resemblance to Callimachus.
κ.τ.λ.: 'he lashed the surface of the water with the spines of this tail, which, with curved points at the extremity, was divided like the horns of the crescent moon.'
: this form, which is not in L. and S., is ἅπ. λεγ. Ap. may have been influenced by the Homeric παρ’ αὐτόθι (παραυτόθἰ.

: for the pleonasm cf. Il. 23. 430, ὡς οὐκ ἀΐοντι ἐοικώς. The ending of the line is an echo of Arat. 857, ἑλισσόμεναι διχόωνται. Aratus seems to have been the first to use the form διχάω (see note to 3.519).

: cf. 658;
Flangini identifies it with the λιμὴν Ἑσπερίδων (Strab. 710, 9).

div.p: 'the next day, at dawn, they saw at once the bend in the land (v. 1581), and the inmost arm of the sea trending inward beyond the projecting bend.'

div.seg: : see note to 2.961. They were now no longer sailing east, but north.
: 'the loud blast'; cf. Il. 4. 276, ὑπὸ Ζεφύροιο ἰωῆς. It is used also of cries, e.g. 3. 708. Curtius refers it to αὔω, for ἰ‐ωv‐ή; others connect it with ἄημι.
: 'the folding-star'; cf. Call. fr. 465, ἀστὴρ Αὔλιος, ὃς δυθμὴν εἶσι μετ’ ἠελίου: Milton, Comus 93, "The star that bids the shepherd fold Now the top of heaven doth hold."
: this use of ἐπί is not Homeric.

: mod. Scarpanto,
a rugged island in the sea between Crete and Rhodes, which was named after it the Carpathian Sea; cf. Il. 2. 676.

: Ap. follows the legend which described Talos as a survivor of the age of bronze. He alone says that he was given by Zeus to Europa to guard Crete. The usual version is that Talos was the workmanship of Hephaestus, and was given to Minos by Zeus or Hephaestus to watch over the island. Cf. Plat. (?) Minos 320, Apollod. 1. 9. 26. The Schol. tells us that according to Simonides and Sophocles (in his Daedalus) Talos slew strangers by becoming fiery hot and wrapping them in his embrace.
: so the Cyclops (Od. 9. 481), ἧκε δ’ ἀπορρήξας κορυφὴν ὄρεος μεγάλοιο.
: σκέπην, ὑφ’ ἧς ὁ ἄνεμος ἄγνυται. Schol. In Od. 5. 404 we have ἐπιωγαί 'load-steads.'
: 'ash-born,' cf. Hes. Op. 143, Ζεὺς δὲ πατὴρ τρίτον ἄλλο γέκος μερόπων ἀνθρώπων Χάλκειον ποίησ’, οὐκ ἀργυρέῳ οὐδὲν ὁμοῖον, Ἐκ μελιᾶν. See also Aen. 8. 315.
: cf. Cat. 55. 14, Non custos si fingar ille Cretum.
: thrice each day; cf. Apollod. l.c., Τάλως τρὶς ἑκάστης ἡμέρας τὴν νῆσον περιτροχάζων ἐτήρει. According to Plato (l.c.) it was thrice a year, ὁ γὰρ Τάλως τρὶς περιῄει τοῦ ἐνιαυτοῦ.

: 'a vein of blood.' The Schol. tells us that Soph. in his Talos had described how he was fated to die when this vein was torn.
Apollodorus says, εἶχε δὲ φλέβα μίαν ἀπὸ αὐχένος κατατείνουσαν ἄχρι σφυρῶν· κατὰ δὲ τὸ δέρμα τῆς φλεβὸς ἦλος διήρειστο χαλκοῖς, and mentions the version of his death that Medea drew out this nail pretending that she would make him immottal.

: 'the thin membrane, which compressed this, controlled the issues of life and death.' For ὅ τε = ὅς τε cf. Od. 12. 40. In Il. 3. 371 ἄγχε … ἱμάς is used of the tight pressure of a helmet strap. The augment could be either used or omitted in the impf. as in ἄγον, ἦγον. The reading of the mss. is certainly corrupt, as it involves governing τήνγε by ἔχε, taking πείρατα in app. with ὑμήν, while ὁ is meaningless. Brunck's ὁ τῆς γε … ὑμήν is not epic.
: 'unless, in addition to this, he possess everlasting life.'

: a difficult phrase, generally explained 'with the oars,' taking ἐπί instrumentally, which is very improbable. Oswald supplies ἥμενοι, comparing 1. 730. The meaning required is 'to rest on the oars.' When they had backed out of range, they were to wait, keeping their oars in the water to steady the ship, the oars serving as it were to anchor her; cf. 2. 1282, νῆ· ἐκέλευσεν ἐπ’ εὐναίῃσιν ἐρύσσαι.

: daughters of Night, ever ravening for blood; cf. Hes. Sc. 249, Κῆρες κυάνεαι, λευκοὺς ἀραβεῦσαι ὀδόντας, Δεινωπαὶ βλοσυραί τε δαφοιναί τ’ ἄπληταί τε … ἵεντο Αἷμα μέλαν πιέειν. In Hom. Κήρ· (also in pl.), as distinct from Αἶσα and Μοῖρα, is the goddess who brings a violent death, especially in battle.

: ἐπάγειν was the word used of setting on a dog, immittere. Here it is appropriately used of the hounds of Hades springing on their victims. The Schol. takes it in a passive
sense, διὰ τῶν φαρμάκων τοῖς ζῶσιν ἐπάγονται.
κ.τ.λ.: "with soul unto mischief shapen she cast The glance of the evil eye upon Talos, his vision to blast" (Way). For θεμένη see note to 3.641.
: this use of μεγαίρειν c. acc. in the sense of βασκαίνειν, fascinare, is quite unique; v. Buttm. Lexil.

: 'gnashed her fury at him.' This is the explanation of Lobeck, who compares Opp. Cyn. 4. 138, θυμὸν ὀδὰξ πρίοντες, 'gnashing with their teeth their fury.' Buttm., who connects πρίω with πρήθω 'to blow, puff,' explains 'she spirted her rage against him.' Hesych. has the gloss πρίεται· φυσοῦται, and πρίστις the spouting-fish (the whale) would be from πρίω in this sense.

: εἴδωλα, φαντάσματα. Schol. 'she sent forth darksome phantoms in the fierceness of her wrath,' i. e. she made these spectres pass before his eyes. Cf. Milton's lines quoted on 442. δείκηλον occurs in 1. 746.
: φέρεται, κεκίνηται. Schol. 'of a truth great wonder thrills my soul.' See on 3. 288. Way tries to preserve the metaphor, "awe as a wind on my spirit bloweth chill."
: 'and even one who is afar off can work us harm.'
: cf. Eur. Cycl. 401, παίων πρὸς ὀξὺν στόνυχα πετραίου λἰθου.

: for this constr. cf. Soph. El. 721, ἔχριμπτ’ ἀεὶ σύριγγα. Elsewhere in Ap. the verb is intrans., e.g. 1567. ἐγχρίμπτειν is intrans. in Ap., e.g. 1512, but trans. in Il. 23. 334. Hom. does not use the simple verb, and where the comp. is intrans. he uses the passive forms.
: for this old form of μόλυβδος cf. Il. 11. 237, μόλιβος ὣς ἐτράπετ’ αἰχμή.
: Aristarch. rejected this augmented form in Hom., v. Schol. on Il. 4. 329.

div.p: With this simile cf. 1. 1003 sqq. The original which our poel develops is Il. 13. 389, ἤριπε δ’, ὡς ὅτε τις δρῦς ἤριπεν ἢ ἀχερωῒς Ἠὲ πίτυς βλωθρή, τήν τ’ οὔρεσι τέκτονες ἄνδρες Ἐξέταμον πελέκεσσι νεήκεσι νήιον εἶναι. Cf. also Il. 4. 483 sqq. Virgil's imitation is well known, Aen. 2. 626 sqq.

div.seg: : cf. Cat. 64. 109, radicitus exturbata (sc. quercus) Prona cadit.
: 'swayed, still standing upright.' For other uses of ἐπισταδόν v. 1. 293, 2. 84.
: cf. Hdt. 1. 181, νύκτα οὐδεὶς ἐναυλίζεται (ἐν τῷ νηᾦ. Ap. also uses αὐλίζομαι, e.g. 2. 1284, and ἐπαυλίζομαι, 3. 929.

: worshipped in Crete,
the island of Minos; cf. 2. 299. Some legends connected the birth of Athene with the river Triton in Crete (Diod. 5. 72).
: this superl. is only found here, though πάμπρωτον is common.

: ὑπερβάλλειν, meaning 'to double a cape,' elsewhere takes the acc. (e. g. Hdt. 7. 168); ὑπέρ may be used as in Od. 14. 300, ἡ δ’ ἔθεεν … Μέσσον ὑπὲρ Κρήτης, where it seems to mean 'out from,' 'keeping clear of' (v. Monro).
: the eastern point of Crete, mentioned in St. Paul's voyage, Acts 27. 7, ὑπεπλεύσαμεν τὴν Κρήτην κατὰ Σαλμώνην.

: ἡ σκοτεινὴ νὺξ κατουλὰς καλεῖται παρὰ τὸ ὀλοόν. καὶ παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ ἐν Ναυπλίῳ "νυκτὶ κατουλάδι." Schol. The deriv. given by the Schol. is clearly that adopted by our poet; but more probably the word means shrouding, 'the blanket of the dark,' from κατείλλω (or κατείλω); cf. ἐξούλη from ἐξείλλω. Hesych. recognizes both meanings.
: 'pierced,' ἅπ. λεγ. Cf. Il. 5. 100, ἀντικρὺ δὲ διέσχε (ὀιστός). ἀμαρυγαί: see note to 2.42.
: 'gloom,' 'murk'; used specially of the nether abyss, e.g. Plat. (?) Ax. 371, where it is coupled with Ἔρεβος: Quint. Smyr. 2. 614. πάντ’ ἐπικιδναμένου χάεος καὶ ἀεικέος ὄρφνης (of the underworld).

: these words have been impugned by many, but the meaning seems to be simply that this pitchy darkness came either from heaven or from Tartarus. Wellauer explains ἄλλη σκοτίη as alter Tartarus, altera inferorum caligo (i.e. a second Tartarus, etc.), comparing ἄλλη Κύπρις, altera Venus, Musaeus 33. Merkel reads οὔλη on the assumption that Ap. is trying to give the meaning of κατουλάδα by the phrases νύκτ’ ὀλοήν, οὔλη σκοτίη.
: 'not even so much' as whether they were in Hades or not. See on 1. 290.
κ.τ.λ.: cf. 1. 418, ἄλλαδὲ Πυθοῖ, Ἄλλα δ’ ἐς Ὀρτυγίην ἀπερείσια δῶρα κομίσσω, where see notes. There was a celebrated temple of Apollo at Amyclae in Laconia (Strab. 311, 38).
: this constr. is common in Hom. also.

: δύο σκόπελοι πρὸς τῇ Θήρᾳ, οὕτως ὀνομαζόμενοι ἀπὸ Μέλαντος
τοῦ κατας χόντος τὴν χώραν. Schol. They are mentioned in Strab. 544, 2.
: 'quick to hear.' It is passive in Call. Del. 308, ἄγαλμα Κύπριδος ἀρχαίης ἀριήκοον ('famous').

div.p: 'and the bow flashed forth a gleaming radiance far and wide.' For the cogn. acc. cf. Luc. Dom. 8, αὐγήν τινα ἡδεῖαν ἀπολάμπει.

div.seg: : the scattered islands in the Aegaean between the Cyclades and Crete.
: i.e. while the bow was flashing.
: the isle of Hippuris is coupled with Anaphe (v. 1717) in Plin. N.H. 4. 12.
: the Homeric form only here; elsewhere εὐναίας, e.g. 1. 1277.

: the 'Isle of the Appearance' is mentioned in Strab.
416, 4, περὶ δὲ τὴν Κρήτην εἰσὶ νῆσοι, Θήρα … καὶ πλησίον ταύτης Ἀνάφη, ἐν ᾗ τὸ τοῦ Αἰγλήτου Ἀπόλλωνος ἱερόν. λέγει δὲ καὶ Καλλίμαχος οὕτως· Αἰγλήτην Ἀνάφην τε, Λακωνίδι γείτονα Θήρᾳ.
: 'they called,' see note to 1.834; here with two accusatives, which Ap., differing from previous poets, also uses with κλείειν, κέκλεσθαι, and ἐνέπειν.
: for the omission of ἄν v. n. 1487, 1. 480. ὃ δή κ.τ.λ.: 'wherefore, when they saw them pouring water (instead of wine) over the burning brands.'
: cf. Od. 8. 326, ἄσβεστος δ’ ἄρ’ ἐνῶρτο γέλως μακάρεσσι θεοῖσι.

div.p:
'And the heroes, well pleased
with their bantering, scoffed at them in language free; and pleasant raillery flashed between them, with rivalry in tossing taunts.'
div.seg: : see note to 3.663; for the augmented iterative form see note to 3.687.
: cf. Il. 2. 275 (of Thersites), λωβητῆρα ἐπεσβόλον: Od. 4. 159, ἐπεσβολίας ἀναφαίνειν.

: 'sport'; cf. 3. 897, 950. In Od. 6. 101 μολπή is explained as παιδιά by the Schol. Aristarchus maintained that μολπή is always used in Hom. of playing a game, and not of singing (v. Lehrs, Aristarch. 138). In 894 supr. and 1. 28 'singing' is the meaning; μέλπω (‐ομαἰ is generally used by Ap. of singing, e.g. 1. 569, 4. 898; sometimes in a wider sense, e.g. 2. 714, 3. 949.

div.p:
Herodotus (5. 83) tells of a similar custom prevailing at Aegina, θυσίῃσί τε (τὰ ἀγάλματἀ καὶ χοροῖσι γυναικηΐοισι κερτομίοισι ἱλάσκοντο. So too Pausanias (7. 27) describing the
worship of the Mysian Ceres at Mysaeum says, ἀφικομένων ἐς τὸ ἱερὸν τῶν ἀνδρῶν, αἱ γυναῖκές τε ἐς αὐτούς, καὶ ἀνὰ μέρος ἐς τὰς γυναῖκας οἱ ἄνδρες γέλωτί τε ἐς ἀλλήλους χρῶνται καὶ σκώμμασιν. Abusive raillery was a feature of the Eleusinian festivals, as we know from the expressions γεφυρίζειν and ὥσπερ ἐξ ἁμάξης.

div.seg: : he reverenced Hermes as being the source of dreams; cf. h. Hom. Merc. 14, where the god is described as ἡγήτορ’ ὀνείρων.

κ.τ.λ.: 'and he wept, imagining that he had union with a virgin whom he had suckled with his own milk.' Brunck adopts κούρη, comparing 1. 269 and Il. 16. 7, τίπτε δεδάκρυσαι Πατρόκλεις, ἠύτε κούρη, but κούρην is confirmed by οὐ κούρη, 1742 infr.

: the Alex. poets always use this word in the sense of ἀπόγονοι, though Apollon. Lex. says that this is an abuse, παράχρουσμα τῶν νεωτέρων ποιητῶν. Curtius refers it to the root νεπ seen in ἀνεψιός, nepos. The meaning is probably the same in Od. 4. 404, φῶκαι νέποδες καλῆς ὁλοσύδνης, where the grammarians give many strange explanations, 'web-footed,' 'footless,' etc.

div.p: The order is τῷ δ’ ἄρα κραδίη μνῆστιν ἐπέβαλε, 'his soul brought back to him the memory of these things.' Brunck compares Opp. Hal. 3. 503 (of a perplexed traveller), κραδίη τέ οἱ ἄλλοτε λαιὴν Ἄλλοτε δεξιτερὴν ἐπιβάλλεται ἀτραπὸν ἐλθεῖν. The meaning there is different, yet it helps to confirm κραδίη against the vulg. κραδίῃ.

div.seg:
: 'glory is thy portion.' This constr. seems to be unique, and is probably modelled on
the intrans. use of λαγχάνειν. For the normal usage v. 3. 4.

div.p: Pindar, P. 4. 38 sqq., tells how this δαιμονία βῶλαξ was washed from the Argo to the island of Thera, from which in later days (c. 630 b.c.) Battus led forth a colony to Cyrene. Cf. Hdt. 4. 147 sqq., Paus. 3. 1. 7, 7. 2. 2.

div.seg: : see note to 1.43. The meaning is that Euphemus' children's children shall dwell in the island.

: cf. Strab. 298, 29, ὦν (sc. τῶν Μινυῶν) τινες μετὰ Θήρα τοῦ Αὐτεσίωνος (ἦν δ’ οὗτος Πολυνείκους ἰπόγονος) πλεύσαντες εἰς τὴν μεταξὺ Κυρηναίας καὶ τῆς Κρήτης νῆσον, "Καλλίστην τὸ πάροιθε, τὸ δ’ ὕστερον οὔνομα Θήρην," ὥς φησι Καλλίμαχος, ἔκτισαν τὴν μητρόπολιν τῆς Κυρήνης Θήραν, ὁμώνυμον δ’ ἀπέδειξαν τῇ πόλει καὶ τὴν νῆσον.

: cf. Strab. 298, 25, Μινυῶν, οἳ τῶν Ἀργοναυτῶν ἀπόγονοι ὄντες
ἐκ Λήμνου εἰς Λακεδαίμονα ἐξέπεσον. Herodotus (4. 145) says that they were driven out by the Pelasgians. Diodorus (10. 19) mentions that the Tyrrhenians deserted the island through fear of the Persians, and handed it over to Miltiades.

: the Schol. explains this by ταχέως, apparently deriving it from ἀ intens. and πτερόν. This meaning satisfies the other passage where the word occurs, Parmen. 17, ὀχῆα Ἀπτερέως ὤσειε πυλέων ἄπο. L. and S. explain it without wings, i.e. without wavering, steadily, resolutely. The note in Et. Mag. 133, 34 is very confused: ἀπτερέως, παρ’ Ἡσιόδῳ, ὥσπερ τὸ ἀψοφέως, σημαίνει τὸ αἰφνιδίως. ἔστιν ἀπωτέρω, ἀπτέρω. οὕτως Ἡρωδιανός. ἔστι ταχέως, ἑτοίμως, ἀφροντίστως. οἱ δέ, ἀπροθύμως, ἐλαφρῶς, ἡδέως. ἔνιοι δέ, ἠμελημένως.

div.p: 'for two things made them hasten, the need of water and the strength of the favouring breeze.'

div.seg: κ.τ.λ.: this custom of the Aeginetans does not seem to be referred to elsewhere.

: 'the sons of the Myrmidons' i.e. the Aeginetans. In Hom. (Il. 1. 180) the Myrmidons are dwellers at Phthia in Thessaly (cf. 1. 55), and followers of Achilles against Troy. Another branch of them may have settled in Aegina. As a name of the Aeginetans, Μυρμιδόνες was connected in various ways with μύρμηκες 'ants'; Strab. 322, 47, Μυρμιδόνας δὲ κληθῆναί φασιν, οὐχ ὡς ὁ μῦθος, τοὺς Αἰγινήτας, ὅτι λοιμοῦ μεγάλου συμπεσόντος οἱ μύρμηκες ἄνθρωποι γένοιντο κατ’ εὐχὴν Αἰακοῦ, ἀλλ’ ὅτι μυρμήκων τρόπον ὀρύττοντες τὴν γῆν ἐπιφέροιεν ἐπὶ τὰς πέτρας, ὥστ’ ἔχειν γεωργεῖν, ἐν δὲ τοῖς ὀρύγμασιν οἰκεῖν φειδόμενοι πλίνθων. The legend of the ants being turned into men in the reign of Aeacus, son of Zeus and the nymph Aegina, is recounted at length in Ov. Met. 7. 517 sqq.
: πόλις Βοιωτίας καταντικρὺ τῆς Ἐὐβοίας κειμένη. Schol. The Argo passed through the Euripus between Euboea and the mainland.
: cf. 1. 69. A list of the Locrian towns subject to Ajax, son of Oïleus, is given in Il. 2. 527-535. Opus was the native city of Patroclus ( Il. 18. 326).
: whence they had started on their voyage, v. 1. 238. Apollodorus (1. 9. 26) says that the voyage lasted four months, εἰς Ἰωλκὸν ἦλθον, τὸν πάντα πλοῦν ἐν τέσσαρσι μησὶ τελειώσαντες.
